courseMetadata.title: Data Visualization for Design Leads
courseMetadata.description: An intermediate course that takes practicing UI/UX designers from making charts to owning data visualization as a discipline. Covers what a dataset actually permits you to claim, the quantitative reasoning behind rates, change and distributions, how the visual system reads marks, how chart forms are composed and selected under real constraints, spatial, hierarchical and network encodings, the obligations of integrity, accessibility and narrative, and how to scale the practice through dashboards, metric governance, design systems, critique and measurement.

prerequisites.description: Working fluency in visual design fundamentals: layout, typography, hierarchy and colour as used in interface work.
Practical experience shipping interface or product design work with real stakeholders and engineering partners.
Basic comfort with tabular data: reading a spreadsheet, understanding rows, columns, totals and averages. No statistics background is assumed.
Comfort with basic arithmetic reasoning: percentages, ratios and averages. No statistics coursework is assumed; the course builds the quantitative reasoning it requires.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: Integrity is seeded in Section 1 as a consequence of grain and aggregation, recurs in Section 3 as overplotting and independent facet scales, and becomes the explicit subject of Section 4. Injecting data-semantics and chart-selection items into the integrity experiences forces learners to recognise the same failure wearing three different costumes. Quantitative reasoning joins this thread because the denominator and base-rate errors taught in section two are integrity failures in the same family as grain collapse and axis truncation.

Accessibility is an encoding decision, not a remediation pass. Interleaving perception and channel-effectiveness items into the accessibility and design-system experiences enforces that claim structurally rather than merely asserting it in prose.

Task framing established in Section 1 is the deciding variable for annotation in Section 4 and for dashboard scoping in Section 5. Injecting Section 1 task items into Section 5 tests whether the habit survived four sections of intervening material.

Chart selection in Section 3 is only defensible if the perceptual evidence from Section 2 is retrievable on demand. Injecting effectiveness-ranking and pop-out items into the selection experiences keeps the justification live rather than recalled once and shelved.

Section 5 synthesises rather than introduces: a design system is encoding-effectiveness made durable and critique is graphical-integrity made social. Heavy injection here converts the final section into a distributed retrieval test across the whole course.

The null-versus-zero rule learned as a column-classification habit in Section 1 must resurface as a clause in an engineering specification in Section 5. This pairing is the course's clearest far-transfer check.

The denominator question is the single idea that recurs most across this course: it decides whether a rate or a count is honest in section two, whether a choropleth shows a phenomenon or a population in section five, and whether a framing is distortive in section six. Injecting across these three makes the recurrence explicit rather than coincidental.

The grammar of graphics is introduced as a selection aid and must be retrieved later as the format of an engineering specification. Injecting grammar items into the spatial and system experiences converts an abstraction into a working notation.

Animation sits across three competencies at once: it is narrative sequencing, it is interaction feedback, and it is an accessibility constraint through reduced-motion. Interleaving prevents it being learned as a single-section topic.

probeQuestions.prompt: A dataset column named `route_id` contains the values 12, 47, 108 and 236. Which encoding is **disqualified** for this variable?
options: A continuous position axis, because the values carry identity only and the axis would assert order and spacing that do not exist.
A categorical colour hue, because hue cannot represent numeric values.
A text label, because numeric values should always be encoded graphically.
None are disqualified — the values are numbers, so any quantitative encoding is valid.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Storage type and measurement scale are different things, and a continuous axis over-claims structure this variable does not have.
Hue is in fact the natural channel for nominal identity — this is the encoding that fits.
Direct labelling is often the strongest option for a small number of identifiers and is never disqualified on principle.
This is the storage-type trap: route IDs are numeric labels, and quantitative encodings assert magnitude they do not carry.

routingRules.action: Advisory: learner may skim the measurement-scale material in the first experience of section one and proceed to the grain and aggregation content.

routingRules.condition: Incorrect, or correct with confidence rated 1 or 2
routingRules.action: Advisory: complete the full data audit experience in section one and schedule its retrieval items at the shortest interval.

probeQuestions.prompt: A file arrives with one row per store per month, containing `avg_basket_value`. What can you **not** determine from this file alone?
options: How basket values were distributed within any month, including whether a few very large baskets are driving the average.
Which stores are included in the file.
Whether the values are expressed in a currency.
How many months of data are present.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The monthly grain has already collapsed the within-month distribution, and no chart built on this file can recover it.
Store identity is present in the file by definition of its grain — one row per store per month.
Units are a metadata question answerable from the file or its documentation, not a consequence of grain.
The time span is directly countable from the rows present.

routingRules.action: Advisory: learner already holds the grain concept; emphasise the aggregation-state and missingness material instead.
Advisory: do the paired record-level versus pre-aggregated worked example in section one before proceeding.

probeQuestions.prompt: A dashboard ranks regions by the **total number** of support tickets raised. The top three regions are also the three with the most customers. What is the most useful observation?
options: The ranking is largely a ranking of customer base size; a rate per customer would answer the question actually being asked.
The ranking is correct as it stands, since totals are the raw facts and rates introduce assumptions.
The regions should be shown on a map so the geographic pattern becomes clear.
The ranking should be reversed so the smallest regions are shown first.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Choosing a count over a rate is a claim about what is being measured, and here it produces a view of the denominator.
Counts confound the phenomenon with the population producing it; presenting them as an answer to an intensity question smuggles in a claim.
Adding geography does not fix the numerator-denominator pairing, and on a map the same problem becomes harder to see.
Sort order does not change which quantity is displayed.

routingRules.action: Advisory: skim the rates-and-denominators experience in section two and proceed to change measures, composition effects and smoothing.
Advisory: complete the full rates-and-denominators experience in section two and schedule its retrieval items at the shortest interval; this material is prerequisite to sections five and six.

probeQuestions.prompt: For judging the **ratio between two quantities**, which visual channel supports the most accurate judgment?
options: Position along a common scale.
Colour hue.
Area.
It depends entirely on the viewer, since these judgments are subjective.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Position on a common scale sits at the top of the empirically measured effectiveness ranking for quantitative magnitude judgment.
Hue carries no intrinsic magnitude ordering and sits at the bottom for this kind of judgment, though it is excellent for categorical identity.
Area judgments are systematically underestimated as values grow, placing area well below position and length.
Individual variation exists, but aggregate error rates by channel have been measured and replicated at scale.

routingRules.action: Advisory: unlock the advanced channel-selection material in section two and reduce time on the introductory ranking content.
Advisory: complete the full channel effectiveness experience in section two, including the caveats on what the ranking does not rank.

probeQuestions.prompt: Why does adding a second highlight colour to a display make the first one less effective?
options: Pop-out depends on the highlight being unique on its distinguishing attribute; competing highlights return the viewer to serial search.
Two colours together produce a simultaneous-contrast effect that lowers apparent saturation.
It does not — additional preattentive attributes are processed in parallel and speed detection up.
The second colour introduces a colour-accessibility conflict that overrides the first.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Highlighting works by subtraction: scarcity is the mechanism, not the attribute itself.
Simultaneous contrast is real but is not what cancels pop-out; the cancellation is about search regime, not apparent colour.
This is the common inversion: multiplying pop-out channels cancels the effect and forces item-by-item checking.
Accessibility is a separate and important concern, but it is not the mechanism by which the first highlight loses force.

routingRules.action: Advisory: treat the preattentive material in section two as review and spend the recovered time on the Gestalt and working-memory content.
Advisory: run the timed find-the-target exercise at one, three and six highlights before continuing.

probeQuestions.prompt: Which statement about zero baselines is correct?
options: Zero is required for length encodings such as bars, where the mark's length is the value, but not for position encodings of quantities with no meaningful zero.
Every quantitative axis must begin at zero, without exception.
Zero baselines are a stylistic convention with no effect on how values are read.
Zero is required whenever the data is volatile, and optional otherwise.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The baseline must match what the encoding claims — that is the principle the familiar rule half-captures.
Applied universally this destroys the signal in exchange rates, temperatures and pH, where zero is not a meaningful reference.
Truncating a length encoding changes the ratio the eye reads, often by several times — the effect is measurable, not cosmetic.
Volatility is not the deciding variable; the encoding type and whether zero is meaningful are.

routingRules.action: Advisory: skim the baseline material in section four and proceed to framing mechanisms and uncertainty representation.
Advisory: complete the paired bars-versus-line baseline drill in section four before the audit exercise.

probeQuestions.prompt: A chart uses a colourblind-safe palette and provides the underlying data as a downloadable table. Which requirement is most likely still unmet?
options: A text alternative conveying the chart's takeaway pattern, and access to required values without a pointer.
None — a safe palette plus the data table covers the requirements.
A higher-resolution export for users who zoom.
A legend positioned closer to the plot area.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Palette and raw data are two pieces; the pattern description and pointer-free access are separate and commonly missing.
A table supplies values, not the structure the chart existed to communicate, and says nothing about keyboard or touch access.
Resolution matters for low-vision users but is downstream of the structural access problems.
Legend proximity reduces reading cost; it is not the outstanding access requirement here.

routingRules.action: Advisory: treat the accessibility criteria in section four as consolidation and focus on the text-alternative writing exercise.
Advisory: complete the four-check accessibility audit in section four on a chart the learner already considers compliant.

probeQuestions.prompt: Before building a map from a dataset containing locations, what is the single most important question to answer?
options: What does the map show that a sorted bar chart would not — is a spatial relationship part of the question?
Which map projection best preserves area for this region?
Which basemap style best matches the product's visual identity?
How many locations are in the dataset?

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Geography costs space and judgment accuracy, and is worth paying for only when adjacency, distance or region is part of the decision.
A genuine question, but it presumes the map — projection cannot rescue a form that does not serve the task.
Basemap styling is a downstream refinement of a decision not yet justified.
Cardinality matters for the encoding, but it does not settle whether geography earns its space.

routingRules.action: Advisory: move quickly through the map-necessity content in section five and prioritise the normalization, areal-unit and network material.
Advisory: complete the geospatial encoding experience in section five in full, including the paired map-versus-bar-chart exercise.

probeQuestions.prompt: Interaction analytics for a dashboard show that most sessions involve no interaction at all. What is the most useful conclusion?
options: The default view carries most of the communicative load and should be designed for one role and one decision.
The interactive features need better discoverability so more users engage them.
Users are not sufficiently trained on the tool.
The dashboard should include more filters to encourage exploration.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Design the default as if it were the only view, then add interaction for the minority of sessions that go further.
Low interaction usually indicates glance-based use rather than a discoverability defect.
Training to use controls that the decision does not require moves cost onto users without improving decisions.
Filters transfer unmade scoping decisions to users with less context and less time.

routingRules.action: Advisory: unlock the advanced dashboard-architecture material in section five and shorten the introductory default-view content.
Advisory: complete the default-view rescue activity in section five before the design-system material.

probeQuestions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for a specific chart type for an upcoming review. In your own words, describe what you would establish before starting, and why the named chart type is not by itself a requirement.
scoringCriteria: Names the decision — the action the audience will take — as the thing to recover first.
Identifies the named chart as a proposed solution rather than a stated need.
Mentions at least two of: audience, analytic task, delivery surface, exploratory versus explanatory mode.
Does not treat the request as either binding or as something to override without inquiry.

routingRules.condition: Response names the decision and at least two further properties
routingRules.action: Advisory: learner may move quickly through the brief-rewriting content in section one and go straight to the practical activity.

routingRules.condition: Response accepts the chart type as the requirement, or proposes overriding it without inquiry
routingRules.action: Advisory: complete the full brief-interrogation experience in section one, including the five-request decision-question drill.

probeQuestions.prompt: Describe how you currently run or participate in design critique for data visualization work, and name one disagreement you have seen that was never resolved.
scoringCriteria: Describes an actual process rather than an ideal.
Indicates whether the artifact's goal and audience are stated before feedback begins.
Bonus: recognises that the named disagreement may be empirically testable.

routingRules.condition: Response describes a criteria-anchored process and identifies the disagreement as testable
routingRules.action: Advisory: prioritise the measurement and success-metrics material in section five over the critique-structure material.

routingRules.condition: Response describes feedback collection without a stated brief
routingRules.action: Advisory: complete the four-pass structured critique activity in section five and run one live session under the brief-gate rule.

competencies.title: Reading data structure and semantics
competencies.description: Determining what a dataset actually is — measurement scales, cardinality, grain, aggregation state, missingness — and what claims it can and cannot support.

desiredOutcomes.description: Classify every variable in an unfamiliar dataset by measurement scale and cardinality, flagging any variable whose storage type misrepresents its semantics.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner correctly identifies at least one numerically-stored nominal or ordinal variable and states the specific encoding it must not receive.

desiredOutcomes.description: Establish the grain and aggregation state of a delivered file and articulate what variation the current grain destroys.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner names the row unit, identifies at least one dimension collapsed by prior aggregation, and states a concrete claim the file cannot support because of it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the column holds numbers, it's quantitative — so I can put it on a continuous axis.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Zip codes, product SKUs, route IDs, survey response codes and calendar years are numeric in storage and nominal or ordinal in meaning. A continuous position axis asserts order, spacing and often a meaningful zero; assigning identity-only values to it states distances that do not exist in the data.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Drill the storage-type-versus-measurement-scale separation on mixed datasets: for each numeric column the learner must answer 'does order mean anything?' and 'does the gap between values mean anything?' before any encoding is chosen. Follow with a contrast case where the same integer column is legitimately quantitative in one dataset and nominal in another.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Ordinal data like a 1–5 satisfaction rating can be averaged and reported as a number.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Averaging requires equal spacing between adjacent values. Ordinal scales explicitly do not guarantee it — the psychological distance from 'poor' to 'fair' need not equal that from 'good' to 'excellent'. The resulting mean encodes an assumption the data never made, and presents it with the authority of a measurement.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Show the same Likert dataset three ways — mean, median with interquartile range, and full response distribution — where the mean is stable while the distribution shifts from unimodal to bimodal. Then require the learner to write the one sentence they would say to a stakeholder who insists on a single number.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The data as handed to me is the data that matters; my job starts at the chart.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Grain and prior aggregation are design decisions someone already made. Inheriting them silently means inheriting their distortions — a pre-averaged table hides the variance the chart then cannot show, and the collapse is usually invisible in the delivered file.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner a pre-aggregated file and the record-level source, ask for a claim from the first, then have them re-aggregate at a different grain and observe the claim reverse. Codify the three questions to ask any data owner: what is a row, what was grouped by which statistic, and what was excluded.

competencies.title: Quantitative reasoning for visual designers
competencies.description: Reasoning correctly about the numbers a chart displays: rates versus counts, denominators and normalization, indexing, percent change versus percentage points, base rates and composition effects, smoothing and seasonality, and scale transforms — so that a design decision is not silently a statistical claim.

desiredOutcomes.description: Determine whether a quantity should be displayed as a count, a rate, a share or an index, and identify the correct denominator for the comparison being made.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner names the population at risk, justifies the denominator against the comparison the chart supports, and identifies at least one conclusion that reverses under a different denominator.

desiredOutcomes.description: Express change correctly, distinguishing percentage change from percentage-point change, absolute from relative effects, and identifying when a composition shift rather than a within-group change is driving an aggregate.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner labels the change measure precisely, and correctly diagnoses at least one case where an aggregate moves in the opposite direction to every subgroup.

desiredOutcomes.description: Choose and disclose smoothing, seasonal adjustment and scale transforms as analytical decisions with stated consequences.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner states what each transform removes as well as what it reveals, and specifies where the disclosure appears in the artifact.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Raw counts show me where the most is happening, so counts are the honest starting point.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Counts confound the quantity of interest with the size of the population producing it. A map or ranking of raw counts is largely a map or ranking of where people are, which is a fact about the denominator rather than about the phenomenon. The choice to display a count rather than a rate is a claim, not a neutral default.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner build the same ranking three times — raw count, rate per capita, and rate against the correct at-risk population — and observe the top of the ranking change each time. Then require every quantity in their next brief to be labelled count, rate, share or index, with the denominator named.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The average tells you what a typical case looks like.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: In a skewed distribution the mean can describe no actual case at all, and can sit above the great majority of observations. Income, wait times, session lengths, order values and claim sizes are all routinely skewed, so a chart of means can move while the typical experience does not, or stay flat while it deteriorates badly.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Show a strongly right-skewed dataset as a mean, a median, and a full distribution, and have the learner state which claims survive each representation. Establish the standing rule that a mean is reported with a shape indicator — median, interquartile range, or the distribution itself.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Percent change is straightforward — a rise from 4% to 6% is a 2% increase.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That is a two percentage-point increase and a fifty percent relative increase, and the two carry very different rhetorical weight. Conflating them, or reporting a relative change without its base, lets a chart imply a large effect from a small one. Relative change on a small base is the most common vehicle for this in practice.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Drill paired statements on the same data — percentage points, relative percent, and absolute counts — requiring the learner to write all three and choose which the decision needs. Require any relative change to be shown alongside its base.

competencies.title: Framing analytic tasks from stakeholder requests
competencies.description: Converting vague or solution-shaped requests into explicit analytic tasks — comparison, trend, distribution, part-to-whole, correlation, deviation, ranking, flow — tied to a named audience and a specific decision.

desiredOutcomes.description: Rewrite a solution-shaped stakeholder request as two or three explicit analytic tasks using a standard task vocabulary.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Rewritten brief names a decision (an action, not a topic), lists tasks from the eight-term vocabulary, and contains no chart type in its requirements.

desiredOutcomes.description: Classify a brief as exploratory or explanatory and justify the classification from audience, decision and delivery surface.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Classification is justified by at least two of audience, decision and surface, and the learner names one requirement that would invert if the mode changed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The stakeholder asked for a pie chart, so the requirement is a pie chart.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A named chart is a guess at a solution, not a statement of need. The requirement is the underlying question and the decision it feeds. Delivering the guess forfeits exactly the expertise the designer was brought in for, and leaves the real requirement untested until review.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Practise the decision question — 'what will you do differently depending on what this shows?' — on five solution-shaped requests, requiring the learner to reach an action verb before proposing anything. Reinforce by having them identify cases where the stakeholder's guess turns out to be correct, so the habit reads as verification rather than contradiction.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More data on screen means more insight — I should show everything available.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Insight comes from the task-relevant comparison being visually available. Unfiltered volume raises visual search cost and lowers the rate at which anything is noticed; the viewer's attention is a fixed budget being spent on irrelevant marks.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner strip a dense dashboard to the single comparison its decision requires, then measure their own time-to-answer on both versions. Pair with the Section 2 material on serial search so the cost has a named mechanism rather than an aesthetic one.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: One well-designed visualization can serve every audience — the analyst and the executive both.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: An exploratory tool and an explanatory graphic optimise for opposite things: flexibility and coverage versus a single unmissable takeaway. Merging them produces an artifact too rigid to explore and too cluttered to explain, and it typically fails both audiences rather than half-serving each.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give one dataset and two audiences, require two separate artifacts, then have the learner list the specific requirements that inverted between them. Follow with a real merged dashboard and ask which audience each element was for.

competencies.title: Perceptual and cognitive foundations
competencies.description: How preattentive attributes, Gestalt grouping, visual search regimes and working-memory limits determine what a viewer notices, in what order, and with what accuracy.

desiredOutcomes.description: Predict the order in which a viewer will perceive elements of a given chart, citing the preattentive attributes and Gestalt principles responsible.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Prediction names at least two specific mechanisms by term and correctly identifies whether the target is found in parallel or by serial search.

desiredOutcomes.description: Defend an encoding decision in review using perceptual evidence rather than preference.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Justification cites a measured effect (judgment accuracy by channel, search regime, working-memory limit) and contains no appeal to taste.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Chart aesthetics are subjective, so perceptual 'rules' are really just someone's taste.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Judgment accuracy for position, length, angle, area and colour has been measured in controlled experiments and replicated at scale. Individual variation exists, but variation between people is not the same as absence of a reliable aggregate effect. These are findings about human vision, not stylistic preferences.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Walk through the Cleveland–McGill methodology, not just its conclusion, so the learner can see what was measured and how. Then have them run a two-minute comparison test on colleagues and observe the effect reproduce on their own sample.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Colour is the most powerful channel, so I should use it for the most important numbers.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Colour is excellent for categorical identity and adequate for coarse magnitude at overview scale, but poor for precise quantitative comparison. Position and length outperform it substantially. Importance and precision are different requirements, and colour serves only one of them.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Separate the two requirements explicitly: have the learner state, for each variable, whether the viewer must identify it or must measure it, and assign channels from that answer. Contrast a heatmap used for cluster detection with a bar chart used for ratio judgment so colour's legitimate role is preserved.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Preattentive attributes are processed fast, so using several of them at once makes a display faster to read.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Pop-out speed depends on scarcity, not on the attribute itself. A highlight works because it is the only one. Multiple simultaneous pop-out channels cancel each other and return the viewer to serial search, which scales linearly with item count.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run a timed find-the-target exercise at one, three and six highlight colours so the learner experiences the cancellation directly. Then introduce the pop-out budget as a hard constraint: one per view, spent on the thing the view exists for.

competencies.title: Channel selection and encoding accuracy
competencies.description: Matching data types to visual channels using effectiveness rankings, expressiveness constraints, colour-scale theory, and scale and axis choices. Includes the grammar of graphics as the unifying abstraction: data, transform, mark, encoding, scale, guide and facet.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose the channel assignments in an existing chart and produce a re-encoding that raises judgment accuracy for that chart's stated task.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Re-encoding removes at least one expressiveness violation, moves the primary-task variable up the effectiveness ranking, and states the task it was optimised for.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select categorical, sequential or diverging colour scales appropriate to a variable's measurement scale and evaluate candidates for perceptual uniformity and CVD safety.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Scale type is justified from the variable's structure, the midpoint of any diverging scale is shown to be meaningful, and the candidate passes a greyscale and CVD check.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Pie charts are bad and bar charts are good.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Context-free verdicts substitute slogans for reasoning. Pies are weak for precise comparison across many slices but adequate for a coarse part-to-whole read with few categories; bars are wrong when the task is trend, distribution or correlation. The form is only assessable against a stated task.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Present four briefs where the same chart form is correct in two and disqualified in the other two, forcing the learner to name the deciding variable each time. Ban the words 'good' and 'bad' from their justifications and require a task reference instead.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The effectiveness ranking is a hierarchy to obey from the top down — always use the highest-ranked channel available.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The ranking measures accuracy of quantitative magnitude judgment and nothing else. When the task is pattern detection, cluster finding, grouping or overview at scale, a lower-ranked channel is frequently the correct choice — a colour-encoded heatmap can beat a position encoding for spotting spatial structure in thousands of values.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Pair every effectiveness-ranking exercise with a task statement, and include at least one case where the correct answer is a low-ranked channel. Require the learner to state what the ranking does not rank before applying it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: 3D, depth effects and area-scaled marks make a chart richer and more engaging.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: These add visual channels that carry no data while degrading judgment accuracy through occlusion, foreshortening and systematic area underestimation. The viewer pays a cost in accuracy and receives no additional information in return.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner estimate values from a 3D pie and its flat equivalent, then check both against the underlying numbers and observe their own error rate. Introduce the data-ink question — what does this channel encode? — as a standing test for any decorative dimension.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A chart type is a single indivisible thing you pick from a list.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Chart forms are compositions, not atoms. Any chart decomposes into data, a transform, a mark type, a set of channel encodings, scales, guides and an optional faceting. A bar chart and a stacked area chart differ by a transform and a mark, not by species. Treating forms as atomic hides which component you would actually change, and makes it impossible to specify a chart precisely for engineering.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner decompose five familiar charts into data, transform, mark, encodings, scales, guides and facets, then produce a new form by changing exactly one component. Require the same decomposition as the format for every engineering specification thereafter.

competencies.title: Chart form selection and multivariate composition
competencies.description: Choosing, combining and composing chart forms — including small multiples, faceting, layering and custom encodings — and justifying the choice against the alternatives that lost. Includes designed tables as a first-class form for precise value retrieval and heterogeneous metrics.

desiredOutcomes.description: Generate a viable set of two to four chart forms for a brief and eliminate all but one with reasons that name a mechanism.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Every elimination cites a named mechanism — baseline loss, legend ceiling, overplotting, cardinality, learning cost — rather than a comparative adjective, and the runner-up is identified.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a defensible visualization for a dataset from an unfamiliar domain, reasoning from data semantics and task rather than from domain precedent.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reasoning proceeds structure to task to decision without appeal to what the field conventionally does, and the learner identifies the one domain question they needed to ask.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: There's one right chart per data shape — a chart-chooser flowchart gives the answer.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Flowcharts key off data structure alone and ignore task, audience and delivery surface, which are the variables that actually decide between several structurally valid options. Identical data structures routinely warrant different answers depending on the decision being served.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give one dataset and three different decisions held by three different roles, and have the learner produce three different correct answers. Then have them locate the point in a published chart-chooser where all three collapse into one recommendation.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A novel or custom visualization signals design sophistication.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Novelty imposes a decoding cost on every viewer on every viewing, while the benefit accrues once to the designer. It is justified only when no conventional form supports the task. Unjustified novelty reads to analytics and engineering partners as self-indulgence and costs the designer credibility they will need later.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Install the novelty test as a required gate: name, in one sentence, the specific task a conventional form would prevent. If the sentence cannot be written, the conventional form is chosen. Reinforce with cases where novelty is genuinely warranted — flow at scale, hierarchical part-to-whole, network structure — so the test reads as calibration, not prohibition.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Showing every data point is more honest than aggregating.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Overplotting hides the distribution as effectively as a bad average does: the dense centre saturates to solid ink while sparse outliers stay fully visible, so the reading is systematically biased toward the rare. Deliberate aggregation with visible variance is frequently the more truthful representation.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner estimate the centre and spread of a heavily overplotted scatter, then reveal the binned version and their own error. Follow immediately with Anscombe's quartet so both failure directions are held at once and the conclusion is 'choose deliberately', not 'always aggregate'.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Falling back to a table means you failed to visualize the data.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A well-designed table is frequently the correct answer, and the effectiveness ranking predicts why: when the task is looking up precise individual values, reading a number beats decoding any graphical channel. Tables also handle mixed units and heterogeneous metrics that no single chart can accommodate, and they support scanning when augmented with alignment, sorting and in-cell marks.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner take a dashboard tile that exists to support value lookup and rebuild it as a designed table with right-aligned figures, deliberate sorting and sparklines, then compare retrieval time against the original chart.

competencies.title: Spatial, hierarchical and relational encodings
competencies.description: Designing for data whose structure has no conventional linear representation: geography, hierarchy, flow and network — including projection and areal-unit effects, normalization on maps, treemaps and sunbursts, Sankey and flow diagrams, and node-link versus matrix representations of networks.

desiredOutcomes.description: Decide whether geography is the right encoding at all, and if so select among choropleth, cartogram, dot density, proportional symbol and non-map alternatives.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner states what the map encodes that a non-spatial form would not, names the normalization applied, and identifies one distortion introduced by the chosen form.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select and justify a representation for hierarchical or network data, including the choice between node-link and matrix forms at a given density.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Choice is justified by the task — path tracing, cluster detection, adjacency lookup — and by graph size and density rather than by appearance.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the data has locations in it, it should be shown on a map.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A map encodes geography, and geography is only worth its considerable space when spatial relationships — adjacency, distance, contiguity, region — are part of the question. When the task is ranking or comparison across a handful of places, a sorted bar chart answers it far more accurately, because area and position on a map are dictated by cartography rather than by the data.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner a location-bearing dataset and require both a map and a non-spatial form, then have them state which questions each answers better. Install the gate question: what does the map show that a sorted bar chart would not?

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The regions on the map are just the regions — they are a neutral container for the data.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Areal units are a choice, and results change with them. The same underlying points aggregated into different boundaries can produce different and even opposite patterns, an effect known as the modifiable areal unit problem. Administrative boundaries also vary enormously in population and area, so equal-looking regions carry wildly unequal weight.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Show one point dataset aggregated at three boundary levels so the pattern visibly changes, then have the learner write the disclosure that must accompany any choropleth: which units, why those, and what the population range across them is.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: In a node-link diagram, where the nodes sit tells you something about the data.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Node position in most force-directed layouts is an artifact of the algorithm, its random seed and its parameters — not an encoding of any variable. Viewers nevertheless read proximity as similarity and centre as importance. At moderate density the layout also degrades into an uninterpretable hairball, at which point a matrix view supports adjacency and cluster tasks far better.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner re-run one layout with different seeds and observe the picture change while the graph does not, then rebuild the same data as an ordered matrix and compare which tasks each supports. Require any published node-link view to state what position does and does not encode.

competencies.title: Graphical integrity and uncertainty
competencies.description: Detecting, preventing and remediating distortion — axis and scale manipulation, aspect-ratio effects, baseline and range selection, misleading aggregation — and representing uncertainty honestly. Includes disclosure control: minimum cell sizes, suppression, and the differencing risk created by interactive filtering.

desiredOutcomes.description: Audit a visualization for distortion and classify each finding by mechanism.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Audit includes at least one framing finding that involves no incorrect number, and each finding is named by mechanism rather than described impressionistically.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select and justify an uncertainty representation appropriate to a specified audience's numeracy and the decision's stakes.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Choice is justified against both numeracy and stakes, and the learner rejects omission with the transfer-of-risk argument rather than an appeal to rigour.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Axes must always start at zero.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: True for length-based encodings like bars, where the mark's length is the value and truncating it breaks that identity. False as a universal law: for position-based encodings of quantities where zero is not a meaningful reference — exchange rates, body temperature, pH — forcing zero compresses the meaningful variation into an unreadable flat line and conceals the signal.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Replace the rule with the principle: the baseline must match what the encoding claims. Drill on paired cases — the same data as bars and as a line — so the learner sees the rule apply and then not apply, and can state which property of the encoding decided it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the underlying numbers are accurate, the chart is honest.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Distortion enters through framing choices — time range, comparison group, denominator, aggregation statistic, aspect ratio — every one of which can mislead while every number remains correct. Arithmetic correctness is a necessary and badly insufficient condition.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give one dataset and require the learner to produce two charts supporting opposite conclusions without falsifying a single value. Then have them write the framing disclosures that would make each chart honest.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Uncertainty confuses non-technical audiences, so it's kinder to leave it out.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Omitting uncertainty does not remove it — it transfers it invisibly to the decision-maker, who then acts on false precision without knowing they are doing so. The premise that intervals are often misread is true; the conclusion that omission solves it is false, because the problem is representation choice, not disclosure.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Present the same forecast as bare point estimates, error bars, a quantile dotplot and a fan encoding, and have the learner match each to an audience and stakes level. Require them to script the sentence they would use to decline an executive's request to remove uncertainty, including the alternative they would offer.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Once the data is aggregated, nobody can be identified, so there is no privacy issue in the chart.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Small cells re-identify. A regional breakdown where one category contains three people, a filter combination that isolates a single team, or two published views that differ by one record can each expose an individual. Aggregation reduces risk; it does not eliminate it, and interactive filtering multiplies the number of views an adversary can difference against each other.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner take a real dashboard and find the filter combination that isolates the fewest records, then implement a minimum-cell threshold with visible suppression rather than silent omission. Add a disclosure-control row to their specification template.

competencies.title: Accessible and inclusive visualization
competencies.description: Designing charts usable across colour-vision deficiency, low vision, screen-reader use, motor constraints and varied numeracy — as a design constraint from the first hour, not a remediation step. Includes internationalization: locale number and date formats, units and currency, label expansion, and right-to-left layout.

desiredOutcomes.description: Evaluate a chart against accessibility criteria — redundant non-colour encoding, contrast, keyboard and touch operability, text alternative — and remediate the failures.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Audit covers all four criteria, and each remediation is an encoding change rather than an added disclaimer or appended data table.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write a text alternative that conveys a chart's takeaway pattern rather than only its values.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Alternative names the chart type, scope and the structural pattern (direction, shape, notable features) in prose, and does not consist of a value list.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A colourblind-safe palette makes a chart accessible.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Palette choice addresses one condition. Contrast ratios, non-colour redundant encoding, text alternatives, keyboard operability, touch target size and reduced-motion handling all remain open. A CVD-safe chart whose values are hover-only is still unusable for a large group.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run the four-check audit — greyscale, pointer-free access, contrast, text alternative — on a chart that already uses a safe palette, so the learner discovers the remaining failures on a chart they had judged compliant.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Accessibility is a QA pass at the end, once the design is stable.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The determining choices are made in the first hour: colour as the sole carrier of meaning, values reachable only on hover, no textual statement of the takeaway. By the time an audit runs, those choices are load-bearing and remediation means redesign rather than adjustment.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner take a finished hover-dependent chart and cost the remediation, then design the same chart accessibly from the wireframe and compare the effort. Move the four criteria into their own definition-of-done for chart work.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Providing the underlying data table satisfies the accessibility requirement.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A table is a fallback for values, not for the pattern the chart exists to communicate. Equivalence means equivalent information, and the information in a chart is structural — a trend, a cluster, a gap. Asking a screen-reader user to reconstruct that from two hundred rows is not equivalent access.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner attempt to state the takeaway of an unfamiliar chart from its data table alone under a time limit, then write the one-sentence pattern description that would have served. Require both the pattern description and the values in every deliverable thereafter.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Making a chart work in other markets is a translation step at the end.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Locale changes the artifact structurally: decimal and thousands separators invert between locales, date orders differ, currencies and units change magnitude and width, translated labels routinely run fifty percent longer and break direct labelling, and right-to-left layout mirrors axis direction and reading order. None of that is fixable by swapping strings in a finished design.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner render one chart with the longest available translation of every label, a right-to-left locale, and a locale using comma decimal separators, then fix what breaks in the layout rules rather than in the copy.

competencies.title: Annotation, framing and explanatory narrative
competencies.description: Directing attention and stating the takeaway through titles, annotation layers, reference marks and sequencing — for both single graphics and multi-step narratives. Includes animation, object constancy through transitions, and multi-step sequenced narrative.

desiredOutcomes.description: Construct a title hierarchy and annotation layer that states the chart's takeaway without asserting more than the data supports.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Title states a specific finding, the subtitle carries units, population, range and comparator, and no element asserts causation the chart cannot establish.

desiredOutcomes.description: Include at least one annotation that complicates the chart's own headline claim where the data warrants it.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Annotation layer contains a reference mark or note that a purely persuasive version would have omitted, and the learner explains why it strengthens credibility.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The data speaks for itself — adding a takeaway would bias the reader.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Every chart already embeds a framing: what was included, aggregated, scaled and compared. Declining to annotate does not produce neutrality, it produces an unguided viewer who supplies their own interpretation from whatever is most visually salient — frequently the wrong thing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Show one chart to several people with only a topic title and collect their stated takeaways, exposing the spread. Then add the accurate takeaway title and repeat, so the learner sees that annotation narrowed the readings toward the supported one rather than away from it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Annotating the takeaway is editorialising, so a neutral topic title is safer.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Stating what the chart shows is different from asserting what it does not. The ethical line is fidelity to the data, not absence of guidance. An explicit takeaway is in fact more auditable than a topic title, because it makes the designer's framing visible and therefore contestable.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Drill the legitimate–illegitimate boundary on paired titles for the same chart, one stating an observed association and one asserting a mechanism. Require the learner to mark where each crosses the line and to rewrite the failing one inside support.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Explanatory and exploratory design are the same problem at different levels of polish.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: They have inverted requirements: one constrains to a single reading, the other preserves many. Treating them as a polish gradient produces underspecified dashboards and overbuilt graphics, because the designer never chose which set of requirements to satisfy.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner list the requirements for each mode side by side and mark every pair that inverts. Then take a merged artifact from their own work and split it into two, noting what each version could finally drop.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Animation and transitions are polish — they make the chart feel nicer.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Transitions carry information. A staged transition that preserves object identity lets the viewer track which mark became which, so a sort or filter is understood rather than merely observed; an abrupt swap forces the viewer to re-read the chart from scratch. Conversely, gratuitous motion competes for the same attention budget as a highlight and can defeat the pop-out it was meant to support.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner build one state change twice — as an instant swap and as a staged transition preserving object constancy — and test which one lets a colleague say what changed. Require every animation to name the relationship it preserves, and to respect reduced-motion preferences.

competencies.title: Interaction design and dashboard architecture
competencies.description: Structuring multi-view systems and interaction — overview and detail, focus and context, brushing and linking, details on demand, filtering, drill-down — including responsive and small-screen behaviour. Includes transition and object-constancy behaviour during filtering and drill-down.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design the information architecture of a multi-view dashboard for a defined role, applying overview and detail, focus and context, and details on demand.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Default view is designed for one role and one decision and stands alone without interaction; every retained control is justified and every removed control's function is accounted for.

desiredOutcomes.description: Specify interaction and responsive behaviour such that no information required to read a chart depends on hover or pointer input.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Specification names where required values live, defines keyboard focus order, and states a responsive drop order including what never drops.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Interactivity compensates for a weak default view — users can always filter to what they need.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Most viewers never interact. The unmanipulated first render carries the majority of the communicative load and is the only view many sessions ever see. In exploratory tools a weak default additionally misdirects explorers about where to look.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner pull interaction analytics from a real dashboard and confront the zero-interaction session share. Then apply the standing test: if interactivity were disabled tomorrow, what percentage of value survives, before and after redesign.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Every dashboard needs a filter panel — that's what makes it flexible.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Filters offload the designer's unmade decisions onto a user with less context and less time. Each one costs the user four things: knowing it exists, what it does, what value is appropriate, and what its current state is. A well-scoped view for a defined role routinely outperforms a configurable one.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require the learner to justify each filter by naming the role whose next question is genuinely unpredictable. Every filter that fails the test is converted into either a default scope or a drill-down, and its function documented.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Tooltips are a fine home for important values — hovering is natural.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Hover is unavailable on touch, invisible to keyboard and screen-reader users, and undiscoverable by anyone not already exploring. It is acceptable for supplementary detail only; anything required to read the chart must be reachable without a pointer.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner attempt their own dashboard on a phone and by keyboard alone, listing every value that became unreachable. Then relocate each one to the mark, an adjacent table, or a focusable element, and record the decision in the specification.

competencies.title: Visualization design systems and governance
competencies.description: Building reusable chart taxonomies, encoding tokens, usage rules, specification formats, engineering handoff, and contribution and review models that scale across an organisation. Includes metric definition and the semantic layer as governed design surface.

desiredOutcomes.description: Define the core of a visualization design system: chart taxonomy with usage limits, semantically assigned encoding tokens, scale and axis rules, accessibility acceptance criteria, annotation standards, and a contribution and review model.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: All six parts are present, colour tokens carry business semantics rather than only visual values, and the taxonomy includes explicit 'when not to use' guidance.

desiredOutcomes.description: Produce an engineering-ready specification covering encoding logic, scale and domain behaviour, and empty, loading, partial, error, stale and overflow states.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Specification includes conditional encoding rules, out-of-range handling, an explicit null-versus-zero policy, a stale-data behaviour, and one line of rationale per decision.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A chart component library is a visualization design system.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Components govern appearance; a system governs meaning. Without encoding rules, semantic colour assignments and selection guidance, teams build consistent-looking charts that contradict each other semantically — the same blue meaning 'forecast' in one product and 'current period' in another, which is worse than visible inconsistency because nobody notices.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner find two charts in their own organisation that use the same visual token for different meanings, then draft the semantic token layer that would have prevented it. Establish the rule that every token carries a business meaning, not only a hex value.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Standardisation kills expressiveness — a system will make all our charts boring.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The purpose of a system is to make routine cases automatic so that scarce design attention goes to the genuinely novel ones. The alternative is not creative freedom; it is redesigning bar charts indefinitely while nobody has time to think about the hard problem.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner audit where their team's chart hours actually went last quarter and classify each as routine or novel. Then design the system to absorb the routine share and reserve a documented exception path for the rest.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A high-fidelity mockup is the specification — if it's pixel-accurate, engineering has what it needs.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A mockup shows one state of a system that has at least a dozen. Encoding logic and conditional rules, scale domain and out-of-range behaviour, empty, loading, partial, error, stale, single-row and overflow states, null-versus-zero policy and responsive drop order are all invisible in it, and will otherwise be decided by whoever is closest to the deadline.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner a polished mockup and the list of production states, and have them find the state the mockup cannot answer. Then require a state inventory table in every handoff, with stale-data behaviour as a named row.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Metric definition is the data team's job — design starts once the numbers exist.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The metric determines what every downstream chart can possibly say. Whether on-time means the train reached the terminal or the rider reached work, whether active user means opened the app or completed an action, whether revenue is booked or recognised — each definition fixes the grain, the denominator and the population, and therefore the entire space of honest visual claims. A designer who declines to engage inherits someone else's unexamined choice and then publishes it.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner take one headline metric in their organisation and reconstruct its definition — grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh — then identify one visual claim currently made that the definition does not support. Add a metric-definition register to the design system's governance scope.

competencies.title: Critique, evidence and practice leadership
competencies.description: Evaluating others' visualization work against explicit criteria, facilitating structured critique, defending decisions with perceptual and empirical evidence, and defining success measures for visualization work.

desiredOutcomes.description: Facilitate a structured critique against explicit criteria in a fixed order and keep preference discussion out until the criteria passes are complete.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Critique runs brief, integrity, encoding, narrative and access in order; every finding names a mechanism; a failed brief pass halts the review.

desiredOutcomes.description: Convert a stalled visualization disagreement into an empirical question and define measurable success indicators for a visualization deliverable.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Test protocol names what is shown, to whom, for how long, what is asked, and a result threshold that would actually change the design; success measures are matched to the artifact's mode.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Critique means identifying what's wrong with the work.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Effective critique tests an artifact against its stated goal and audience. Without that anchor it degrades into preference exchange, produces contradictory direction, and erodes the team's trust in the process — so the next review gets fewer honest submissions.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Make the brief pass a hard gate: if audience, decision, task and mode are not stated, the review stops and the session becomes brief-writing. Have the learner facilitate one session under that rule and report what changed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Disagreements about charts come down to taste, so they're settled by whoever is most senior.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Most visualization disputes are empirical — about judgment accuracy, task fit, comprehension or data validity — and are resolvable with the literature or a short test. Settling them by status forfeits a cheap and better answer and teaches the team that evidence is decorative.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner take a live disagreement, phrase it as a testable question, and run a fifteen-minute study with five participants. Require them to pre-register the result that would change their own mind.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: You can't really usability-test a visualization — comprehension is too subjective.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Comprehension tests, timed value retrieval, comparison-accuracy tasks, prediction tasks and misconception probes are established protocols that routinely overturn confident internal opinion. Five participants surfaces most catastrophic comprehension failures at very low cost.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run a timed takeaway-recall test on the learner's own chart with five colleagues and compare the recalled messages against the intended one. The gap is usually large enough to settle the objection without argument.

sections.title: Data Foundations and Analytic Tasks
sections.description: What the data permits, and what the stakeholder actually needs — before any chart exists. Establishes measurement scale, cardinality, grain, aggregation state and missingness as the properties that constrain every later decision, and the practice of recovering a decision and its analytic tasks from a solution-shaped request.

learningObjectives.description: Classify every variable in a supplied dataset by measurement scale and cardinality, and flag variables whose stored type misrepresents their semantics.
Explain how a dataset's grain and aggregation state constrain the claims a visualization can support, given a record-level and a pre-aggregated version of the same data.
Distinguish absence of measurement from a measured zero, and state the encoding consequence of each.
Rewrite an ambiguous, solution-shaped stakeholder request as two or three explicit analytic tasks using a standard task vocabulary.
Specify audience, decision and delivery surface for a given brief, and classify the brief as exploratory or explanatory with justification.
Apply the data audit and brief-recovery procedure to a dataset from an unfamiliar domain without relying on domain precedent.

motivationHooks.prompt:
Most bad charts are not drawing failures. They are decisions made before anyone opened a design tool.

You will be handed a spreadsheet and a request. If you begin by choosing a chart, you have skipped the two questions that determine whether *any* chart can succeed: what does this data actually measure, and what question is this person trying to answer? Get those wrong and no amount of typographic care rescues the output — you will have built a beautiful, confident, wrong artifact, and you will have to defend it in a room containing an analyst who knows exactly why it is wrong.

This is also where your leverage is highest and least contested. Anyone on the team can argue about a colour ramp. Very few people in a product org will notice that the "average customer satisfaction" being plotted is an average of ordinal ranks, or that the dataset was pre-aggregated in a way that destroys the very variation the chart is meant to reveal.

Catching that is a design contribution, and it is the one that earns you standing with the data team.

Here is a claim to hold on to and test as you go:

> **A transit authority reports that a bus route ran 86% on time last quarter. The figure is arithmetically correct. Publishing it in a board deck is still a serious error.**

Write down now, in one line, what you think the error is. You will find out before the section ends — and the gap between your answer and the real one is roughly the size of this section's contribution.

**The resolution.** The 86% was a monthly average across every hour the route runs. Grouped by hour of day, it resolves into 96% off-peak and **61% during the 7–9am peak** — the window in which most riders travel.

Nothing was falsified. The error was in the **grain**: the file's row unit had already collapsed the variation the decision depended on, and that collapse was invisible in the delivered file.

If your prediction was "they cherry-picked the period" or "the sample was too small," you were reasoning about the *numbers*. The error was one level up, in what a row represented — which is the level this section is about, and the level the MTA case study shows operating at civic scale.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following.

**Storage type is not measurement scale.** A column full of numbers may be nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio, and the classification — not the data type — determines which encodings and which arithmetic are licensed.

**Grain is the most consequential property in any delivered file.** It fixes what can be summed, what an average means, and which variation still exists to be shown. Aggregation destroys variation permanently, and no chart recovers it.

**Arithmetic correctness and truth are different standards.** Every number in the Route 47 chart was right. So was every number in the MTA reporting. Both misled, and both did so through decisions made before any chart existed.

**A named chart type is a guess at a solution, not a requirement.** The requirement is the decision — the thing with an action verb in it — and the analytic tasks that follow from it.

**Exploratory and explanatory are a fork with inverted requirements**, decided in the brief rather than discovered in review.
keyTakeaways: Classify by meaning, not by storage type: nominal → ordinal → interval → ratio.
A visual channel must not imply more structure than the scale carries.
Ask three questions of every file: what is a row, what was grouped and excluded, what does a missing value mean.
Distinguish 'not measured' from 'measured as zero' — never plot the first as the second.
Recover the decision before the design; a decision contains a verb.
Name audience, delivery surface and mode before choosing anything visual.
Match grain to the task, not to what arrived and not to the finest available.

furtherReading.title: On the Theory of Scales of Measurement
furtherReading.author: S. S. Stevens
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The original nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio paper. Short, and worth reading in the original for how carefully the operations-per-scale argument is constructed — it is the source of the 'what arithmetic is licensed' framing used throughout this section.

furtherReading.title: Visualization Analysis and Design, Chapters 2–3
furtherReading.citation: Munzner, T. (2014). CRC Press.
furtherReading.author: Tamara Munzner
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The most rigorous available treatment of data abstraction and task abstraction. Chapter 3's what–why–how framing is essentially the academic version of the design brief you built in this section; read it if you want the formal grounding.

furtherReading.title: A Multi-Level Typology of Abstract Visualization Tasks
furtherReading.citation: Brehmer, M. & Munzner, T. (2013). IEEE TVCG, 19(12).
furtherReading.author: Matthew Brehmer, Tamara Munzner
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The formal version of the eight-task vocabulary, with the why/what/how decomposition. Useful when you need to write a brief precise enough that two designers would produce compatible artifacts from it.

furtherReading.title: Low-Level Components of Analytic Activity in Information Visualization
furtherReading.citation: Amar, R., Eagan, J. & Stasko, J. (2005). IEEE InfoVis.
furtherReading.author: Robert Amar, James Eagan, John Stasko
furtherReading.rationaleNote: An empirically derived task taxonomy built by observing what analysts actually do. Read it alongside Brehmer & Munzner to see how a bottom-up and a top-down taxonomy converge.

furtherReading.title: Data Organization in Spreadsheets
furtherReading.citation: Broman, K. W. & Woo, K. H. (2018). The American Statistician, 72(1), 2–10.
furtherReading.author: Karl Broman, Kara Woo
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Short, practical, and will immediately improve how you talk to whoever hands you the file. Its section on distinguishing empty cells from zeros is the most directly applicable thing you can read after this section.

furtherReading.title: MTA Subway Performance Dashboards
furtherReading.citation: Metropolitan Transportation Authority. Performance metrics portal.
furtherReading.author: MTA
furtherReading.rationaleNote: A live artifact of this section's case study. Browse the current metrics and count how many are passenger-centred rather than train-centred — you are looking at the outcome of a grain decision that took years of public pressure to change.

furtherReading.title: How Charts Lie, Chapter 1
furtherReading.citation: Cairo, A. (2019). W. W. Norton.
furtherReading.author: Alberto Cairo
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The most readable book-length treatment of framing-based distortion, and the one to hand a stakeholder rather than read yourself. Chapter 1 covers the 'correct numbers, wrong claim' pattern that this section introduces and Section 6 develops fully.

furtherReading.title: Exploratory Data Analysis (selected chapters)
furtherReading.citation: Tukey, J. W. (1977). Addison-Wesley.
furtherReading.author: John Tukey
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Optional and old, and still the clearest statement of why you look at data before summarising it. Skim rather than read; the value is in the disposition, which is exactly the one this section is trying to install.

learningExperiences.title: What the numbers actually are

contentBlocks.content:
A regional transit authority hands you a CSV. Seven columns, forty thousand rows. The Director of Service Planning says: *"Can you make a pie chart of ridership by route for the board deck?"*

Before you answer, look at what you actually have. Here is one row.

contentBlocks.caption: One row from the transit dataset

contentBlocks.content:
Five of those seven columns hold numbers. They are not five of the same kind of thing.

**`route_id` = 47.** A number, not a quantity. Route 47 is not *more* than route 12, and the average of routes 47 and 12 is not route 29.5.

**`stop_sequence` = 3.** This has order — stop 3 comes after stop 2 — but the gaps are not equal. Stop 2 to stop 3 might be 400 metres; stop 3 to stop 4 might be six kilometres.

**`rider_rating` = 4.** A 1–5 satisfaction response. Ordered, with no guaranteed equal spacing: the distance from "poor" to "fair" is not reliably the same as from "good" to "excellent", and it varies by respondent.

**`boardings` = 218.** A count. Zero means zero, and 400 is genuinely twice 200. This is the only column here you can freely add, average and ratio.

**`temp_c` = 11.** Equal intervals — 11°C to 12°C is the same step as 20°C to 21°C — but zero is a convention, not an absence of heat. 20°C is not twice as warm as 10°C.

One row, four different kinds of number.

## The abstraction

What separates those columns is their **measurement scale** — the kind of information the values carry, independent of how they happen to be stored.

contentBlocks.caption: The four measurement scales, in order of increasing structure

contentBlocks.title: The rule that follows
contentBlocks.content:
**A visual channel must not imply more structure than the scale carries.**

A continuous position axis implies order, *and* spacing, *and* usually a meaningful zero. Putting nominal data on it is a false claim about the data, told in a visual grammar the viewer trusts.

Notice where that error entered: not in a manipulated axis, but in a variable classification made in the first ten minutes.

## Three more properties, before any chart exists

Scale is one of four things you need to establish.

**Cardinality** — how many distinct values a variable has. `route_name` might have 6 values or 340. This single number rules chart forms in and out before any aesthetic consideration: a legend works at 6 and fails at 340.

**Grain** — what one row represents. One boarding? One stop-visit? One route-day? Everything downstream depends on it, and it is the property people most often forget to ask about. The next experience is devoted to it.

**Aggregation state** — whether these are raw observations or the output of someone else's summarising.

And one property that is really a question rather than a value: **missingness** — not just how many values are absent, but *why*. A null in `rider_rating` because nobody surveyed that stop is a different fact from a null because the stop had zero riders. The first is an absence of measurement; the second is a measurement of zero. Charting them identically merges two different realities.

contentBlocks.altText: Two line charts of the same sensor series. In the first, a four-hour instrumentation gap is shown as a break in the line with the period shaded and labelled 'sensor offline'. In the second, the same missing hours are plotted as zero, producing a deep V-shaped dip to the axis that reads as a sudden collapse in activity and then a recovery. The dip is an artifact of the encoding, not an event in the data.
contentBlocks.caption: Absence of measurement is not a measurement of zero.

terms.definition: The kind of information a variable's values carry — nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio — independent of the data type used to store them.
A measurement scale carrying identity only: categories with no order.
A measurement scale carrying ordered categories with no guaranteed equal spacing between them.
A measurement scale with equal spacing and an arbitrary zero; differences are meaningful, ratios are not.
A measurement scale with equal spacing and a true zero, so ratios between values are meaningful.
The number of distinct values a variable takes; frequently rules chart forms in or out before any aesthetic consideration.
The pattern of absent values and, critically, the reasons for their absence — unmeasured is not the same as measured as zero.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. "It's stored as a number, so it's quantitative."** *(ds-numeric-means-quantitative)* — Zip codes, SKUs, route IDs, survey codes and calendar years are all numeric in storage and non-quantitative in meaning. Classify by what the value *means*.

**2. Averaging ordinal data and presenting the result as a measurement.** *(ds-ordinal-averaging)* — "Average satisfaction: 3.7" silently asserts equal spacing between response options. Report distributions, medians or top-box shares instead — and if a mean is organisationally mandated, show the distribution beside it so the assumption stays visible.

**3. Plotting nulls as zeros.** *(ds-numeric-means-quantitative, and an integrity failure)* — "We didn't measure" and "we measured nothing" are different facts. A line dipping to zero across an instrumentation gap invents an event.

**4. Choosing the channel before classifying the variable.** — Every subsequent decision in this course depends on the classification. It costs two minutes and it is the cheapest error to avoid.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Storage type is not measurement scale. Classify by meaning: **nominal → ordinal → interval → ratio**, each adding order, then equal spacing, then a true zero.
- A visual channel must not imply more structure than the scale carries.
