interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: write the two or three sentences you would actually say in a review to justify moving a variable from colour to position. Assume the person you are talking to is not hostile, just unconvinced.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
A version that tends to work: *"The main thing this chart is for is comparing these two numbers. People read ratios off position roughly twice as accurately as off colour — that's been measured repeatedly since the eighties. So I've put the comparison on position and moved region onto colour, which is what colour is actually good at."*

Three features make it land: it names the task first, it cites a measured effect without turning into a lecture, and it gives colour a job rather than taking it away. The last one matters more than it sounds — a proposal that removes something feels like loss, and a proposal that reassigns it does not.

workedExamples.problem: A hospital dashboard shows 12 wards. Each ward's bed occupancy rate is encoded as the fill colour of a ward tile, on a light-to-dark ramp. Ward name is text; ward type is tile border colour. Executives use it to decide where to open surge capacity. Diagnose and re-encode.
steps: **State the task.** Deciding where to open surge capacity is a **ranking** plus **deviation** task: which wards are highest, and which exceed the threshold where surge is warranted.
**Classify the variables.** Occupancy rate: ratio, 12 values. Ward name: nominal, 12 values. Ward type: nominal, small number of values.

**Check expressiveness.** Occupancy on a luminance ramp is ordered data on an ordered channel — expressiveness passes. Ward type on border hue is nominal on nominal — passes. No disqualifications, so we proceed to effectiveness.

**Check effectiveness against the task.** Occupancy — the quantity the decision turns on — sits on **shading, rank 7**. The task requires ranking 12 values and judging distance from a threshold. This is exactly the judgment shading is worst at.
**Check the pop-out budget.** Ward type is encoded as border hue across all 12 tiles, so hue is fully consumed by a context variable. There is no pop-out available for the state that matters.

**Re-encode the primary variable to position.** A sorted dot plot or bar chart: wards on a categorical axis ordered by occupancy, occupancy on a common-scale position axis. Rank 7 → rank 1, on the variable the decision depends on.

**Add a reference mark.** A threshold line at the surge-trigger level. This converts "is 91% a lot?" — an absolute judgment requiring domain knowledge — into "is this bar past the line?", which is immediate.
**Re-encode ward type onto a muted, low-salience channel.** Small shape markers or a light grouping band. It is context, not the decision variable, and it must stop consuming hue.
**Spend the pop-out once.** Saturated accent for wards past threshold **and** still rising. Everything else muted.
**Keep the numbers.** Direct-label each bar with its percentage. Position gives the comparison; the numeral gives the exact value for the conversation that follows.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The tile grid was not badly executed. It was well-executed with the decision variable on the seventh-ranked channel.**

That is the most common encoding failure in enterprise dashboards, and it is invisible if you evaluate charts on appearance: the tile grid is compact, tidy and colourful, and it puts the thing the executives are deciding on into the channel humans read least accurately.

The general procedure the example demonstrates:

1. Name the task.
2. Classify the variables.
3. Eliminate on expressiveness.
4. Ask which variable the **decision** depends on, and check where it sits on the ranking.
5. Move it up. Move context variables down.
6. Add a reference mark to convert absolute judgments into comparative ones.
7. Spend the pop-out once.

Steps 4 and 5 are where most of the gain lives, and both require Section 1's task statement before they can be executed at all.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Give the top four channels in the effectiveness ranking for quantitative data, in order.
What does the effectiveness ranking measure, and name two tasks it says nothing about.
Define expressiveness, and state its relationship to effectiveness in one sentence.
Why does the effectiveness ranking roughly invert for nominal data? Give an example of a channel that moves.
State the two-step check that catches the most common enterprise encoding failure: which variable does the decision depend on, and…?

learningExperiences.title: Colour, properly

contentBlocks.content:
Colour is where most encoding damage happens, because it feels expressive and is perceptually treacherous. Designers arrive at this material with more confidence than any other part of the course, and it is the part where confident intuition most reliably fails.

Three scale types, matched to three data situations.

contentBlocks.caption: Colour scale types and where each belongs
rows: Distinct hues at roughly equal luminance
One hue (or an ordered multi-hue path) varying monotonically in **luminance**
Data with a genuinely meaningful midpoint
Two sequential ramps meeting at zero, a target, or a baseline
Continuous; the midpoint must be real

contentBlocks.title: The diverging trap
contentBlocks.content:
Use a diverging scale **only when the midpoint is genuinely meaningful** — zero, a target, a baseline, a break-even point.

The palette's pivot reads as a **threshold**. On data with no natural centre, a diverging scale invents a boundary and manufactures a story: values on one side look categorically different from values on the other, when the underlying data is a smooth continuum.

This is an integrity failure delivered through a colour picker, and Section 6 treats it as one.

contentBlocks.altText: Three rows. Categorical: six distinct hues at roughly equal lightness, for nominal identity. Sequential: a single-hue ramp darkening steadily from pale to deep blue, for ordered data. Diverging: two ramps meeting at a pale neutral midpoint, brown on one side and blue on the other, with the midpoint marked and labelled as needing to be meaningful.
contentBlocks.caption: Three colour scale types, three data situations.

contentBlocks.content:
## Perceptual uniformity, and why luminance carries ordering

A **perceptually uniform** scale is one where equal steps in the data produce equal *perceived* steps in colour. Most naive gradients fail this badly.

The requirement is **monotonic luminance**: brightness must rise (or fall) steadily across the ramp. Luminance is the channel humans read ordinally — it is what survives greyscale conversion, what survives most colour-vision deficiencies, and what the visual system uses to judge "more" and "less."

The classic failure is the **rainbow / jet** colormap. Its luminance is non-monotonic: it rises toward yellow and falls again. That creates bright bands mid-scale which viewers read as boundaries or peaks **in the data**, when they are artifacts of the palette. It also collapses under common colour-vision deficiencies and prints unusably in greyscale.

Perceptually uniform alternatives — viridis, cividis, magma, the ColorBrewer sequential ramps — order by luminance and survive both tests.

contentBlocks.altText: Two colour ramps shown with their measured luminance plotted beneath. The rainbow ramp's luminance rises from dark blue, peaks sharply at yellow in the middle of the scale, then falls again toward dark red, producing a bright band mid-scale that readers perceive as a peak in the data. The viridis ramp's luminance rises steadily from dark purple to bright yellow with no reversal, so equal steps in the data produce equal perceived steps.
contentBlocks.caption: Computed relative luminance profiles for the two ramps.

contentBlocks.content:
## Two things that break palettes validated on swatches

**Simultaneous contrast.** The same fill reads lighter against a dark surround and darker against a light one. A palette signed off on large swatches in a design tool can fail on the actual marks.

**Small marks lose saturation.** A three-pixel scatter dot does not read as the colour it is. Anything encoded in saturation at small mark sizes is being encoded much more weakly than it appears in review.

The practical consequence: **validate palettes at the mark size and against the background they will actually be used at.** Not in a swatch grid.

## Colour-vision deficiency as an encoding constraint

Roughly 8% of men of northern European descent and about 0.5% of women have some form of colour-vision deficiency, most commonly red–green. In an enterprise product with a hundred thousand users, that is thousands of people.

So red/green as the *sole* carrier of a good/bad distinction is not a nice-to-have failure. It is an encoding failure for a substantial share of any large audience.

The structural fix is **redundant encoding**: carry the meaning in a second channel — position, shape, direct label, luminance difference — so that colour reinforces rather than bears the load.

**The fastest proxy test:** render it in greyscale. If it still reads, it survives most CVD. This takes ten seconds and catches most of the failures.

Section 6 develops this fully, along with contrast minimums, pointer-free access and text alternatives. What matters here is the framing: **this is an encoding decision made in the first hour, not a remediation pass at the end.**

contentBlocks.altText: A red and green status pair and a blue and orange status pair, each shown three ways: as designed, converted to greyscale, and under a deuteranopia simulation. The red and green pair converts to two nearly identical greys and becomes indistinguishable under deuteranopia, losing the entire good-versus-bad distinction. The blue and orange pair remains clearly separable in both conditions.
contentBlocks.caption: The ten-second test: greyscale and colour-vision simulation.

terms.definition: A set of distinct hues at roughly equal luminance, used for nominal identity; practically limited to about six to eight distinguishable categories.
A colour ramp varying monotonically in luminance, used for ordinal or ratio data running from low to high.
Two sequential ramps meeting at a meaningful midpoint such as zero, a target or a baseline; illegitimate when the midpoint is arbitrary.
The property that equal steps in the data produce equal perceived steps in colour; requires monotonic luminance across the ramp.
The shift in a colour's appearance depending on its surround, which is why palettes validated on large swatches can fail on small marks.
Reduced ability to distinguish certain hues, most commonly red and green; makes hue-only encoding of meaning a structural failure for part of any large audience.
Carrying the same meaning in two or more channels so that no single channel is load-bearing.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Rainbow or jet colormaps for continuous data.** *(ee-3d-adds-richness — same family: visual variation that is not data)* — Non-monotonic luminance creates false boundaries readers take for features. Also fails CVD and greyscale.

**2. Diverging scales on data with no meaningful midpoint.** — The pivot becomes a claim that a threshold exists. If the midpoint is arbitrary, the claim is fabricated.

**3. Categorical palettes past about eight categories.** — Beyond the ceiling, do not encode identity in colour at all. Facet instead — Section 4 covers this.

**4. Using brand colours as a data palette.** — Brand palettes are chosen for identity and contrast against a background, not for perceptual uniformity, ordering or CVD safety. They almost never satisfy all three.

**5. Letting hue alone be load-bearing.** *(vp-colour-for-precision)* — If removing colour destroys the chart, colour is carrying more than it should.

**6. Validating a palette on swatches.** — Simultaneous contrast and small-mark desaturation both break swatch-validated palettes at real sizes.

**7. Treating CVD as an edge case.** — Roughly one in twelve men. In any large audience it is thousands of people.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Three scale types for three data situations: **categorical** for nominal, **sequential** for ordered, **diverging** only where the midpoint is real.
- **Perceptual uniformity requires monotonic luminance.** Luminance is the channel that carries ordering.
- Rainbow ramps create false features, fail CVD, and fail greyscale. Use viridis, cividis, magma or ColorBrewer.
- Validate palettes at real mark size against the real background — simultaneous contrast and desaturation break swatch approvals.
- **Redundant encoding** is what makes colour safe. Never let hue alone be load-bearing.
- Greyscale rendering is a ten-second proxy test for most CVD failures.
- Three tests, in order, before you evaluate whether you *like* a continuous scale: **type matches structure, luminance orders monotonically, midpoint aligns with the data's meaningful zero.**

interactionSequence.prompt: Which statement about diverging colour scales is correct?
options: They are appropriate only when the data has a genuinely meaningful midpoint such as zero, a target or a baseline.
They should be used whenever the data spans both high and low values, since the contrast aids reading.
They are interchangeable with sequential scales as long as the endpoints are distinguishable.
They are preferable to sequential scales because more hues carry more information.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The pivot is read as a threshold, so an arbitrary midpoint fabricates a boundary the data never contained.
All continuous data spans high and low — that describes range, not a meaningful centre.
A diverging scale makes a structural claim about a centre; a sequential scale claims monotonic order. Different claims, not interchangeable styling.
Visual variation that carries no additional data is cost without informational return.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A quick field test: **can you name what the middle colour means?** If the answer is "zero," "on target," "break-even" or "the national average," the diverging scale is earning its place. If the answer is "the middle of the range," it is not — the range's midpoint is an artifact of whatever data happened to be included, and it will move when the data updates.

interactionSequence.prompt: A weather service maps rainfall anomaly — deviation from the thirty-year normal — using a rainbow colormap running dark blue through green and yellow to dark red. **Predict:** which regions will appear most visually prominent to a reader, and will that match the regions with the largest anomalies? One line.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The question to ask is where the ramp is *brightest*, not where the data is most extreme. In a rainbow ramp the luminance peak sits around yellow — the middle of the scale. So regions of **moderate** anomaly appear more prominent than regions of extreme anomaly in either direction. The worked example below walks the full diagnosis.

interactionSequence.prompt: A product team wants to use their brand's five accent colours as the categorical palette for all charts. What is the strongest objection?
options: Brand palettes are selected for identity and background contrast, not for equal luminance, distinguishability under CVD, or ordering — they rarely satisfy all three.
Brand colours should never appear in charts under any circumstances.
Five categories is too few for any realistic dataset.
Charts should use only greyscale so that no brand association is implied.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it is a solvable problem: derive a data palette that is brand-adjacent and perceptually validated, rather than reusing the UI palette directly. Section 7 makes this a design-system requirement.
Too absolute. Brand-derived data palettes are entirely workable; the requirement is that they be validated against perceptual criteria first.
Five is comfortably within the categorical ceiling; the issue is the palette's construction, not its size.
This discards colour's genuine strength at categorical identity to solve a problem that palette design solves better.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The underlying distinction — worth carrying to Section 7 — is that **UI colour and data colour are different problems**. UI colour signals interactivity, state and hierarchy. Data colour encodes values, and must satisfy ordering, uniformity and CVD constraints that UI colour never faces. Systems that reuse one palette for both produce charts whose colours mean two things at once.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: take one chart you have shipped and describe what happens to it in greyscale. If you cannot say without checking — check now, then answer. What was carrying the meaning?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The two most common findings: a multi-series line chart where all the lines become the same mid-grey and the legend becomes useless; and a red/green status encoding that becomes two indistinguishable greys, so the chart loses its entire meaning rather than some of its polish.

Both are fixed the same way — add a second channel. Dash patterns and direct labels for the series case; an icon, position or explicit text for the status case. Neither costs anything visually for readers with full colour vision, which is what makes redundant encoding such a cheap discipline once it is habitual.

workedExamples.problem: A regional weather service publishes a map of rainfall anomaly — deviation from the thirty-year normal — using a rainbow colormap from dark blue to dark red. Diagnose it and prescribe.
steps: **Classify the variable.** Anomaly is ratio-scaled with a genuinely meaningful zero: *normal*. Positive and negative both occur and mean opposite things.

**Does the data have a natural midpoint?** Yes — zero anomaly. So a **diverging** scale is warranted. This is one of the cases where diverging is correct rather than decorative, and the scale *type* is right.

**Test luminance monotonicity.** Fail. The rainbow's luminance rises toward yellow and falls again, so a viewer sees bright bands mid-scale. Regions of **moderate** anomaly appear more visually prominent than regions of **extreme** anomaly.

**Test midpoint alignment.** Fail. The ramp's perceptual centre is the bright yellow band, which does not correspond to zero anomaly. The palette's visual pivot and the data's meaningful pivot are in different places, so the reader's sense of 'normal' is anchored to the wrong value.

**Test CVD and greyscale.** Fail both. Under red–green deficiency the two ends converge, so drought and flood become indistinguishable — the single most consequential distinction on the map. In greyscale the ramp is non-monotonic and unreadable.

**Prescribe.** A perceptually uniform diverging ramp with its neutral point anchored **exactly at zero anomaly** — for example a blue–white–brown ramp with symmetric luminance either side. Blue–brown is chosen over red–green specifically because it survives the most common CVD.
**Add redundancy.** Contour lines at fixed anomaly intervals, so magnitude is readable without any colour judgment at all, and the map survives greyscale reproduction in print.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**Correct scale type, wrong implementation** — and that is the useful diagnosis, because it tells you what to change and what to keep.

The general procedure for any continuous colour scale, applied in this order:

1. **Type matches data structure** — is there a real midpoint?
2. **Luminance orders monotonically** — does brightness rise steadily across the ramp?
3. **Midpoint aligns with the data's meaningful zero** — is the palette's pivot where the data's pivot is?

Only after all three pass do you evaluate whether you like it. Note that a designer working from taste alone would likely have replaced the rainbow with something more attractive and could easily have picked another scale failing tests 2 and 3 — the aesthetic instinct and the perceptual requirement are not correlated.

fadedVariant.problem: A logistics dashboard maps warehouse pick-rate performance across 60 sites, using a green-to-red diverging scale centred on the **median site's** performance. Sites above the median are green, below are red. Diagnose it against the same three tests, plus the accessibility check.
givenSteps: Pick rate is a ratio-scaled performance measure.
The scale is diverging, centred on the median of the sites currently included.
blankedStepPrompts: Apply test 1 — does the data have a genuinely meaningful midpoint, and is the chosen midpoint it?
State the specific consequence of the midpoint choice for how sites are read, and what happens when the data updates.
Apply the CVD and greyscale tests to the green-to-red ramp, and state the practical consequence.
Prescribe a fix, addressing both the midpoint problem and the palette problem.
blankedStepAnswers: **Fail on both counts.** Pick rate may well have a meaningful midpoint — a target rate, a contractual SLA, or a break-even throughput — but the **median of the current sites is not it**. The median is an artifact of which sites happen to be included, not a property of the performance measure.

By construction, **half the sites are always red**, regardless of whether performance is good. A fleet where every site exceeds target still renders half its sites as failing. And because the midpoint moves when the data updates, a site can change colour without changing performance — its neighbours changed. Colour is encoding relative rank while appearing to encode absolute status, which readers will not detect.

**Green-to-red is the worst common choice for CVD**, since red–green deficiency is the most prevalent form; the two ends converge and the entire good/bad distinction collapses. In greyscale, a green-to-red ramp is also close to non-monotonic — mid-saturation greens and reds convert to similar greys — so print reproduction fails too.

**Midpoint:** re-anchor to the actual target or SLA, and state it in the subtitle ('relative to the 120 picks/hour target'). If no target exists, that absence is a finding to report, and a **sequential** scale should be used instead of inventing a threshold. **Palette:** replace with a CVD-safe diverging ramp such as blue–white–orange, and add **redundant encoding** — a shape marker or explicit label for below-target sites — so status survives greyscale and CVD. Section 5 adds a further concern: on a map, site marker size may also need to reflect throughput, since a small site and a large one currently look equally important.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the three tests a continuous colour scale must pass before you evaluate whether you like it, in order.
When is a diverging scale legitimate, and what field test tells you quickly?
Why does a rainbow colormap create features that are not in the data? Name the property that fails.
What is the fastest proxy test for redundant encoding, and roughly what share of a large audience does it protect?
Why is a brand or UI palette usually the wrong basis for a data palette? Name two constraints data colour faces that UI colour does not.

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Audit and re-encode one real chart from your own work, producing a defence that cites mechanisms rather than preferences.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: Use a chart currently in production in a product you work on. Choose one you did not design if possible — the failures are easier to see and the exercise stays honest.
instructions: **Part A — Channel inventory (10 min).** Build a table with one row per visual channel in use — position-x, position-y, length, area, hue, luminance, saturation, shape, size, texture, motion, enclosure. For each: the variable it encodes, that variable's measurement scale, and a verdict of **matched**, **over-claiming** (channel implies more structure than the scale carries), or **decorative** (varies but encodes nothing).

**Part B — Pop-out budget (5 min).** Count the elements competing for preattentive attention. Then write one sentence: what is the one thing this chart exists to make unmissable? If more than one element is competing, you are over budget — say which one you would keep.

**Part C — Colour tests (5 min).** If any continuous scale is present, run the three tests: type matches structure, luminance monotonic, midpoint aligned. Then render or simulate the whole chart in greyscale and note what stops working.

**Part D — Re-encode (10 min).** Produce a revised encoding that removes every decorative channel, fixes every over-claim, moves the decision variable up the effectiveness ranking, and spends the pop-out exactly once. Add a reference mark if any absolute judgment can be converted into a comparative one.

**Part E — Defence (5 min).** Write three sentences justifying the change, each referencing a mechanism or measured finding rather than a preference. This is the paragraph you would actually say in a review.
materialsOrPrerequisites: One real chart from a product you work on.
A greyscale rendering method — a screenshot filter, a CVD simulator, or printing it.
The effectiveness ranking and the three colour tests from this section.
reflectionPrompts: How many channels turned out to be decorative? Were any of them ones you would have defended before this section?
Was the decision variable on a high-ranked channel, or did a context variable get the best channel?
What broke in greyscale — some polish, or the meaning?
Does your Part E defence contain any sentence beginning 'I think it looks'? If so, rewrite it.

verification.mode: self-assessment against explicit criteria, with the Part E defence tested by reading it aloud to a colleague
selfAssessmentCriteria: At least one decorative channel is identified and eliminated.
The decision variable's channel is named with its position on the effectiveness ranking, before and after.
Every over-claiming channel is justified as such by reference to the variable's measurement scale.
The greyscale check was actually run, not estimated.
The pop-out budget is spent exactly once, and what was demoted to make room is named.
The defence contains no appeal to taste.

learningExperiences.title: Case study: how a default changed a field

contentBlocks.content:
## The situation

For decades, the default colormap in widely-used scientific plotting environments was a rainbow-style ramp. It appeared in an enormous volume of published medical imaging, climate science and geoscience figures — not because anyone chose it, but because it was what came out of the software.

From the 2000s onward a sustained critique accumulated. The luminance is non-monotonic, so it introduces bright bands readers perceive as structure in the data. It is not perceptually uniform, so equal data steps produce unequal perceived steps. It degrades severely under colour-vision deficiency and in greyscale reproduction. Reviewers documented cases in scientific and medical imaging where the artificial banding coincided with consequential thresholds.

## What actually changed the outcome

The critique was published, repeatedly, in journals practitioners read. It changed some behaviour.

What changed most behaviour was a version bump. **Matplotlib's 2.0 release changed its default colormap to viridis** — designed explicitly for monotonic luminance, perceptual uniformity and CVD robustness. That single change flipped the default for a very large share of scientific figure production. Several journals and scientific societies subsequently issued guidance discouraging rainbow ramps for continuous data.

The order matters: guidance persuaded the people who read guidance. The default reached everyone else.

contentBlocks.title: Three things a design lead should extract
contentBlocks.content:
**1. The failure was perceptual, not aesthetic.** Nobody's complaint was that the rainbow was ugly. The claim was that readers saw boundaries that did not exist in the data — a **graphical integrity** failure delivered through a colour choice.

**2. Defaults are the real intervention.** The highest-leverage act available to a design lead is frequently to change what happens when nobody is thinking. Section 7 builds a whole competency on this.

**3. The evidence was portable.** Practitioners could point to specific, checkable properties — the luminance profile, a CVD simulation, a greyscale conversion — rather than to preference. **Portability is what let the argument win**, and it is the model for every encoding argument you will make.

## Being fair about the other side

The rainbow ramp was not adopted out of carelessness, and it does one thing well that its replacements do not: it has **many perceptually distinct steps**, so a reader can discriminate more separate levels within it than within a monotonic luminance ramp. For tasks that genuinely require reading many discrete bands — some kinds of interferometry, certain medical modalities — practitioners argued that discriminability mattered more than uniformity, and that argument was not frivolous.

The resolution was not that the critics were simply right. It was that **the default should serve the common case**, and the common case is a reader forming an impression of shape and magnitude, not counting bands. Specialists who need discriminability can still choose it deliberately.

That is a more useful lesson than "rainbow bad": **a default is a claim about what most users are doing**, and it should be argued on those grounds.

terms.definition: The property that equal steps in the data produce equal perceived steps in colour; requires monotonic luminance across the ramp.
A colour ramp varying monotonically in luminance, used for ordinal or ratio data running from low to high.
Reduced ability to distinguish certain hues, most commonly red and green; makes hue-only encoding of meaning a structural failure for part of any large audience.
Carrying the same meaning in two or more channels so that no single channel is load-bearing.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors this case illustrates
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Arguing encoding from taste when evidence is available.** *(vp-perception-is-taste)* — 'I find it garish' loses. 'Here is the luminance profile and here is the CVD simulation' wins.

**2. Assuming a published guideline changes behaviour.** — It changes the behaviour of people who read guidelines. Most production output comes from defaults.

**3. Treating the opposing case as obviously stupid.** — The discriminability argument for rainbow ramps is real. Understanding why a bad default persisted is what lets you replace it without a fight.

**4. Fixing the palette and leaving colour load-bearing.** — A perceptually uniform ramp is still a single channel. If the figure needs to survive print and CVD, add contours or labels.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- The rainbow colormap's failure was **measurable**: non-monotonic luminance producing features that were not in the data.
- Published critique changed some behaviour. **Changing the library default changed most of it.**
- Portable evidence — luminance profile, CVD simulation, greyscale conversion — is what makes an encoding argument winnable.
- The counter-argument for discriminability was legitimate; the resolution was that **defaults should serve the common case** while specialists opt out deliberately.
- This is Section 7's governance argument arriving early: ship the better thing as the default, not as advice.

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these by expected leverage in getting forty product teams to stop using a problematic palette — highest leverage first.
options: Publish a written colour guideline document
Ship the corrected palette as the default in the shared charting library
Run a lunch-and-learn on colour accessibility
Add a palette check to the design review checklist

optionFeedback.feedback: **Third.** Necessary as a reference and as something the review gate can point at — but read by a minority.
**First.** Defaults propagate to everyone, including teams that never read anything. This is the viridis lesson exactly.
**Last on leverage** — highest engagement per attendee, smallest and least durable reach. Not worthless: it builds the constituency that lets the other three survive.
**Second.** A recurring gate tied to shipping applies whether or not anyone remembers the training.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Note that the lunch-and-learn ranks last on **leverage**, not on value. Sessions like it are how you build the group of people who will defend the default when someone asks to override it. The ordering is about reach per unit of effort, not about worth.

Section 7 returns to this as the core of visualization governance.

interactionSequence.prompt: A senior colleague dismisses your palette proposal as 'a matter of taste, and I prefer ours.' Using this case as a model, what do you bring to the next conversation — and what do you deliberately not argue about?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Bring:** the luminance profile of both palettes side by side; both rendered in greyscale; both under a CVD simulation; and, if you can get it, thirty seconds of someone unfamiliar reading values off each. Every one of these is checkable by the other person, which is what makes them arguments rather than assertions.

**Do not argue about:** which palette is more attractive. You will lose that argument even if you win it, because you have accepted the framing that this is a preference question. The move is to concede the aesthetic point entirely — *"yours may well look better, and it produces bands readers will mistake for data"* — which puts the disagreement on ground where evidence exists.

This is the core of Section 7's critique material: **convert the status contest into an empirical question.**
hints: What could the other person check for themselves?
Which part of their claim can you simply concede?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you this would work in your organisation?

interactionSequence.prompt: What is the default in your own environment that nobody chose — a charting library palette, a template, a component's out-of-the-box settings? What would change if it were corrected?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Common answers: the default categorical palette in whichever BI tool the company standardised on; the default axis behaviour of a charting component, which frequently truncates baselines automatically; slide template chart styles carrying 3D and gradient fills; a design system's chart component that offers no threshold reference line, so nobody adds one.

That last pattern is worth noticing — **defaults shape output by omission as much as by commission.** A component that makes a good practice unavailable suppresses it more effectively than any guideline could encourage it.

workedExamples.problem: Build the evidence pack that would win the rainbow-versus-viridis argument in your own organisation, without relying on anyone's authority.
steps: **Extract the luminance profile of both ramps.** Plot luminance against position along the scale. Viridis rises monotonically; the rainbow rises and falls. This single chart is the whole argument in one image, and it requires no expertise to read.
**Render a real figure from your product in both palettes.** Use actual data, not a gradient strip — the artifact under discussion should be one your audience recognises.

**Convert both to greyscale.** The viridis version remains readable because luminance carried the ordering. The rainbow version becomes ambiguous, with mid-scale values appearing lighter than the extremes.

**Run both through a CVD simulator** for deuteranopia and protanopia. Note specifically what distinction collapses, in domain terms — not 'colours look similar' but 'high and low readings become indistinguishable'.
**Time three colleagues reading values off each version.** Five minutes of work. Report accuracy, not opinion.

**Name the legitimate counter-case yourself, before anyone else does.** If your product genuinely has a task requiring many discriminable bands, say so and propose the rainbow as an opt-in for that view. Raising the opposing argument first is what makes the rest of the pack credible.
**Propose the change as a default, with an override.** Not a ban.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**Six pieces of evidence, roughly ninety minutes of work, and none of it requires anyone to accept your judgment.**

That is the whole model this section has been building toward. The luminance profile, the greyscale render, the CVD simulation and the timing test are all things the other person can verify or repeat. A preference cannot be verified, which is why arguing from preference puts you at the mercy of whoever outranks you.

Note the final two steps especially. Naming the counter-case yourself and proposing a default rather than a prohibition are what turn a correct argument into an adopted one — and the difference between those two outcomes is most of what distinguishes a design lead from a designer who is right.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why did changing a library default change more behaviour than years of published critique? State the general principle.
Name three pieces of portable evidence you can bring to a colour dispute, and say what makes each one portable.

learningExperiences.title: Section quiz: perception and visual encoding

contentBlocks.content: Answer from memory. This section supplies the evidence base you will draw on for the rest of the course — Section 4 selects chart forms with it, Section 6 audits with it, and Section 7 defends decisions with it. Confident errors here propagate.

contentBlocks.title: How this is scored
contentBlocks.content: These items are formative and shape your review queue. The graded assessments for this section are `assess-visual-perception` and `assess-encoding-effectiveness`, which run after this check.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Because people disagree about which charts look better, the channel effectiveness ranking is essentially a matter of taste.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Individual judgments vary, but aggregate error rates by channel have been measured in controlled experiments and replicated at scale. Variation between people is not the absence of a reliable effect.
Correct. The ranking reports measured aggregate accuracy, replicated since 1984. Disagreement about appearance is a different question from how accurately people read magnitudes.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. The ranking reports measured aggregate accuracy, replicated since 1984. Disagreement about appearance is a different question from how accurately people read magnitudes.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Adding a second highlight colour makes both highlights easier to find.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Pop-out depends on the highlight being unique on its distinguishing attribute. A second highlight makes both weaker, and enough of them return the viewer to serial search.
Correct. Highlighting works by subtraction — emphasis is a budget of roughly one per view, and adding to it spends it.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Highlighting works by subtraction — emphasis is a budget of roughly one per view, and adding to it spends it.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** A perceptually uniform colour scale requires luminance to change monotonically across the ramp.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Luminance is the channel humans read ordinally, so if it rises and falls, mid-scale bright bands appear as false features in the data.
Incorrect. Monotonic luminance is precisely the requirement — it is what makes equal data steps produce equal perceived steps, and what makes the ramp survive greyscale.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Luminance is the channel humans read ordinally, so if it rises and falls, mid-scale bright bands appear as false features in the data.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** The effectiveness ranking applies in the same order to nominal data as to quantitative data.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. For nominal data the ordering roughly inverts: hue and shape are strong identity channels, while position and length imply magnitude that categories do not have.
Correct. The ranking measures quantitative magnitude judgment. For categories it effectively inverts, which is why hue is the right channel for identity and the wrong one for ratios.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. The ranking measures quantitative magnitude judgment. For categories it effectively inverts, which is why hue is the right channel for identity and the wrong one for ratios.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** If an encoding fails expressiveness, a sufficiently accurate channel can compensate.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Expressiveness is a precondition, not a trade-off. A precisely-read false claim is worse than an imprecisely-read true one.
Correct. Expressiveness comes first: the encoding must convey all and only the structure in the data before accuracy is even considered.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Expressiveness comes first: the encoding must convey all and only the structure in the data before accuracy is even considered.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Selecting a colour-vision-safe palette is enough to make a chart's colour usage accessible.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. A safe palette addresses one condition. Contrast, redundant non-colour encoding, pointer-free access to values and text alternatives all remain open — Section 6 covers them.
Correct. Palette choice is one requirement among several, and a CVD-safe chart whose meaning still rests on hue alone has not solved the problem.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Palette choice is one requirement among several, and a CVD-safe chart whose meaning still rests on hue alone has not solved the problem.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Whitespace between bars is a spacing preference rather than an encoding decision.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Proximity groups. Gap sizes determine which bars viewers see as belonging together, which is a claim about the data whether or not it was intended.
Correct. Proximity is always operating, so gap size is a data-semantic decision — in grouped bars the between-group gap must be clearly larger than the within-group gap.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Proximity is always operating, so gap size is a data-semantic decision — in grouped bars the between-group gap must be clearly larger than the within-group gap.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** An analyst proposes encoding a scatterplot's third variable — region, seven categories — as point size, 'so the important regions look important.' In two or three sentences, diagnose the proposal and say what you would do instead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Diagnosis:** region is nominal and size is an ordered channel, so the encoding asserts magnitude and ranking among categories that have neither — an **expressiveness** failure, which disqualifies rather than trades off.

**The second problem:** 'look important' reveals that the real goal is emphasis, not encoding. Importance is an editorial judgment about which region matters, not a property of the variable, and smuggling it into the data encoding makes it invisible and unchallengeable.

**Instead:** identity goes on hue, or — at seven categories with overplotting risk — into faceting, which Section 4 covers. If one region genuinely warrants emphasis, spend the single pop-out on it explicitly and mute the rest, so the editorial choice is visible as a choice.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** State the two-step check that catches the most common enterprise dashboard encoding failure, and give one example of the failure.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**The check:** (1) Which variable does the decision depend on? (2) Where does that variable sit on the effectiveness ranking?

**The failure:** the decision variable sits on a low-ranked channel while a context variable occupies a high-ranked one. The canonical example is the KPI tile grid — the quantity everyone is deciding on encoded as tile fill colour (rank 7), while position on the grid encodes nothing at all, or encodes alphabetical order.

The fix is nearly always the same: sort by the decision variable and put it on position. It usually makes the dashboard less pretty and much more useful, which is a trade you should be prepared to defend explicitly rather than hoping nobody notices.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which item here did you answer confidently and get wrong? Name the belief you held instead — that is what your review queue will target.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The two that most often catch experienced designers are the nominal-inversion item and the expressiveness item. The first because the ranking is usually taught as a single list without its scope, and the second because 'trade-off' is such a natural way for designers to think about competing constraints that a hard precondition feels unfamiliar.

Both reappear immediately: Section 4 uses expressiveness as the first elimination step when generating a viable set of chart forms, so a shaky grasp of it will show up there within the hour.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the encoding procedure in order: classify, then what, then what?

sections.title: Chart Selection and Composition
sections.description: Forms are composed, not chosen from a catalogue. Introduces the grammar of graphics as the unifying abstraction, the four selection inputs and the viable-set discipline, composition strategies including small multiples and their shared-scale requirement, density handling, designed tables as a first-class form, and the learning-cost test that governs when novelty is justified.

learningObjectives.description: Decompose any chart into data, transform, mark, encoding, scale, guide and facet, and identify which component a proposed change actually alters.
Given a dataset and analytic task, generate a viable set of three genuinely different forms and defend a selection on task fit, audience and encoding accuracy rather than convention.
Eliminate rejected candidates with named mechanisms rather than comparative adjectives, and identify the runner-up.
Apply small multiples, faceting and layering to multivariate or high-cardinality data, maintaining shared scales and justifying panel order.
Diagnose overplotting as a distortion and select an appropriate density remedy for the stated task.
Determine when a designed table is the correct form, and specify the alignment, sorting and in-cell marks that make it designed.
Apply the novelty test to determine whether a custom encoding is warranted, and state the learning cost it imposes on the specific audience.
Design a defensible visualization for a dataset from an unfamiliar domain, reasoning from structure and task rather than from domain precedent.

motivationHooks.prompt:
This is the pivot of the course. Sections 1 to 3 gave you three independent constraint systems — what the data permits, what the numbers mean, and what the eye can do. **This section is the first place you must satisfy all three at once, under pressure, with a stakeholder waiting.**

It is also where the gap between a designer and a design lead becomes visible. A designer picks a chart. A lead generates the viable set, eliminates its members with stated reasons, and can explain in one sentence why the survivor beat the runner-up.

That capability is what makes you useful in a room where a director wants a treemap and a data scientist wants a violin plot: you are the only person who can adjudicate on grounds both of them accept.

It is also where the most seductive failure lives. Custom, novel, signature visualizations are how visualization work gets noticed — and how it gets quietly ignored by the people who were supposed to use it.

The test in this section will tell you which one you are building, and it says yes often enough that it is not a rule about taste.

Hold this and test it as you go:

> **A national grid operator has one dataset: two years of hourly demand, generation by source, price and temperature. Three people ask for 'a view of how renewables are performing' — a regulator, a control-room operator, and a trader.**

Write one line now: can one well-designed artifact serve all three? If you think not, name the property of their requests that makes it impossible.

**The resolution.** No — and the reason is not that the data is insufficient. The data is identical for all three.

Their **tasks** differ (trend, deviation, correlation-plus-distribution), their **modes** differ (explanatory, glanceable, exploratory), and their **surfaces** differ (print, a wall display read at four metres, dual monitors). Every one of those pairs has inverted requirements.

If you predicted that one artifact could work with enough interactivity, note what the control-room surface does to that idea: an operator under time pressure at four metres cannot interact, and Section 7 will show that most viewers of any dashboard never do.

**The structural point:** data structure is identical across all three, so anything that selects a form from structure alone — every chart-chooser flowchart ever printed — produces one answer where three are needed. **Structure eliminates; task selects.** That five-word rule is what this section is built on.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following.

**Charts are compositions, not species.** Data, transform, mark, encoding, scale, guide, facet. Forms that seem categorically different usually differ by one or two components — and naming which ones exposes the real cost, as stacking exposes the loss of the common baseline.

**Structure eliminates; task selects.** Audience and delivery surface adjust and eliminate again. Chart-chooser flowcharts fail because they see only the first input.

**The deliverable is the viable set, not the winner.** Two to four genuinely different candidates, eliminated with named mechanisms, and an explicitly identified runner-up.

**Superpose to compare series to each other; facet to see each series' shape.** Shared scales are mandatory, and independent panel scales are an integrity failure wearing a layout costume.

**There is no neutral representation.** Overplotting hides the distribution; summary statistics hide the shape. You are always choosing which structure to reveal.

**A designed table is a first-class form**, and novelty carries a learning cost paid by every viewer every time — justified only by naming the task a conventional form would prevent.
keyTakeaways: Decompose before you argue: which component are you actually changing, and what does it cost?
Generate three genuinely different candidates, not three variants of one.
Eliminate with mechanisms — baseline loss, legend ceiling, overplotting, cardinality, learning cost — never adjectives.
Name the runner-up and why it lost. That is what lets you adapt when the brief changes.
Facet for shape, superpose for comparison; shared scales always.
Sort facet panels by something meaningful — panel position is a free channel.
Overplotting is aggregation by ink opacity, done badly. Bin, blend, contour or facet.
Run the novelty test per audience: the same form is conventional for one reader and novel for another.

furtherReading.title: The Grammar of Graphics
furtherReading.citation: Wilkinson, L. (2005). 2nd edition, Springer.
furtherReading.author: Leland Wilkinson
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The origin of the decomposition this section opens with. Dense and more formal than most designers need — read the early chapters for the argument that charts are built rather than chosen, and leave the rest as reference.

furtherReading.title: Vega-Lite: A Grammar of Interactive Graphics
furtherReading.citation: Satyanarayan, A., Moritz, D., Wongsuphasawat, K. & Heer, J. (2017). IEEE TVCG, 23(1).
furtherReading.author: Arvind Satyanarayan, Dominik Moritz, Kanit Wongsuphasawat, Jeffrey Heer
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The most practical modern expression of the grammar, and worth reading even if you never write a line of Vega-Lite: its specification format is very close to the seven-row decomposition you will hand engineers in Section 7.

furtherReading.title: Envisioning Information, chapter on small multiples
furtherReading.citation: Tufte, E. (1990). Graphics Press.
furtherReading.author: Edward Tufte
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Still the clearest statement of why small multiples work. Read it for the argument rather than the aesthetics — the claim that a repeated structure lets the reader learn an encoding once is the whole basis for faceting.

furtherReading.title: Visualization Analysis and Design, Chapters 12–13
furtherReading.citation: Munzner, T. (2014). CRC Press.
furtherReading.author: Tamara Munzner
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The rigorous treatment of superposition versus juxtaposition versus partitioning, with explicit trade-off analysis. The chapter on reducing items and attributes covers the density material with more options than this section had room for.

furtherReading.title: Graphs in Statistical Analysis
furtherReading.citation: Anscombe, F. J. (1973). The American Statistician, 27(1), 17–21.
furtherReading.author: Frank Anscombe
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Four pages, and still the most efficient argument for plotting your data ever written. Read the original rather than the reproduced quartet image — the framing is what makes it land.

furtherReading.title: Same Stats, Different Graphs
furtherReading.citation: Matejka, J. & Fitzmaurice, G. (2017). ACM CHI.
furtherReading.author: Justin Matejka, George Fitzmaurice
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The Datasaurus Dozen. The method for generating datasets with matching statistics is as interesting as the result, and it makes the Anscombe point impossible to dismiss as a curiosity.

furtherReading.title: Scatterplot Matrix Techniques for Large N
furtherReading.citation: Carr, D. B., Littlefield, R. J., Nicholson, W. L. & Littlefield, J. S. (1987). JASA, 82(398).
furtherReading.author: Daniel Carr and colleagues
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The origin of hexagonal binning. Useful background on why binning is a statistical decision rather than a rendering trick — which is the argument you will need when someone calls it 'hiding the data'.

furtherReading.title: Show Me the Numbers: Designing Tables and Graphs to Enlighten
furtherReading.citation: Few, S. (2012). Show Me the Numbers, 2nd edition. Analytics Press.
furtherReading.author: Stephen Few
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The best available treatment of tables as a designed form — alignment, sorting, grouping, and when a table beats a graph. Dated in its visual examples and correct in its reasoning; read the table chapters specifically.

furtherReading.citation: Burn-Murdoch, J. and the FT Visual & Data Journalism team (2020).
furtherReading.author: John Burn-Murdoch
furtherReading.rationaleNote: A rare public record of chart-selection reasoning made under pressure, including the reversals. Read the team's published explanations alongside the charts themselves — the reasoning is the artifact worth studying.

learningExperiences.title: Charts are compositions, not species

contentBlocks.content:
A designer says: *"let's switch from a grouped bar chart to a stacked area chart."*

That sentence treats charts as **species** — as though you were choosing between a horse and a bicycle. It is the way almost everyone talks, and it makes two things impossible: reasoning precisely about what you are changing, and specifying the result to an engineer.

Charts are not species. They are **compositions**, and a grouped bar chart and a stacked area chart differ by exactly two components.

## The seven components

The **grammar of graphics** decomposes any chart into a small set of independent choices. Change one and you get a different chart; the rest stay put.

contentBlocks.caption: The grammar, with the questions each component answers
rows: None; aggregate to monthly; stack; bin; rank; smooth
Point, line, bar/rect, area, arc, path, text
Which variable goes on which channel?
x = month, y = demand, colour = source
How do data values map to channel values?
Linear, log, ordinal, sequential colour; domain and range
How does the reader decode the scale?
Axis, legend, gridline, reference line, direct label
Is this repeated across a variable?
None; one panel per source; grid by region × year

contentBlocks.title: What this buys you
contentBlocks.content:
**Precision in argument.** "Stacked area versus grouped bar" becomes: *transform gains a stacking step, mark changes from rect to area.* And now the real cost is visible — **stacking is what removes the common baseline from every series except the first**, which is a rank-1-to-rank-3 demotion on the effectiveness ranking from Section 3.

**Precision in specification.** An engineer cannot build from "a stacked area chart." They can build from the seven components, and Section 7 uses exactly this decomposition as the handoff format.

**Generativity.** Once forms are compositions, you can construct one that has no name. Change the mark on a bar chart from rect to point and you have a dot plot. Add a facet and you have small multiples. Nothing has to exist in a catalogue first.

contentBlocks.altText: Two charts of the same generation-by-source data. The grouped version places four source bars side by side in each month, all sharing the chart's baseline. The stacked version places them on top of one another; a highlighted line traces the moving baseline that the wind series must be read against, showing that only the bottom series retains a common origin.
contentBlocks.caption: One transform apart.

contentBlocks.content:
## Scale and guide are where the arguments actually happen

Two components deserve special attention because they carry most of the disputes you will have.

**Scale** is not a styling layer. It contains the domain (what range of data is shown), the transform (linear or log), and the mapping to channel values. Section 6's baseline arguments are scale arguments. Section 2's index base period is a scale argument. The choice to clamp outliers to an axis edge is a scale argument. When someone says a chart is misleading, they are usually objecting to a scale.

**Guide** is the reader's decoder. Axes, legends, gridlines, reference lines, direct labels. Sections 3 and 6 both live here: direct labelling instead of a legend is a guide decision, and the threshold reference line that converts an absolute judgment into a comparative one is a guide decision. Guides are the cheapest place in the whole grammar to buy comprehension, and the most frequently left at defaults.

terms.definition: The abstraction that treats any chart as a composition of data, transform, mark, channel encodings, scales, guides and faceting rather than as an indivisible type.
The geometric primitive a chart draws — point, line, bar, area, arc, path — one component of the grammar.
An axis, legend or annotation that lets a viewer decode a scale; the readable counterpart of an encoding.
The overall structural type of a visualization: bar, line, scatter, area, treemap, Sankey and so on.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Treating chart types as indivisible objects.** *(ee-chart-types-are-atomic)* — It hides which component you would actually change, and makes precise specification impossible.

**2. Thinking the grammar tells you which chart to build.** — It does not. It gives you a vocabulary for describing and modifying charts. **Selection** needs the four inputs in the next experience.

**3. Treating scale as styling.** — Domain, transform and clamping behaviour are analytical decisions with integrity consequences.

**4. Leaving guides at their defaults.** — Guides are the cheapest comprehension you can buy, and the component most often left untouched.

**5. Assuming the decomposition is unique.** — Some charts decompose more than one way, and that is fine. The value is in having *a* precise description, not the One True Parse.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Any chart decomposes into **data, transform, mark, encoding, scale, guide, facet**.
- Forms that seem categorically different usually differ by one or two components — and naming which ones exposes the real cost.
- **Stacking is a transform**, and its cost is the common baseline for every series but the first.
- **Scale** carries most integrity disputes; **guide** is the cheapest comprehension available and the most neglected.
- The grammar is a vocabulary for describing and modifying charts, not a procedure for choosing them.
- This decomposition is the specification format for engineering handoff in Section 7. Learn it here; use it there.

interactionSequence.prompt: Using the grammar, what is the difference between a grouped bar chart and a stacked bar chart of the same data?
options: A stacking transform is added; everything else — data, mark, encodings, scales — can stay the same.
They are different chart types and share no common structure.
The mark changes from bar to area.
The data must be reshaped from wide to long format.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct — and naming it as a transform exposes the cost immediately: stacking removes the common baseline from every series above the first.
They share six of seven components. Treating them as unrelated types is what makes the trade-off invisible.
The mark is rect in both. Changing the mark to area would give you a stacked *area* chart, which is a further step.
Both forms are built from the same tidy data; reshaping is an implementation detail, not a grammar difference.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the whole payoff in one example. "Should we group or stack?" sounds like a preference question. **"Should we add a stacking transform, given that it costs the common baseline for five of our six series?"** is a question with an answer, and the answer depends on whether the task is reading the total or reading each series.
hints: Which component would you edit to turn one into the other?
What does the mark do in each — is it actually different?

interactionSequence.prompt: Which grammar component carries most of the disputes about whether a chart is misleading?
options: Scale — domain, transform and clamping determine what range is shown and how values map to the channel.
Mark — whether the data is drawn as bars, lines or points.
Facet — how many panels the chart is split into.
Data — which rows were loaded.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Baseline arguments, log-versus-linear, index base periods and outlier clamping are all scale decisions, and Section 6 treats them as the core distortion mechanisms.
Mark choice matters for accuracy, but a bar and a line drawn on the same honest scale rarely differ in whether they mislead.
Faceting can mislead — independent panel scales are a real failure — but note that this is itself a *scale* problem showing up inside a facet.
Row selection genuinely can mislead, and Section 1 covered it as grain and range. It is a smaller share of chart-level disputes than scale.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Worth noticing about option C: independent facet scales are a scale failure wearing a layout costume. That is a general pattern with the grammar — once you decompose, apparently different problems turn out to be the same component misbehaving in different contexts, which is exactly what makes the vocabulary worth learning.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: decompose one chart from your current work into the seven components. Then name the single component you would change first, and what changing it would cost.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Two things people usually discover doing this. First, the **guide** row is often nearly empty — default axis, default legend, no reference line — which means the cheapest available improvement has not been made. Second, writing the **transform** row forces you to state what aggregation happened, and a surprising number of designers cannot answer that about charts they maintain, which is Section 1's grain problem surfacing again.

Keep this decomposition. You will use the same seven rows as the skeleton of an engineering specification in Section 7.

workedExamples.problem: A national grid operator has two years of hourly data: total demand, generation by source (six categories), wholesale price, and temperature. Decompose two candidate views of renewable performance into grammar components, and use the decomposition to expose their trade-offs.
steps: **Candidate A — stacked area of generation by source over time.** *Data:* hourly generation, aggregated to monthly. *Transform:* aggregate to month, then **stack** by source. *Mark:* area. *Encoding:* x = month, y = generation, colour = source. *Scale:* linear y from zero; categorical colour for six nominal sources. *Guide:* axis, legend. *Facet:* none.

**Candidate B — line of renewable share over time.** *Data:* hourly generation, aggregated to monthly. *Transform:* aggregate to month, then **compute renewable share** = renewable ÷ total. *Mark:* line. *Encoding:* x = month, y = share. *Scale:* linear y, 0–100%. *Guide:* axis, direct label, prior-year reference series. *Facet:* none.
**Compare the transform rows.** A stacks; B computes a ratio. That single difference determines what each can answer: A shows composition and total, B shows one derived quantity precisely.

**Price the stacking transform.** Only the bottom band of a stacked area sits on a common baseline. Every band above it is read against a wiggling baseline, so judging any individual source's trend requires comparing lengths without a shared origin — rank 1 down to something well below rank 3 in practice. **That is the cost of one transform, and it is invisible if you call this 'a stacked area chart'.**

**Price the encoding row in A.** Six nominal categories on colour is at the practical ceiling for a legend, and it forces a working-memory round-trip per lookup (Section 3). B uses one series and needs no legend at all.

**Note what B's guide row buys.** A prior-year reference series converts "is 31% good?" into "is this above or below the grey line?" — an absolute judgment becoming a comparative one, for the price of one guide component.
**State what each cannot do.** A cannot support precise per-source trend. B cannot show which renewable source drove the change, and cannot show total demand at all.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The decomposition converted a style question into a costed comparison.**

Neither chart is better in the abstract. A answers *what is the generation mix and how large is total demand*; B answers *is renewable share rising*. The grammar made the difference precise — one transform, one encoding row, one guide row — and made each cost nameable rather than felt.

Notice what the grammar did **not** do: it did not tell you which to build. Six components could have gone either way and the decomposition is silent on which is right. That decision needs the four selection inputs, which is the next experience.

Also note that these seven rows, filled in like this, are already most of an engineering specification. Section 7 adds state behaviour and responsive rules; the encoding logic is here.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the seven grammar components, in order.
Which grammar component does stacking belong to, and what does it cost?
Which component carries most 'this chart is misleading' disputes, and name three decisions it contains.

learningExperiences.title: Generating candidates and eliminating them with reasons

contentBlocks.content:
## Why chart-chooser flowcharts fail

You have seen the posters. *How many variables? Is one of them time? → line chart.*

They fail for one reason: **they key off data structure alone**, and data structure is necessary and radically insufficient.

The grid dataset from the last experience has one structure — a time series with a categorical breakdown. Here are three people who need something from it:

- **Regulator, quarterly report.** *Has renewable share risen year on year?* → **trend**, explanatory, print and PDF.
- **Control room, live.** *Is generation matching demand right now, and where is the margin?* → **deviation**, glanceable, wall display.
- **Trading desk, analysis.** *Under what temperature and wind conditions does price spike?* → **correlation** and **distribution**, exploratory, dual monitors.

Identical structure. Three different correct answers. A flowchart cannot produce that, because the variables that decide are not in its inputs.

contentBlocks.caption: The four selection inputs and what each does
rows: What forms this audience reads fluently

contentBlocks.title: Structure eliminates; task selects
contentBlocks.content:
That five-word rule is the core of this section.

Cardinality rules out a legend at 340 categories. Nominal scale rules out a position axis. A print surface rules out hover. **None of these tell you what to build** — they narrow the field.

What picks the winner from the survivors is the **task**: which judgment must the viewer make. And what makes your choice defensible is being able to name **the runner-up and why it lost**.

## The viable set discipline

**Generate two to four genuinely different candidates. Eliminate all but one with reasons that name a mechanism.**

Three rules make it work:

**Genuinely different.** Three variants of one idea is not a viable set. If all your candidates share a mark and a transform, you have generated one option and coloured it three ways.

**Mechanisms, not adjectives.** "Less clear," "busier," "harder to read" are verdicts, not reasons. Name the mechanism: baseline loss, legend ceiling, overplotting, cardinality, learning cost, expressiveness failure, occlusion. A mechanism can be checked; an adjective can only be disputed.

**Name the runner-up.** If you cannot say which option came second and why it lost, you did not run a selection — you had a preference and worked backwards. The runner-up is also what you reach for when the brief changes, which happens constantly.

terms.definition: The two to four defensible chart forms generated before selection, from which one is chosen with stated reasons and a named runner-up.
The overall structural type of a visualization: bar, line, scatter, area, treemap, Sankey and so on.
The decoding effort a non-standard encoding imposes on every viewer on every viewing, paid repeatedly while the benefit accrues once.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Selecting from a chart-chooser flowchart.** *(csc-flowchart-decides)* — Flowcharts see structure and are blind to task, audience and surface — the variables that actually decide among structurally valid options.

**2. Generating three variants of one idea.** — A viable set needs genuinely different candidates, or the elimination step is theatre.

**3. Eliminating with adjectives.** — "Cluttered" cannot be checked or defended. Name the mechanism.

**4. Choosing the form before recovering the decision.** *(atf-chart-type-is-requirement)* — The Section 1 error, recurring here in more expensive form because now you have built something.

**5. Applying context-free verdicts.** *(ee-pie-bad-bar-good)* — "Never use pie charts" eliminates without reference to task, which is the same defect as the flowchart.

**6. Not knowing your runner-up.** — Then you cannot adapt when the surface or audience changes, and you cannot defend the choice under challenge.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Four inputs: **structure** (eliminates), **task** (selects), **audience and convention** and **delivery surface** (adjust and eliminate again).
- Chart-chooser flowcharts fail because they see only the first one.
- Generate **two to four genuinely different** candidates, then eliminate with **named mechanisms**.
- Mechanisms are checkable: baseline loss, legend ceiling, overplotting, cardinality, learning cost, expressiveness failure.
- **Name the runner-up and why it lost.** That is the deliverable, not the winner alone.
- Anticipate the follow-up question — where its answer lives is a design decision, not a courtesy.

interactionSequence.prompt: The three grid stakeholders above all want 'a view of how renewables are performing' from the same dataset. **Predict:** could one well-designed artifact serve all three? Answer yes or no with one line of reasoning.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The tasks are trend, deviation, and correlation-plus-distribution; the modes are explanatory, glanceable, and exploratory; the surfaces are print, wall display, and dual monitors. Every one of those pairs has inverted requirements.

This is the Section 1 fork arriving with teeth: an artifact serving all three would need to be simultaneously constrained to one reading and open to many, and legible at four metres and at arm's length. Three artifacts is not a failure to consolidate — it is the correct answer.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which of these is a valid elimination reason in a viable-set write-up?
options: Rejected: stacking removes the common baseline for five of six series, and the task is per-source trend.
Rejected: too cluttered for this audience.
Rejected: pie charts are not appropriate for professional reporting.
Rejected: the team has not used this form before.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. It names a mechanism, ties it to the stated task, and can be checked by anyone who knows the effectiveness ranking.
'Cluttered' is a verdict, not a reason. It cannot be checked, and it invites a preference argument you have no evidence for.
A context-free chart verdict eliminates without reference to task — the same defect as a chart-chooser flowchart.
Unfamiliarity is a real cost — it is the learning-cost input — but stated this way it is an appeal to habit rather than an estimate of what the cost buys.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
A useful test on your own write-ups: **could a reader disagree with this reason by checking something?** If yes, it is a mechanism. If the only possible response is "I don't find it cluttered," you have written a preference.

Note that option D is close to legitimate. "Rejected: this form imposes a learning cost on a quarterly audience who will see it four times a year, and the accuracy gain over a sorted bar chart is small" **is** a mechanism-based rejection. The difference is estimating the cost against the benefit rather than invoking habit.

interactionSequence.prompt: A public-health agency must show the trend in vaccination rate for **each of nine districts** to a mixed technical audience in an interactive web report. Rank these forms from most to least suitable.
options: Stacked area chart
Small multiples with shared scales
Superposed line chart with a nine-item colour legend
One pie chart per district

optionFeedback.feedback: **Third.** Stacking sacrifices the common baseline for eight of nine districts, defeating the per-district trend judgment — and stacking rates is arithmetically meaningless anyway, since they do not sum to anything.
**First.** The task is per-series shape at a cardinality above the legend ceiling; faceting handles both.
**Second.** Supports trend and cross-district comparison, but occlusion and nine-item legend round-trips degrade it noticeably.
**Last.** A part-to-whole form applied to a trend task is a category error — it cannot represent change over time at all.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Note what drives the entire ordering: the stated task (per-district trend) and the cardinality (nine). Change the task to "total coverage and composition" and the stacked area rises sharply.

That is precisely why a chart-chooser flowchart cannot produce this ranking — it sees a time series with a categorical breakdown and emits one recommendation, having never been told what anyone needs to judge.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: take a chart you shipped recently and write its elimination note — the runner-up form, and the named mechanism that ruled it out. If you never generated a runner-up, say what you would have considered.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Most designers find they did not generate a viable set — they arrived at a form quickly, and it was often the right form. That is not a failure of judgment; experienced instinct is usually good. The problem is that an instinct cannot be **defended**, **adapted**, or **taught**, and a design lead needs all three.

The runner-up is also load-bearing practically: when a stakeholder says "this needs to work on mobile too," the person who knows why the second option lost can answer in thirty seconds. The person who does not starts over.

workedExamples.problem: Build the regulator's chart: trend in renewable share, year over year, for a print and PDF regulatory report.
steps: **Structure — eliminate.** Time (ordered, ~17,500 hourly points per source), source (nominal, 6), generation (ratio). The hourly cardinality immediately rules out any form needing one distinguishable mark per hour.

**Re-grain to the task.** "Year over year" does not need hourly resolution. Monthly preserves seasonality — which matters enormously for wind and solar — and yields 24 points per source. This is a Section 1 decision made in service of the task, not for convenience.

**Generate three genuinely different candidates.** **(a)** Stacked area of generation by source over time. **(b)** Line of renewable share over time, with prior-year overlay. **(c)** Small multiples, one panel per source, shared y-scale.

**Eliminate (a).** Only the bottom band sits on a common baseline; judging any individual source's trend means comparing lengths without a shared origin. It does show total demand and composition well. **Verdict: strong for total and mix, weak for the stated task.**

**Eliminate (c).** Excellent for per-source trend comparison — but it answers a question the regulator did not ask, and costs six panels of report space. **Verdict: right answer to a different question.**

**Select (b).** Puts the exact quantity the decision hinges on — renewable share — on position along a common scale, rank 1. Single series, so no legend round-trip. Direct-labelled, so it survives greyscale print.

**Adjust for audience and surface.** Regulators read line charts fluently, so no learning cost. Print means no hover and possible greyscale reproduction — both favouring a single direct-labelled series over anything hue-dependent.
**Anticipate the follow-up.** The regulator's first question after seeing (b) will be *"driven by which source?"* Keep **(c)** as an appendix figure.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**Selected: (b), a share-over-time line with the prior year as a muted reference series, direct-labelled. Runner-up: (a), rejected because stacking sacrifices the common baseline the primary judgment requires.**

That sentence is the deliverable. It names the winner, the loser and the mechanism, and it can be defended to anyone.

Two further points. First, the re-graining in step 2 did more work than the form choice — most of the design happened before any candidate was generated.
