Second, keeping (c) for the appendix is not politeness: **anticipating the follow-up question and deciding where its answer lives is a design decision**, and the alternative is being asked for it in the meeting and having nothing.

fadedVariant.problem: The control room needs the second view: *is generation matching demand right now, and where is the margin?* Deviation task, glanceable, wall display read at four metres by operators under time pressure, updating every five minutes. Work the same procedure.
givenSteps: The same underlying dataset is available at any grain, including live.
The task is deviation — margin against demand — with a secondary ranking of where the margin is thinnest.
blankedStepPrompts: Which structural or surface constraints eliminate options before any candidate is generated?
Generate three genuinely different candidates, one line each.
Select one and name the mechanism that decides it.
Name the runner-up and the mechanism that ruled it out.
blankedStepAnswers: **Surface eliminates hardest here.** Four-metre viewing distance rules out anything requiring small marks, dense labels or precise value reading — so no scatterplots, no tables, no multi-series legends. Time pressure rules out any form needing interaction or interpretation. The five-minute refresh means the form must be stable under updating: anything whose scale rebases on new data will make the display jump, so the scale domain must be **fixed**, not data-driven. Structure contributes less than usual, since the grain is whatever we choose.

**(a)** A single large gauge or bullet chart of current margin against demand, with threshold bands. **(b)** A sorted bar chart of margin by region or interconnector, worst first, with a threshold reference line. **(c)** A dual-line chart of generation and demand over the last six hours, with the gap shaded.

**Select (b)**, the sorted bar with threshold line — or (a) if a single system-wide number genuinely suffices. The deciding mechanism is that the task is **deviation plus a secondary ranking**: operators need to know not only whether margin is adequate but *where* it is thinnest, and only (b) supports both. Length on a common baseline is rank 1–3, readable at four metres, and the threshold line converts an absolute judgment into a comparative one that needs no domain arithmetic under pressure.

**Runner-up: (c)**, the dual-line trend. Rejected because reading a *gap between two lines* is a length judgment without a common baseline — the same demotion stacking causes — and at four metres under time pressure the operator must estimate a difference rather than see a state. It remains the right form for the post-incident review, where the question becomes *how did we get here*, which is trend rather than deviation. **(a)** is rejected as the third option because a single system-wide gauge answers 'is there margin' and discards 'where', which is the operator's actual next action.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the four selection inputs and say what role each plays — eliminate, select or adjust.
Why can a chart-chooser flowchart not produce the right answer? Name what it sees and what it is blind to.
List five named mechanisms you can use to eliminate a candidate form, and say what makes a mechanism different from an adjective.
Why is naming the runner-up part of the deliverable rather than an academic exercise? Give two practical reasons.

transferExercises.context: Museum visitor research — no energy-sector vocabulary transfers.
transferExercises.scenario: A large museum has 18 months of anonymised indoor-positioning data: one row per visitor per gallery-entry event, with visit_id, gallery_id (32 galleries), entry_time and dwell_seconds. The curatorial director asks for 'something showing how people move through the building' ahead of a decision about relocating a major exhibit.
transferExercises.task: Produce: **(a)** the decision question and the analytic tasks it implies; **(b)** a viable set of three genuinely different forms, one line each on what it makes visible and what it hides; **(c)** your selection, your runner-up, and the named mechanism that ruled the runner-up out; **(d)** one property of this dataset's missingness that could invalidate the whole analysis.
successCriteria: The decision line contains an action verb.
Three candidates are structurally different, not three variants of one idea.
Every elimination names a mechanism rather than an adjective.
The runner-up is explicitly identified.
The missingness point recognises that a visitor outside all sensor ranges produces no rows — absence of data is not absence of visitors.
No reliance on museum-sector precedent.

learningExperiences.title: When one view isn't enough

contentBlocks.content: Three ways to use more than one view, in increasing order of what they ask from the viewer.

contentBlocks.caption: Composition strategies and their costs
rows: One form repeated across a categorical variable, on **shared scales**
The task is seeing each series' **shape**
Screen space; cross-series comparison becomes harder
Series overlaid in one coordinate space
The task is comparing a **few** series to **each other**
Occlusion and legend load past 4–5 series
Different forms side by side, usually coordinated
Viewer must learn each encoding separately and join them mentally

contentBlocks.title: The rule that settles most arguments
contentBlocks.content:
**Superpose when the task is comparing series to each other. Facet when the task is seeing each series' shape.**

One sentence, and it resolves the majority of composition disputes you will have. Everything else — cardinality, space, occlusion — is a secondary constraint on top of it.

## Small multiples are the most underused technique in product design

Their power is perceptual, not aesthetic. Because every panel is structurally identical, the viewer learns the encoding **once** and then performs pure pattern comparison across panels — no legend, no round-trip, no colour discrimination.

That is why faceting scales gracefully to dozens of categories where a legend collapses at six. It is the single best answer to high cardinality, and designers reach for it far less often than they should because it looks less impressive in a review than one dense chart.

**Shared scales are not optional.** Panels with independent y-scales look comparable and are not. The grid layout itself makes a comparison claim — proximity and similarity from Section 3 are doing the work — and independent scales invalidate that claim while leaving it visually intact. That is an integrity failure hiding inside a layout choice, and Section 6 treats it as one.

If shared scales flatten some panels, **that flatness is the finding**, not a problem to style away.

contentBlocks.altText: Above: nine series superposed on one axis with a nine-item colour legend; lines cross and occlude one another and no individual shape is readable. Below: the same nine series as small multiples on shared scales, each panel showing one series in dark ink against the other eight drawn in light grey for context, sorted so the grid also conveys ranking. No legend is required.
contentBlocks.caption: Superpose to compare series; facet to see each series' shape.

contentBlocks.altText: Four regional trend panels shown twice. On shared scales, Region A sits high, Region D sits very low, and their differing growth is visible. With each panel scaled to its own data, all four lines look near-identical in slope and position, concealing that Region A grew by eight units while Region D grew by two.
contentBlocks.caption: Independent panel scales: comparable-looking, not comparable.

contentBlocks.content:
## The superposition ceiling

Superposition degrades fast past about four or five series, for two independent reasons that compound:

**Occlusion.** Lines cross and hide one another; later-drawn series obscure earlier ones. Which series is on top is a rendering-order decision that becomes a data-visibility decision.

**Legend load.** Section 3's working-memory round-trip, once per lookup, times the number of series. Past six, viewers stop consulting and start guessing.

The transition point is therefore not arbitrary: **when superposition passes the legend ceiling, move to faceting.** You lose direct cross-series comparison and gain per-series legibility, which is the trade the rule above describes.

A hybrid worth knowing: facet, and in each panel draw all the other series in light grey behind the highlighted one. Each panel then supports both shape and context, at the cost of ink.

terms.definition: Repetition of one chart form across values of a categorical variable, on shared scales, so the viewer learns the encoding once and then compares patterns.
Identical axis domains across faceted panels, without which the panels look comparable and are not.
Overlaying multiple data series within a single coordinate space; suited to comparing a small number of series to each other.
Placing different chart forms side by side, usually coordinated; powerful but expensive, since the viewer must learn each encoding separately.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Faceting with independent scales.** *(csc-flowchart-decides — structure-only thinking)* — Panels that look comparable and are not. The layout makes a claim the scales invalidate.

**2. Superposing more than about five series.** — Occlusion plus legend load. Past the ceiling, facet.

**3. Reaching for juxtaposition first.** — It is the most expensive strategy, because the viewer must learn two encodings and join them. Try faceting before you try two different forms.

**4. Treating panel order as arbitrary.** — Sorting facets by a meaningful quantity turns a grid into a ranking for free. Alphabetical order throws that away.

**5. Styling away an inconvenient flat panel.** — If shared scales make a panel look flat, the panel *is* flat relative to its peers. That is information.

**6. Assuming faceting always costs space.** — Nine tiny panels frequently occupy less area than one chart with nine legible superposed series and a legend.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **Superpose to compare series to each other; facet to see each series' shape.**
- Small multiples work because the viewer learns the encoding once, then compares patterns — which is why they scale past the legend ceiling.
- **Shared scales are mandatory.** Independent panel scales are an integrity failure wearing a layout costume.
- Superposition degrades past 4–5 series through occlusion and legend load.
- Sort facets by a meaningful quantity; the grid becomes a ranking at no cost.
- Juxtaposition is the most expensive strategy — the viewer learns two encodings and joins them mentally. It is dashboard territory, covered in Section 7.

interactionSequence.prompt: A logistics team wants to compare month-over-month shipment volume for fourteen distribution centres, seeing the shape of each centre's year. Which composition strategy is correct?
options: Small multiples — fourteen panels on shared scales — because the task is per-series shape and faceting scales past the legend ceiling.
A single line chart with all fourteen series superposed and a colour legend.
Small multiples with each panel scaled to its own data, so every centre's pattern is clearly visible.
A stacked area chart, so total volume is visible alongside each centre.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct on both counts: the task is per-series shape, and fourteen categories is far beyond the working-memory ceiling for legend use.
Occlusion plus a fourteen-item legend forces repeated memory round-trips; superposition is for comparing a few series to each other.
The most dangerous option here. Independent scales make panels look comparable while destroying comparability — the layout makes a claim the scales invalidate.
Only the bottom band has a common baseline; the other thirteen are read against a wiggling one, which is exactly the judgment this task requires.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Option C is worth dwelling on because it is the one experienced designers pick. It comes from a good instinct — every panel should be legible — applied to the wrong level. The panels become individually legible and jointly meaningless, and nothing on the screen signals that to the reader.

When shared scales flatten some panels, the honest move is to say so in the subtitle: *"panels share a common scale; five centres are near-flat at this scale."*
hints: Is the task comparing centres to each other, or seeing each one's shape?
What does a grid layout imply to a reader about comparability?

interactionSequence.prompt: You are faceting sales performance into 24 panels, one per region. What ordering should the panels use?
options: Sorted by a meaningful quantity — total sales, or change since last year — so the grid also communicates a ranking.
Alphabetical, so readers can find a specific region quickly.
Geographic arrangement, so the layout resembles a map.
Random, to avoid implying a ranking that the data does not support.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Panel position is a free encoding channel, and leaving it unused wastes it. Sorted facets deliver shape and rank simultaneously.
Defensible **if** the primary task is lookup of a named region — which is a real task. But if the task is comparison, alphabetical order discards a free channel.
Sometimes excellent, and it is a genuine trade: geographic arrangement supports spatial reasoning at the cost of the ranking. Section 5 covers when geography earns its space.
Randomness does not avoid implying order — readers read grids in reading order regardless — it just makes the implied order meaningless.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The general principle: **position is always encoding something.** In a faceted grid, the reader will infer meaning from panel order whether or not you put meaning there. Your choice is between an ordering that carries information and one that carries an accident of the alphabet.

Note that option B is legitimately correct for a lookup task, which is the recurring lesson: task decides.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: find one chart in your product with more than five superposed series. Describe what would be gained and lost by faceting it, and say which you would choose given its actual task.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The common finding is that the multi-series chart exists because someone asked to "see them all together" — which sounds like a comparison task and usually is not. When you check what people actually do with it, they typically look at one series and glance at whether it is above or below the others, which faceting-with-grey-context serves better than superposition.

The usual objection is space. Test it rather than accepting it: nine small panels frequently occupy less area than one chart with nine legible series and a legend, because the legend and the whitespace needed to keep nine lines distinguishable are not free.

workedExamples.problem: A grid operator wants to show how each of six generation sources performed across 24 months. The current chart superposes six lines with a legend. Improve it.
steps: **Identify the task.** "How each source performed" is per-series shape — with an implicit secondary interest in relative size.
**Apply the rule.** Task is shape, not cross-series comparison, so **facet**.

**Check the cardinality against the ceiling.** Six series is right at the legend ceiling, which explains why the current chart is borderline usable rather than obviously broken. Faceting removes the legend entirely.
**Set shared scales.** All six panels share a y-domain covering the full range. Solar and wind will look small next to gas; that is true, and the shared scale is what makes it visible.
**Decide panel order.** Sort by total generation, descending. The grid now delivers ranking for free, in addition to shape.

**Recover the lost comparison.** Faceting costs direct cross-series comparison, which the secondary interest wanted. Add each panel's context: all six series drawn in light grey behind the highlighted one. Each panel now answers *what shape* and *how large relative to the others*.
**Handle the flat panels honestly.** If two sources are near-flat at the shared scale, state it in the subtitle rather than rescaling those panels.
**Check space.** Six panels at roughly a third the width of the original, in two rows, occupy comparable area to the original chart plus its legend.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The faceted version answers the stated task better and the secondary task about as well, without a legend.**

The grey-context trick is worth keeping: it is the standard answer to "but I lose the comparison," and it costs only ink. Note that it also removes the last dependence on hue — the highlighted series is distinguished by *being the dark one in its own panel*, which means the whole chart survives greyscale and colour-vision deficiency without any palette work at all.

That is the pattern to notice: a composition decision made for perceptual reasons in Section 3's terms also resolved an accessibility requirement from Section 6, without anyone designing for it. Good encoding decisions tend to compound.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the one-sentence rule for choosing between superposition and faceting.
What is the non-negotiable requirement when faceting, and why is violating it an integrity failure rather than a styling choice?
Name the two independent reasons superposition degrades past about five series.
Why is panel order in a faceted grid a free encoding channel, and when is alphabetical order nonetheless correct?

learningExperiences.title: Density, tables, and when to invent something

contentBlocks.content:
## Overplotting is a form of hiding

The trading desk wants to know under what temperature and wind conditions wholesale price spikes. The obvious form is a scatterplot: temperature on x, price on y, ~17,500 hourly points.

Predict the failure. At that density in a typical plot area, the dense central region saturates to solid ink. Everything about the **distribution** — where the mass is, what shape it has — is destroyed, while the sparse outliers remain fully visible.

**The chart systematically over-represents the rare and under-represents the typical.**

contentBlocks.title: "Show every point, it's more honest"
contentBlocks.content:
This is intuitive and wrong. An overplotted scatter is not showing you 17,500 points. It is showing you a black blob plus the outliers, and the viewer's impression of central tendency is being formed by an artifact of ink density.

**Deliberate aggregation with visible variance is frequently the more truthful representation.**

Nothing was lost from the *file*. Nearly everything was lost from the *reading*, and completeness is not communicativeness.

**Remedies, cheapest first:**

- **Alpha blending** — partial transparency so density accumulates. Simple, and still breaks at extreme density.
- **Two-dimensional binning** (hexbin or grid heatmap) — aggregate to cells, encode count by luminance. Density becomes explicit and quantified. Note this is a *deliberate* use of a low-ranked channel, justified by task exactly as Section 3 argued.
- **Density contours** — shows shape at the cost of hiding individual outliers, so pair with a sparse outlier layer.
- **Faceting by a third variable** — split by wind-output quartile. The conditional structure the trader actually asked about becomes directly readable.

contentBlocks.altText: Three scatterplots of the same 1,600 observations. The raw version shows a solid black mass through the dense central region with sparse outliers clearly visible above it. Alpha blending reveals gradation within the mass. Two-dimensional binning encodes count per cell as colour intensity, making density explicit and quantified, with the extreme price events restored as distinct red marks on top.
contentBlocks.caption: Overplotting hides the distribution and keeps the outliers.

contentBlocks.content:
## The other direction: Anscombe

**Anscombe's quartet** is four datasets with nearly identical means, variances, correlation and regression line, whose scatterplots are wildly different — one linear, one curved, one linear with a single outlier, one essentially a vertical line plus a leverage point. The **Datasaurus Dozen** extended this by constructing datasets with matching summary statistics that plot as, among other things, a dinosaur.

*Lesson: summary statistics without a plot conceal structure.*

The overplotting case is the mirror image. *Lesson: plotting without aggregation can also conceal structure.*

**The reconciliation: you are always choosing which structure to make visible. There is no neutral representation.** A lead's job is to know which structure the task requires, choose deliberately, and say so out loud when defending it.

contentBlocks.altText: Four scatterplots with the same fitted regression line. The first is a loose linear relationship. The second is a clean curve, not a line at all. The third is a tight straight line with one distant outlier pulling the fit. The fourth has all points at a single x value except one far-right point that alone determines the slope. All four share the same means, variances, correlation and regression line.
contentBlocks.caption: Anscombe's quartet — identical summary statistics.

contentBlocks.content:
## Tables are a first-class form

A well-designed table is frequently the correct answer, and the effectiveness ranking predicts why: **when the task is looking up a precise individual value, reading a number beats decoding any graphical channel.**

Tables also handle what no single chart can — mixed units and heterogeneous metrics in one view, which is most of what finance and operations actually need.

A **designed table** is not a data dump. It uses:

- **Right-aligned numerals** with consistent decimal places, so digits line up and magnitude is readable by column width
- **Deliberate sorting**, by the quantity the decision turns on
- **In-cell marks** — sparklines, small bars, direction arrows — adding shape without leaving the row
- **Restrained rules and grouping**, using proximity rather than borders
- **Emphasis spent once**, exactly as in any other chart

Falling back to a table is not a failure to visualize. Choosing one for a lookup task is the same discipline as choosing a bar chart for a comparison task.

contentBlocks.altText: A five-row cost-centre table with right-aligned figures at consistent decimal places, a twelve-month sparkline in each row, and a percentage change column in which only the two rows exceeding ten percent are emphasised. Rules are light, rows are sorted, and emphasis is spent once.
contentBlocks.caption: A designed table is a chart.

contentBlocks.content:
## Novelty and learning cost

Every non-standard encoding imposes a **learning cost**: the viewer must decode the mapping before extracting any information, and re-pays some of it on each return visit.

Conventional forms — bar, line, scatter, table — have near-zero learning cost for professional audiences. That is not a small advantage. Two consequences:

- **A conventional chart that supports the task beats a custom chart that supports it slightly better.** The margin must be large, because the cost is paid by every viewer every time while the benefit accrues once to the designer.
- **Novelty is justified when no conventional form supports the task.** Genuine cases exist: hierarchical part-to-whole at depth, flow between states at scale, network structure, high-dimensional comparison. Notice these are cases where the *data's structure* has no conventional representation — not cases where the designer wanted something fresher. Section 5 is entirely about them.

**The test to apply to yourself:** *if I chose the conventional form instead, what specific task would the viewer be unable to perform?* If you cannot name it in one sentence, choose the conventional form.

terms.definition: Marks obscuring one another at high density, destroying the visible distribution while preserving outliers.
Partial mark transparency so that overlapping marks accumulate into visible density.
Aggregating points into spatial cells, often hexagonal, and encoding the count, which makes density explicit and quantified.
Four datasets with nearly identical summary statistics whose plots are radically different; the standard demonstration that statistics without a plot conceal structure.
A table treated as a first-class visualization form, using alignment, sorting, grouping and in-cell marks to support precise value retrieval and heterogeneous metrics.
The decoding effort a non-standard encoding imposes on every viewer on every viewing, paid repeatedly while the benefit accrues once.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Plotting every raw point in the belief that it is more honest.** *(csc-raw-points-more-honest)* — Overplotting conceals the distribution while preserving outliers, biasing the reading toward the rare.

**2. Over-correcting into summary statistics alone.** — Anscombe exists to show that matching summaries can hide radically different structures. Both failure directions are real.

**3. Treating a table as a failure to visualize.** *(csc-table-is-a-failure)* — For precise value lookup and heterogeneous metrics, a designed table is the correct form.

**4. Shipping a data dump and calling it a table.** — Alignment, sorting, in-cell marks and restrained rules are what make it designed. An unsorted grid of numbers is not a table any more than an unlabelled scatter is a chart.

**5. Reaching for a custom encoding to signal sophistication.** *(csc-novelty-signals-skill)* — Every viewer pays the learning cost, every time. Name the task a conventional form would prevent, or use the conventional form.

**6. Believing novelty is never justified.** — The opposite error. Some data structures genuinely have no conventional representation, and refusing them costs the reader more than the learning cost would.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **Overplotting hides.** It destroys the distribution while preserving outliers, biasing the reading toward the rare.
- Remedies in order of cost: alpha blending, 2D binning, density contours plus outlier layer, faceting by a third variable.
- Anscombe and overplotting cut in opposite directions. **There is no neutral representation** — you always choose which structure to reveal.
- A **designed table** is a first-class form and the right answer for precise lookup and heterogeneous metrics. Alignment, sorting and in-cell marks are what make it designed.
- **Novelty carries a learning cost paid by every viewer every time.** Justify it by naming the specific task a conventional form would prevent.
- If you cannot name that task in one sentence, use the conventional form.

interactionSequence.prompt: A scatterplot of 60,000 loan records shows a solid black mass in the centre with scattered points at the edges. A colleague argues that any aggregation would be less honest. Your response?
options: The overplotted version already hides the distribution while preserving the outliers, so it over-represents the rare; binning or density with a separate outlier layer is more truthful.
They are right — every data point should always be shown so nothing is lost.
They are right, but the chart should be enlarged until the points separate.
Replace it with summary statistics, which are more rigorous than any plot.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it names the mechanism rather than asserting a preference — which is what makes it usable in review.
Nothing is lost from the file, but nearly everything is lost from the reading — the viewer sees ink density, not data.
At 60,000 points this only postpones saturation, and it fails entirely on any fixed delivery surface.
This over-corrects into the opposite error: Anscombe's quartet exists precisely to show that matching summary statistics can hide radically different structures.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The sentence that ends this argument: **"the version you are defending is already an aggregation — it aggregates by ink opacity, and it does it badly."** Once someone sees that the overplotted chart is making a summarising decision rather than avoiding one, the disagreement becomes about *which* aggregation is right, which is a design conversation rather than a moral one.

interactionSequence.prompt: A dashboard tile exists so finance staff can look up the exact figure for a named cost centre among forty. A designer proposes replacing the current table with a bar chart. Evaluate.
options: The table is correct: when the task is precise value lookup, reading a number beats decoding any graphical channel, and forty rows exceeds what a bar chart labels comfortably.
The bar chart is better, because visualizing data is always preferable to tabulating it.
The bar chart is better, because bars sit near the top of the effectiveness ranking.
Either works equally well, since the underlying numbers are identical.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct — and the effectiveness ranking itself predicts it, since the ranking concerns judging magnitudes rather than retrieving exact values.
Tables are a first-class form. Treating them as a failure discards the best tool for lookup and for heterogeneous metrics.
Length ranks highly for *comparing magnitudes*, which is not the task, and forty labelled bars is beyond comfortable direct labelling.
Identical numbers do not imply identical task support; the whole discipline is that representation determines what is readable.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The strongest version of this answer keeps the table **and** adds a sparkline column, so the row supports lookup and the column supports shape. That is usually the real requirement hiding behind the request — someone wanted trend visible and reached for 'make it a chart' as the only tool they knew.

Section 7 returns to this: an organisation with no table component in its design system will keep converting tables into charts, because the system made one option available and the other not.

interactionSequence.prompt: A designer proposes a custom radial encoding for a quarterly revenue-by-region report, arguing it will make the deck memorable. What is the correct evaluation?
options: Apply the novelty test — name the specific task a conventional form would prevent. Revenue by region is a ranked comparison a sorted bar chart handles at top-ranked accuracy, so the learning cost is unjustified.
It is a good idea: a distinctive visualization signals design sophistication to executives.
Radial encodings are always invalid and should never be used.
Accept it if the executives like it, since audience preference is the deciding factor.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Novelty is justified by structural necessity, not memorability — the cost is paid by every viewer while the benefit accrues to the designer.
To analytics and engineering partners this typically reads as self-indulgence and costs credibility you will need later.
Radial forms are appropriate for genuinely cyclical data — hours of the day, months of the year — where linear layout misrepresents wraparound.
Audience *fluency* is an input to selection; audience *preference* between forms is the judgment you are being paid to make on their behalf.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Worth being precise about what the novelty test is not: it is not a prohibition. Section 5 spends ninety minutes on forms that exist precisely because conventional charts cannot represent hierarchy, flow or network structure — and there the test passes easily, in one sentence.

The test exists to distinguish those cases from this one. Applied honestly it says yes reasonably often, which is what stops it being a rule about taste.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: describe a chart in your product that should probably be a designed table, or a table that should have in-cell marks added. What is the task it actually serves?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The most common real answer is a KPI tile grid or a bar chart of many named entities that people scan for *their* row — a cost centre, their region, their team. The tell is when users ask "can you add the numbers on top of the bars?" That request means the graphical encoding is not serving the task and they are working around it.

When you hear it, the honest response is usually not to add labels to the bars. It is to ask whether the chart should have been a sorted table with a sparkline column all along.

workedExamples.problem: Build the trading desk's view: under what temperature and wind conditions does wholesale price spike? Correlation plus distribution, exploratory, large screen, ~17,500 hourly observations.
steps: **Start with the naive form and predict its failure.** Scatterplot of temperature against price. At 17,500 points the central mass saturates; distribution is destroyed, outliers survive intact.
**Name what that costs for this task.** The trader's question is conditional — *under what conditions* — which is a question about where the mass sits. That is precisely what overplotting removes.
**Apply alpha blending first.** Cheapest remedy. Helps, and still saturates in the densest region, because the dense region is where most of the hours are.

**Move to two-dimensional binning.** Hexbin, count encoded by luminance. Density becomes explicit and quantified. This is a deliberate use of a low-ranked channel, justified because the task is pattern detection rather than ratio judgment.

**Recover the conditional structure by faceting.** Split into four panels by wind-output quartile, shared scales. The trader's actual question — how the temperature-price relationship changes with wind — is now directly readable rather than inferred.
**Restore the outliers as a separate layer.** Binning hides individual extremes, and price spikes are the events the desk cares most about. Plot spike events as distinct marks over the hexbin base.
**Check the composition against the rule.** The task is seeing each wind regime's shape, not comparing the four to each other — so faceting is right, and shared scales are mandatory.

**Apply the novelty test to the whole thing.** Is a hexbin a custom encoding? For a trading desk, no — it is conventional in quantitative finance. For a public report it would need justification. **Audience fluency, not the form itself, decides the learning cost.**
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The final design shows fewer raw marks and more information.**

A hexbin base for density, faceted into four panels by wind quartile for conditional structure, with spike events layered on top as individual marks.

The general principle worth carrying: **"show everything" and "hide nothing" are not the same instruction.** Overplotting hides. The question is never raw-versus-aggregated in the abstract; it is which representation makes the task-relevant structure visible.

And note step 8, because it generalises further than it looks: the learning cost of a form is a property of the **audience**, not of the form. The same hexbin is conventional for one reader and novel for another, which means the novelty test has to be run per-audience rather than answered once and filed.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why is an overplotted scatterplot a distortion rather than merely a legibility problem? Name what it preserves and what it destroys.
Name four remedies for overplotting, in increasing order of cost.
What do Anscombe's quartet and the overplotting problem jointly establish?
When is a designed table the correct form, and name three things that make a table designed rather than dumped.
State the novelty test in one sentence, and say what determines whether a given form counts as novel.

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Run the full viable-set discipline on a real brief and produce a defensible selection rationale.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: Use a live brief from your own work — ideally the one you rewrote in Section 1's activity, so the decision statement is already available.
instructions: **Part A — Constraints (5 min).** Write the four selection inputs explicitly, one line each: structure summary, primary analytic task, audience and convention notes, delivery surface.

**Part B — Generate three (12 min).** Sketch three genuinely different viable forms — not three variants of one idea. Constraint: at least one must use a composition strategy (facet, layer or juxtapose), and at least one must be considered as a designed table. Label each with what it makes visible and what it hides.
**Part C — Decompose (8 min).** Write the seven grammar components for your leading candidate. This is the row set you will hand to engineering.

**Part D — Eliminate (8 min).** For each rejected form, write one sentence naming a specific mechanism. 'Less clear' and 'busier' do not count — use baseline loss, legend ceiling, overplotting, cardinality, learning cost, expressiveness failure or occlusion.

**Part E — Stress test (7 min).** Answer three questions about your selection: what happens at ten times the current cardinality, and which choice breaks first? What happens in greyscale? What is the first follow-up question your audience will ask — and where does its answer live?
materialsOrPrerequisites: A real brief with a stated decision, audience and delivery surface.
Paper or a sketching tool — the candidates should be rough, not built.
The four selection inputs and the seven grammar components from this section.
reflectionPrompts: Were your three candidates genuinely different, or three versions of the form you had already decided on?
Did any elimination sentence turn out to be an adjective in disguise?
Did the table option get a fair hearing, or was it dismissed reflexively?
Is the answer to your follow-up question a planned artifact, or 'they could always ask us'?

verification.mode: self-assessment against explicit criteria, with the selection rationale read aloud to a colleague who does not know the brief
selfAssessmentCriteria: Three structurally distinct candidates were generated, not three variants.
Every elimination cites a named mechanism.
The runner-up is explicitly identified with the reason it lost.
The grammar decomposition is complete across all seven components.
The stress test identifies which specific choice breaks first at scale.
The final rationale fits the pattern: given [structure] and the task of [task] for [audience] on [surface], I selected [form]; the runner-up was [form], rejected because [mechanism].

learningExperiences.title: Case study: chart selection under pressure, in public

contentBlocks.content:
## The situation

In early 2020 the *Financial Times* published a series of charts tracking case and mortality trajectories across countries, led by John Burn-Murdoch. They became among the most widely reproduced statistical graphics of the period.

What makes them worth studying is not that they were good. It is that the team **explained their decisions publicly as they iterated**, and revised them repeatedly in response to comprehension feedback — so there is a rare public record of chart selection being done under time pressure, in front of an audience, with the reasoning visible.

## Three decisions worth studying

**1. Aligning on a common start point rather than calendar date.**

Countries entered the outbreak at different times, so a calendar x-axis made trajectories incomparable — the primary task was *comparison of growth trajectories*, and calendar alignment defeated it. Re-indexing the x-axis to "days since the Nth confirmed case" made the comparison direct.

In grammar terms this is a **transform** plus a **scale** change, not a new chart type. And it is the same move as re-graining the regulator's data to monthly: **task-driven axis definition**, decided before any form was chosen.

**2. A logarithmic y-axis.**

On a linear scale, exponential growth compresses early differences into an unreadable floor while the leading country dominates the plot area. On a log scale, *slope* corresponds to *growth rate* — which was the quantity the comparison actually concerned.

This was contested. Log scales carry real comprehension risk with general audiences, as Section 2 noted. The team addressed it with heavy annotation and reference lines showing doubling times, **rather than abandoning the scale**. Note the trade being made explicitly: comprehension risk accepted, mitigated by guides, because no linear alternative supported the task.

**3. Superposition, then faceting.**

The headline chart superposed a limited set of countries — under the five-series ceiling — with lines direct-labelled at their endpoints, eliminating legend round-trips. As the country count grew, the team published **small-multiple** versions with shared scales and a muted "all other countries" backdrop in each panel.

That is exactly the superposition-to-faceting transition from this section, including the grey-context trick, arriving under deadline rather than from a textbook.

contentBlocks.title: What a design lead should take from it
contentBlocks.content:
**Every decision had a named cost, taken because a specific analytic task demanded it, and was defended publicly on those grounds.**

The log axis was not chosen because it looked better. It was chosen because slope had to mean growth rate, and the comprehension cost was paid down with guides rather than denied.

And the charts were **revised repeatedly** in response to how people actually read them — which is the critique-and-measurement loop of Section 7 operating in real time and in public.

## Being fair about the criticism

The log-scale decision drew sustained objection from people who were not being unreasonable. Research on how general audiences read logarithmic axes is genuinely mixed, and there is evidence that many readers interpret them as linear — which, on a growth chart, systematically understates how bad the top end is.

So the critics had a real point, and the resolution was not that they were wrong. It was a **judgment under uncertainty**: the task required slope-as-growth-rate, no linear form supplied it, and the team chose to accept a known comprehension risk and mitigate it, rather than choose a form that could not answer the question at all.

That is what most real chart decisions look like. **You will rarely choose between a right and a wrong option. You will choose which cost to pay, and your job is to name it, mitigate it, and be able to say why.**

terms.definition: A scale transform on which equal distances represent equal ratios, making proportional change comparable across magnitudes; carries real comprehension risk with general audiences.
Repetition of one chart form across values of a categorical variable, on shared scales, so the viewer learns the encoding once and then compares patterns.
Identical axis domains across faceted panels, without which the panels look comparable and are not.
Placing series labels on the marks themselves rather than in a legend, eliminating working-memory round-trips.
An axis, legend or annotation that lets a viewer decode a scale; the readable counterpart of an encoding.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors this case illustrates
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Treating axis definition as formatting.** — Re-indexing to a common start point was the decision that made the comparison possible at all.

**2. Choosing a scale for appearance rather than for what slope should mean.** — The log axis was a task decision with a stated cost, not a stylistic one.

**3. Denying a cost instead of mitigating it.** — The team could have argued that log scales are fine. They accepted the risk and spent guides on it, which is the stronger position.

**4. Superposing past the ceiling as the audience grows.** — The transition to small multiples was forced by cardinality, exactly as this section predicts.

**5. Treating publication as the end.** — The charts were revised repeatedly against how readers actually behaved.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **Task-driven axis definition** — aligning to a common start point — was the decision that made the primary comparison possible.
- The **log scale** was chosen so slope would mean growth rate, with its comprehension cost accepted and mitigated by annotation and reference lines.
- The **superposition-to-faceting** transition happened under deadline, driven by cardinality, with grey context in each panel.
- Every decision was named, costed and defended in public.
- The criticism was legitimate. Most real selections are choices about **which cost to pay**, not between right and wrong.

interactionSequence.prompt: Re-indexing the x-axis from calendar date to 'days since the Nth case' is which grammar change, and what justified it?
options: A transform plus a scale change, justified because the task was comparing growth trajectories and calendar alignment made them incomparable.
A change of chart type from a time series to a different species of chart.
A mark change, justified by making the lines easier to distinguish.
A guide change, justified by making the axis labels shorter.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Two components moved, everything else held, and the justification came from the analytic task rather than from appearance.
Both versions are line charts of a series over an ordered dimension. Describing it as a type change hides which component actually moved.
The mark stayed a line throughout. Distinguishability was handled by direct labelling, which is a guide decision.
Guides did a lot of work in these charts, but the re-indexing changed what the x position *means*, which is transform and scale.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the grammar paying off on a real artifact. "They changed the x-axis" is vague enough to sound like formatting. **"They added a transform that re-indexes each country to its own outbreak start, and changed the scale's meaning from calendar time to elapsed time"** makes visible that the underlying data was recomputed — and that every country's line now begins at a different real-world date, which is a substantive claim readers need to understand.

interactionSequence.prompt: You are proposing a log axis for a public-facing chart and a colleague objects that readers will misread it. Using this case as a model, what do you propose — and what do you concede?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Concede the substance:** the evidence on general-audience log comprehension is genuinely mixed, and many readers do interpret log axes as linear. Denying that puts you on ground you cannot hold.

**Propose:** state what the linear alternative cannot do — if slope must mean growth rate and the series spans orders of magnitude, no linear form answers the question. Then spend guides on the risk: doubling-time reference lines, explicit annotation of what the axis means, direct labels at the endpoints, and a stated subtitle. Offer a linear companion view if the surface allows.

**And offer to test it.** A five-person comprehension check settles this faster than the argument will, which is Section 7's move: **convert the disagreement into an empirical question.** Note that this is also the honest outcome — if the test shows readers misreading it badly, you should change the chart.
hints: Which part of their objection is simply true?
What can no linear form do?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you this would resolve it in your organisation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Recall a chart decision you made where you chose which cost to pay rather than between a right and a wrong option. Did you name the cost out loud at the time? What happened as a result?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The usual pattern is that the cost was noticed and not stated — and then surfaced later as someone else's objection, at which point it looked like an oversight rather than a decision.

Naming a cost when you make it does two things. It makes the decision reviewable, which is what a lead owes their team. And it inoculates: an objection you raised yourself, with a mitigation attached, is far harder to use against you than one you appeared not to have considered.

workedExamples.problem: Reconstruct the FT team's selection reasoning for the headline trajectory chart using this section's four inputs, then identify the point at which the design had to change.
steps: **Structure.** Daily cumulative counts per country. Time is ordered and continuous; country is nominal with cardinality rising over time from a handful to dozens; counts are ratio-scaled and span several orders of magnitude.
**Task.** Comparison of growth trajectories across countries — explicitly comparative, and specifically about *rate* rather than level.
**Audience and surface.** General newspaper readership, including many non-technical readers; web and print; viewed briefly, shared widely, often as a screenshot without surrounding article text.
**First elimination — calendar x-axis.** Fails the task: countries at different outbreak stages are not comparable on calendar dates. Eliminated by task, not by appearance.
**Second elimination — linear y-axis.** Fails the task: compresses early differences into a floor and lets the largest country dominate. Slope no longer corresponds to growth rate.

**Selection with a named cost.** Log y-axis and re-indexed x-axis, accepting a comprehension risk that no linear alternative avoids while still answering the question. **Mitigation spent on guides:** doubling-time reference lines, direct endpoint labels, explicit annotation.

**Identify the breaking point.** As countries were added, superposition passed the legend and occlusion ceiling — around five series, exactly as this section predicts. That is a **cardinality** trigger, and it is predictable in advance rather than something to discover in the wild.
**The forced transition.** Small multiples on shared scales, each panel highlighting one country against a muted backdrop of all others. Shape per country, plus context, without a legend.

**Note the screenshot problem.** Because these charts travelled as images stripped of their article, the guides had to carry the entire interpretive load. That is a delivery-surface constraint most designers never account for, and it argues for annotation inside the plot area rather than in surrounding copy.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The design did not change because taste changed. It changed because cardinality crossed a threshold that was predictable from the outset.**

That is the most useful thing in this case for your own practice. The superposition ceiling is not a rule of thumb you discover when a chart gets ugly — it is a constraint you can name in advance, which means you can plan the transition rather than being forced into it mid-crisis.

And step 9 deserves keeping. **A chart that will be screenshotted is a chart whose surrounding text does not exist.** If the interpretation depends on a caption, and the caption is croppable, the interpretation is not protected. Guides inside the plot area survive; everything outside it is optional as far as the reader is concerned. Section 6 develops this into the annotation layer, and Section 7 into what a default view owes its reader.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why was re-indexing to 'days since the Nth case' a task decision rather than a formatting one? Name the task it enabled.
What is the stronger response to a known comprehension cost — denying it or mitigating it? Give the reason and one example of a mitigation.
Why does a chart likely to be shared as an image change where annotation must live?

transferExercises.context: Competitive esports — high-cardinality, rapidly changing, and nothing about energy or museums transfers.
transferExercises.scenario: A tournament organiser has, for 400 matches: match_id, map (7 values), team_a and team_b (24 teams), per-round economy values, and round outcomes. An analyst wants to explore whether certain teams underperform on specific maps.
transferExercises.task: In under 250 words: identify the analytic task; state whether the primary artifact should be exploratory or explanatory and why; choose between superposition, faceting and juxtaposition with a named justification; and specify what happens to your design if the team count rises from 24 to 200 — naming which of your choices survives and which breaks first.
successCriteria: Identifies the task as comparison across a team-by-map matrix, with distribution as a secondary concern.
Classifies the artifact as exploratory and justifies it from the word 'explore' and the analyst audience.
Chooses faceting or a matrix layout with a named mechanism, not an adjective.
Correctly predicts that panel count, not encoding, breaks first at 200 teams.
Considers a designed table or heatmap matrix as a candidate rather than dismissing it.
No reliance on esports domain knowledge.

learningExperiences.title: Section quiz: chart selection and composition

contentBlocks.content: Answer from memory. This section is the course pivot — it is the first place all four prior competencies had to be used at once, and Section 5 assumes every habit here is available without prompting.

contentBlocks.title: How this is scored
contentBlocks.content: These items are formative and shape your review queue. The graded assessments for this section are `assess-chart-selection-composition` and `assess-encoding-effectiveness`.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** When faceting into small multiples, giving each panel its own y-scale is acceptable if the axis labels are clearly shown.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Labels do not repair the implication. The grid layout itself makes a comparison claim, and viewers compare panel shapes preattentively — long before reading any axis.
Correct. Independent scales make panels look comparable while destroying comparability. If shared scales flatten some panels, that flatness is the finding.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Independent scales make panels look comparable while destroying comparability. If shared scales flatten some panels, that flatness is the finding.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** A conventional chart form that adequately supports the task should usually be preferred over a custom form that supports it marginally better.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The learning cost of a custom form is paid by every viewer on every viewing, so the performance margin must be large rather than marginal.
Incorrect. The cost of novelty is paid repeatedly by every reader while the benefit accrues once to the designer, so a marginal gain does not justify it.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. The learning cost of a custom form is paid by every viewer on every viewing, so the performance margin must be large rather than marginal.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** There exists a neutral chart that simply presents the data without emphasising any particular structure.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Every representation reveals some structures and conceals others — summaries hide shape, raw points hide distribution, aggregation hides variance, faceting hides cross-series comparison.
Correct. Choosing deliberately, and saying which structure you chose to reveal, is the discipline. Anscombe and overplotting establish this from opposite directions.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Choosing deliberately, and saying which structure you chose to reveal, is the discipline. Anscombe and overplotting establish this from opposite directions.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Falling back to a table means you failed to find a way to visualize the data.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. For precise value lookup and for heterogeneous metrics, a designed table is the correct form — reading a number beats decoding any graphical channel.
Correct. A designed table is a first-class form, and choosing one for a lookup task is the same discipline as choosing a bar chart for a comparison task.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. A designed table is a first-class form, and choosing one for a lookup task is the same discipline as choosing a bar chart for a comparison task.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** A grouped bar chart and a stacked bar chart differ by a transform, not by chart type.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct — and naming it as a transform exposes the cost immediately: stacking removes the common baseline from every series above the first.
Incorrect. They share six of seven grammar components; only the transform differs. Treating them as separate types is what hides the trade-off.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct — and naming it as a transform exposes the cost immediately: stacking removes the common baseline from every series above the first.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Data structure is sufficient to determine the correct chart form.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Structure eliminates options; task selects among the survivors, and audience and delivery surface adjust further. Identical structures routinely warrant different answers.
Correct. This is why chart-chooser flowcharts fail — they see structure and are blind to the variables that actually decide.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. This is why chart-chooser flowcharts fail — they see structure and are blind to the variables that actually decide.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** You are handed hourly air-quality readings from 60 monitoring stations across a city over three years. A councillor asks for a chart showing whether air quality is improving. In four or five sentences, walk through your selection and name your runner-up.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Structure:** time at very high cardinality, 60 nominal stations far past the legend ceiling, ratio readings. Re-grain from hourly to monthly or seasonal — a three-year improvement question does not need hourly resolution.

**Task:** trend, with an implied deviation against a regulatory threshold.

**Audience and surface:** non-technical councillor, explanatory report, likely print or slide.

**Selection:** a citywide trend line on a common-scale position axis, direct-labelled, with a threshold reference line — plus a faceted small-multiple set on shared scales as a planned secondary figure.

**Runner-up:** superposed lines for a small selected set of stations, rejected on legend-ceiling and occlusion grounds at 60 series.

Strong answers add two things: averaging 60 stations into one line hides uneven improvement across the city — a Section 2 concern — and the councillor's predictable follow-up (*improving everywhere?*) is exactly why the faceted figure is planned rather than optional.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** Explain in two or three sentences why a chart-chooser flowchart could not have produced your answer above.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Flowcharts key off **data structure alone**, and the structure here — a time series with a categorical breakdown — is identical to structures warranting completely different answers depending on task, audience and surface.

Two specific decisions were decisive in the answer above and have no representation in a flowchart's inputs: the **re-graining from hourly to monthly**, which came from the task, and the **explanatory classification**, which came from the audience. A flowchart sees neither, so it emits one recommendation for three different correct answers.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which item did you answer confidently and get wrong? Name the belief you held instead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The independent-facet-scales item catches the most people, because it is the one where a genuinely good instinct — *every panel should be legible* — produces the wrong answer. If that was yours, the thing to hold is that legibility and comparability are different goals, and the grid layout has already promised the reader comparability before they read a single axis.

It returns immediately: Section 5 faces the same problem with map colour scales across regions, and Section 6 classifies it explicitly as a distortion mechanism.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the selection rationale pattern: given [?] and the task of [?] for [?] on [?], I selected [?]; the runner-up was [?], rejected because [?].

sections.title: Spatial, Hierarchical and Relational Forms
sections.description: Data whose structure has no conventional linear representation — geography, hierarchy, flow and network. Covers the map-necessity gate, normalization and areal units on maps, projection distortion, treemaps and Sankey diagrams as legitimate passes of the novelty test, and node-link versus matrix representations of networks.

learningObjectives.description: Decide whether geography is the right encoding at all by applying the map-necessity gate question, and name the specific spatial relationship that justifies a map.
Select the population at risk as the denominator for a mapped quantity, and flag units whose counts are too small to rank on.
Explain the modifiable areal unit problem and produce the three disclosures every choropleth owes its reader.
Determine when projection choice becomes a quantitative error, and select an equal-area projection for area-encoded quantities.
Choose among choropleth, cartogram, dot density, proportional symbol and non-map alternatives, naming the loss each choice accepts.
Select and justify a representation for hierarchical or flow data, distinguishing what the form encodes from what is layout artifact.
Choose between node-link and matrix representations by task and graph density, and specify the controls that determine what a node-link diagram asserts.
Reason from structure and decision to a defensible spatial or relational design in an unfamiliar domain, without relying on domain precedent.

motivationHooks.prompt:
These are the forms where the novelty test from Section 4 says **yes** — where the data's structure genuinely has no conventional representation, and a custom encoding is the correct answer rather than an indulgence.

They are also the forms where designers most reliably produce something that looks impressive and communicates nothing. A hairball network diagram, a choropleth of raw counts, a treemap used for ranking — each of these ships regularly, each looks like sophisticated work, and each fails at the task it was built for.

The difference is not talent. It is whether four specific questions were asked before anyone opened a tool.

Maps in particular carry an authority that other charts do not. Readers treat them as depictions of reality rather than as encodings with choices in them — which means the choices you make disappear from view rather than being scrutinised.

That is precisely why the failures here reach the public more often than any other kind. A misjudged bar chart is argued with. A misleading map is believed.

Hold this and test it as you go:

> **A research team aggregates the same 420 incident locations twice — once into census tracts, once into postal districts. The two maps show noticeably different patterns: the cluster appears in a different place, with a different extent.**

Write one line now: which map is wrong? If you think neither, write what obligation that places on whoever publishes either one.

**The resolution.** Neither is wrong. Both are computed correctly from identical observations.

The pattern is **partly a property of the units**, not only of the incidents — the modifiable areal unit problem, with a scale component (how large the units are) and a zoning component (where the lines fall at a given size). It applies to every choropleth ever made, and it cannot be escaped.

What follows is an obligation rather than a fix. Every choropleth owes its reader **which units, why those units, and the range of exposure across them** — and where a finding matters, you re-aggregate at a second boundary level and report whether it holds.

If you predicted that the finer aggregation must be more accurate, note the trade: finer units reduce aggregation effects and worsen small-count instability and disclosure risk. Finer is not better, it is different — which is the same shape as the grain decision from Section 1, arriving with a coastline drawn around it.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following.

**Geography must earn its space.** Ask what the map shows that a sorted bar chart would not. If you cannot answer in one sentence naming a spatial relationship, build the bar chart. A map spends screen space and judgment accuracy, and a great many maps buy nothing with it.

**Normalization decides what a map is a map of**, and a map hides its own denominator — which makes the counts-versus-rates failure far harder for a reader to detect here than anywhere else.

**Areal units are an analytical choice, usually inherited.** The modifiable areal unit problem is unavoidable, so disclose the units, the reason, and the exposure range, and test stability where the finding matters.

**Any area-based encoding inherits the projection's area distortion** as a quantitative error.

**Treemaps and Sankeys pass the novelty test legitimately** — and each has a large region of misuse. Area is rank 5, so treemaps are for composition rather than ranking; in a Sankey only width and height encode, while position and crossings are layout that readers nonetheless interpret.

**Node position in a force-directed layout is an algorithm artifact.** Encode centrality explicitly, fix the seed, filter before rendering, and say what position means — or use a matrix, which has no layout to misread.
keyTakeaways: Apply the gate question before every map: what does this show that a sorted bar chart would not?
Choose the population at risk, and put the denominator in the subtitle — the map cannot show it.
Disclose which units, why those units, and the exposure range across them.
Use an equal-area projection whenever a quantity is encoded by area or by shading of areas.
Name the loss each map form accepts: recognisability, lookup precision, or spatial relationship.
Treemaps answer 'what is this made of', never 'which is biggest'.
In Sankeys and node-link diagrams, state what position does not encode.
A request for a network diagram often resolves into a computed scalar and a sorted bar chart.

furtherReading.title: How to Lie with Maps
furtherReading.citation: Monmonier, M. (2018). 3rd edition, University of Chicago Press.
furtherReading.author: Mark Monmonier
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The standard work on cartographic distortion, and the direct ancestor of this section. The chapters on data classification and on the choices hidden in choropleth breaks are the ones to read first — they cover a decision this section only gestures at.

furtherReading.author: Cynthia Brewer
furtherReading.rationaleNote: Practical and specific on colour, classification and layout for thematic maps, by the author of ColorBrewer. The most directly usable reference if you are building maps rather than critiquing them.

furtherReading.citation: Openshaw, S. (1984). CATMOG 38, Geo Books.
furtherReading.author: Stan Openshaw
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The foundational treatment. Short, and worth reading in the original for how thoroughly the scale and zoning effects are separated — most secondary accounts blur them together.

furtherReading.title: Worldmapper and the cartogram tradition
furtherReading.citation: Worldmapper. Cartogram collection.
furtherReading.author: Worldmapper / Benjamin Hennig and colleagues

learningExperiences.title: When geography earns its space, and what it costs

contentBlocks.content:
A land-management agency hands you parcel records for a large region: ownership category, current use class, area, and a decade of change events. Every row has coordinates.

The request is "a map showing how land use is changing."

The presence of coordinates in a dataset is the most reliable trigger for an unexamined design decision in this entire field. Locations are *in* the data, therefore a map — and the question of whether geography is the right encoding never gets asked.

contentBlocks.title: The gate question
contentBlocks.content:
**What does the map show that a sorted bar chart would not?**

Ask it before anything else. A map spends a great deal of screen space and a great deal of judgment accuracy on encoding *position by geography* — and that is only worth paying for when a **spatial relationship** is part of the question: adjacency, contiguity, distance, catchment, route, or region.

If the task is ranking or comparison across a handful of named places, a sorted bar chart answers it strictly more accurately, because position on a common scale is rank 1 and area-constrained colour is rank 7.

contentBlocks.altText: On the left, a grid of regions shaded by rate. On the right, the same regions as a sorted bar chart with values labelled. The bar chart makes ranking and magnitude directly readable through position and length, while the map requires comparing shaded areas of differing size and shape.
contentBlocks.caption: Does geography earn its space?

contentBlocks.content:
Notice what the map cannot do in that comparison. Region sizes are dictated by cartography, so a large sparsely-populated region shouts and a small dense one whispers, regardless of their values. Colour is doing the quantitative work at rank 7. And the reader cannot rank anything without scanning the whole map and holding values in memory.

The map does one thing the bar chart cannot: it shows you **where**, and whether the high values sit next to each other. If your decision does not turn on that, you are paying for geography and receiving nothing.

## Normalization decides what the map is a map of

This is Section 2 arriving in spatial form, and it is the single most common failure in published cartography.

A **choropleth** shades defined areal units by value. If that value is a raw count, the map is substantially a map of wherever the denominator is largest — population, area, number of parcels. The pattern a reader sees is the denominator's pattern, not the phenomenon's.

contentBlocks.altText: Two choropleths of the same region grid. Shaded by total cases, the darkest region is the most populous one. Shaded by cases per thousand residents, a different and much smaller region is darkest, and the previously dominant region becomes mid-toned. Both maps use identical data.
contentBlocks.caption: A map of counts is largely a map of population.

contentBlocks.content:
The rule from Section 2 carries over unchanged: **choose the population at risk**. For habitat loss that is hectares of habitat, not hectares of region. For access to services it is residents within a catchment, not residents in an administrative unit. For crop disease it is planted area of that crop, not farmland.

And small denominators bite harder on maps than anywhere else, because a map gives every unit equal visual standing regardless of how many observations produced it. A region with nine parcels and one change event renders as an extreme value in exactly the same ink as a region with nine thousand. Flag low-count units visibly — hatching, reduced opacity, or an explicit "insufficient data" category — rather than letting them lead the ranking. Section 6 returns to this as **small cell suppression**, where the concern becomes disclosure rather than stability.

## The boundaries are a choice, not a container

Here is the part that surprises most designers.

Aggregate the *same* point observations into different boundary sets and the spatial pattern changes — sometimes substantially, occasionally reversing. This is the **modifiable areal unit problem**, and it has two components: the *scale* effect (how big the units are) and the *zoning* effect (where the lines fall at a given size).

It is not an edge case or a statistical curiosity. It applies to every choropleth ever made.

contentBlocks.altText: A scatter of 420 point observations with a cluster toward the lower left, shown alongside two aggregations of those identical points: one into a four-by-four grid and one into a seven-by-six grid. The apparent location, extent and intensity of the cluster differ noticeably between the two aggregations even though no observation changed.
contentBlocks.caption: The same points, two boundary sets.

contentBlocks.title: What follows from this
contentBlocks.content:
You cannot escape the modifiable areal unit problem. You can only **disclose** it.

Every choropleth owes its reader three things in the subtitle or method note: **which units**, **why those units**, and **the range of population or exposure across them**.

Where the finding matters, test its stability: re-aggregate at a second boundary level and report whether the pattern holds. If it does not, that is the finding — and reporting it is the difference between a map and an argument.

## Projection, and why it is a quantitative problem

Every **projection** flattens a curved surface and distorts some combination of area, shape, distance and direction. You cannot preserve all of them.

For a designer the consequence is specific: **any area-based encoding inherits the projection's area distortion as a quantitative error.** Choropleth shading, dot density and bubble size all read partly as "how much space this occupies," and on a Mercator-style projection that space is inflated toward the poles by a large factor.

contentBlocks.altText: Two grids of circles representing equal true areas. On the equal-area projection all circles render identically. On the Mercator-style projection the circles inflate progressively toward the top of the map, so equal ground areas appear several times larger at high latitudes.
contentBlocks.caption: Every projection distorts something.

contentBlocks.content:
The practical rule is short: **if the map encodes a quantity by area or by shading of areas, use an equal-area projection.** Web-mapping defaults are almost universally Mercator-based, because they preserve local shape and angle for navigation — which is the right trade for finding a street and the wrong one for comparing regional quantities.

This is a default nobody chose, exactly like the rainbow colormap in Section 3. It is worth checking what your mapping library does before assuming.

## The form choices, and what each accepts

Three ways to put a quantity on a map, each trading something different away.

contentBlocks.altText: The same regional data shown as a choropleth with rate encoded by shading, as a cartogram in which each region's area is scaled to its population so visual weight matches where people are, and as a dot density map in which each dot represents a fixed number of cases and distribution within each region is visible.
contentBlocks.caption: Three ways to put a quantity on a map.
Map form trade-offs
rows: Area distortion; visual weight ∝ region size, not value; implies uniformity within each unit
Making visual weight match population or exposure
Recognisability; readers may not find their own region
Count of marks placed within units
Precise value lookup; dot placement within a unit is usually arbitrary
Size of a mark at a point
Comparing places of very different area
Area is rank 5; occlusion where places cluster

terms.definition: A map encoding a value by shading defined areal units; requires normalization, since raw counts render as a map of the denominator.
A map deliberately distorting geographic area to encode a variable such as population, trading spatial fidelity for quantitative fidelity.
A map placing marks in proportion to a count within each area, conveying magnitude and rough distribution without area-based shading.
The effect whereby aggregating the same point data into different boundary sets produces different, sometimes opposite, spatial patterns.
The transformation from a curved surface to a flat one; every projection distorts some combination of area, shape, distance and direction.
Expressing a quantity relative to a base — population, area, time or a reference period — so that groups of different size can be compared.
The population or exposure a count is divided by; choosing it is an analytical claim, not a formatting decision.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Mapping because the data has coordinates.** *(srf-map-is-the-default)* — Geography costs space and accuracy. Pay for it only when a spatial relationship is part of the decision.

**2. Choropleths of raw counts.** *(qr-counts-are-comparable)* — The map becomes a map of the denominator. This is Section 2's error with a coastline drawn around it.

**3. Treating administrative boundaries as neutral.** *(srf-boundaries-are-given)* — Units are an analytical choice and the pattern changes with them. Disclose which and why.

**4. Letting tiny units drive the ranking.** — A unit with nine observations renders as confidently as one with nine thousand. Flag low counts visibly.

**5. Using a Mercator-style projection for an area-encoded quantity.** — The projection's area distortion becomes a quantitative error in your encoding.

**6. Implying uniformity within a unit.** — A choropleth says the whole region has that value. Dot density and point maps do not make that claim.

**7. Sequential ramps where the data diverges, or vice versa.** — Section 3's midpoint rule applies unchanged, and on maps a fabricated midpoint reads as a boundary between two kinds of place.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **The gate question:** what does the map show that a sorted bar chart would not? If nothing, do not build a map.
- Geography is worth its cost when **adjacency, contiguity, distance, catchment or region** is part of the decision.
- **Normalization decides what the map is a map of.** Counts produce a map of the denominator.
- Choose the **population at risk**, and flag low-count units rather than letting them lead.
- **Areal units are a choice.** The modifiable areal unit problem is unavoidable, so disclose the units, the reason, and the exposure range — and test stability at a second level where the finding matters.
- **Any area-based encoding inherits the projection's area distortion.** Use an equal-area projection for quantities.
- Choropleth, cartogram, dot density and proportional symbol each accept a different loss. Name the one you accepted.

interactionSequence.prompt: A conservation team wants to compare protected-area funding across twelve regions for a budget decision. **Predict:** should this be a map? Answer yes or no and give the one question your answer depends on.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The question your answer should depend on is whether any **spatial relationship** enters the decision. If the budget is allocated region by region on the merits, twelve values ranked by position answers it better and faster. If the decision involves corridors, adjacency between protected areas, or catchments crossing regional lines, geography is doing real work and a map earns its place.

Note that "the stakeholders expect a map" is a real constraint and not an answer to this question. It is a reason to build one *and* to be clear about what it cannot support.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that call?
