**2. Believing accurate numbers guarantee an honest chart.** *(gi-accurate-numbers-honest)* — Range, comparison group, denominator, statistic and aspect ratio all mislead while every value stays correct.

**3. Auditing only the axis.** — The axis is the most visible mechanism and rarely the most consequential. Framing choices are invisible and do more work.

**4. Treating aspect ratio as layout.** — It sets perceived slope. Resizing is a substantive edit.

**5. Assuming distortion implies bad faith.** — Most of these are made by people applying a half-remembered rule or fitting a chart into a template. Diagnosing intent gets you a defensive room and no fix.

**6. Fixing the axis and leaving the claim.** — A chart with a corrected baseline under a title asserting more than the data supports has been half-repaired.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **Lie factor** = effect shown in the graphic ÷ effect in the data. It makes distortion arguable rather than assertable.
- **The baseline must match what the encoding claims** — zero for length, the data's meaningful reference for position.
- Distortion enters through **framing**: range, comparison group, denominator, statistic, exclusions. Every number stays correct.
- **Aspect ratio is quantitative.** Banking to about 45° is the principled default.
- Audit the framing before the axis. The axis is visible; the framing is not.
- Most distortion is inherited or template-driven rather than intended. Diagnose the mechanism, not the motive.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Predict:** the two bars represent 52.1% and 48.4%, and the chart's axis starts at 40. Roughly what ratio will a reader perceive between them, and what is the actual ratio? Give both numbers.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Perceived: roughly **3 to 1**, because the visible bar lengths are 12.1 and 8.4 units above the floor. Actual: **1.08 to 1**.

The ratio of those two ratios is the lie factor, roughly 2.8. If your estimate of the perceived ratio was close, note that you computed it from the truncation rather than seeing the chart — which is precisely what a reader cannot do.

interactionSequence.prompt: A line chart of a currency exchange rate over six months uses a y-axis from 1.28 to 1.34. A reviewer demands it start at zero. What is the correct response?
options: The zero rule applies to length encodings, where the mark's length is the value. This is a position encoding of a quantity with no meaningful zero, so a zero baseline would compress the signal into an unreadable flat line.
The reviewer is right: all quantitative axes must begin at zero to avoid exaggeration.
The reviewer is right, but only because currency data is volatile.
It does not matter, because the axis is labelled with its actual range.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it states the principle rather than the exception — which is what stops the same argument recurring next month.
Applied universally this destroys signal in exchange rates, temperatures and pH, where zero is not a meaningful reference point.
Volatility is not the deciding variable. Whether the encoding is length-based, and whether zero is meaningful, are.
Viewers read mark geometry preattentively, long before reading axis labels — labels do not repair a misleading geometry.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The reviewer is doing something valuable and applying it imprecisely, which is worth acknowledging out loud. The instinct that a truncated axis exaggerates is correct and catches real problems; the rule they learned just does not have its scope attached.

Giving them the principle rather than an exception is also the more generous move — they leave the conversation with something that works, instead of a special case they will now have to remember.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which of these is a genuine integrity finding even when every number in the chart is arithmetically correct?
options: The time range begins at a local trough, so the subsequent series reads as recovery rather than as normal fluctuation.
The chart uses a typeface that does not match the report's body text.
The legend sits to the right rather than above the plot area.
The chart shows four series where three would have been sufficient.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Range selection shapes the reading without altering a single value — one of the classic mechanisms alongside comparison group, denominator, statistic and aspect ratio.
A typographic inconsistency is a craft issue, not a claim about the data.
Legend placement affects reading cost, not the truth of what is claimed.
Series count affects clarity and search cost; it is not by itself a distortion of the underlying relationship.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The general test: **could this change the conclusion a reader draws, while leaving every value correct?** Framing choices pass that test. Craft issues do not.

It is worth being disciplined about the distinction in review, because mixing craft notes into an integrity finding weakens the integrity finding — the room starts hearing the whole list as preferences.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: find a chart in your organisation with a truncated axis. Is the encoding length-based or position-based? Was the truncation a distortion, or was it correct? Write the sentence you would say to whoever made it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Both outcomes are common, and finding a *correct* truncation is the more useful result — it means you have a concrete example to reach for the next time someone applies the zero rule universally.

On the sentence: something like *"these are bars, so the length is the value — truncating makes the gap look about three times bigger than it is"* works far better than citing a rule, because it names what the reader will experience rather than what the designer violated.

workedExamples.problem: Audit the drug efficacy slide: two bars at 52.1% and 48.4%, y-axis from 40, titled "Superior response demonstrated." Produce findings and a remediation.
steps: **Identify the encoding.** Length, via bar height. Therefore length must run from zero.
**Compute the lie factor.** Displayed ratio ≈ 3:1. Data ratio = 52.1 ÷ 48.4 ≈ 1.08:1. Lie factor ≈ **2.8**. *Finding: baseline truncation on a length encoding.*
**Examine the comparison.** "Comparator" is unnamed. Which drug, which dose, which population? *Finding: comparison-group ambiguity.*
**Examine uncertainty.** Two bars, no intervals. A 3.7-point difference in response rate may or may not exceed sampling variability, and the chart is silent. *Finding: uncertainty omitted.*
**Examine the annotation.** "Superior response demonstrated" asserts a statistical conclusion — *superior*, *demonstrated* — that the chart does not support. *Finding: annotation over-claims.*

**Remediate the encoding, not just the axis.** Re-encode as a **dot plot with confidence intervals**. Position on a common scale is rank 1, there is no length semantics, so a non-zero axis range is legitimate and the real difference is visible without exaggeration.
**Show the quantity of interest.** The difference *is* the finding, so add a second panel showing the difference with its interval. A reader should not have to subtract two intervals in their head.
**Repair the framing.** Name the comparator and dose in the subtitle.
**Rewrite the title inside what the data supports.** *"Response rate 3.7 points higher than [comparator, dose]; 95% CI −0.4 to 7.8."*
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The remediated chart shows the same accurate numbers and makes a much weaker-looking claim — which is the correct outcome, because the weaker claim is the true one.**

Note the pattern: the fix required **changing the encoding**, not just the axis. Integrity failures are usually encoding failures wearing an axis costume, and a designer who only adjusts the baseline leaves a chart that is technically defensible and still built to overstate.

Also note that three of the four findings had nothing to do with the axis. The truncation is what an auditor sees first and it was the least consequential of the four.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the corrected baseline rule as a principle rather than two cases.
Give the lie factor formula, and say what having a number for it buys you in a review.
Name five framing choices that can mislead while every number remains correct.
Why is resizing a chart to fit a slide a substantive edit rather than a layout change?

transferExercises.context: Municipal utilities — a public-facing, regulated setting.
transferExercises.scenario: A city publishes a dashboard of lead concentrations in tap water, sampled quarterly from 1,200 homes. The headline chart is a bar chart of the citywide mean concentration by quarter, y-axis from 8 to 14 µg/L, titled 'Water Quality Monitoring'. The regulatory action level is 15 µg/L and the distribution is strongly right-skewed: most homes are very low, a few are very high.
transferExercises.task: Produce a full audit: **(a)** every integrity finding, classified by mechanism; **(b)** why the mean is the wrong statistic here and what it conceals, connecting to Section 2; **(c)** a rewritten takeaway title that stays inside what the data supports; **(d)** the one change that most improves the chart, and why.
successCriteria: Identifies baseline truncation on a length encoding and estimates the exaggeration.
Identifies that a citywide mean over a right-skewed distribution conceals the homes that breach, which is the entire public-health concern.
Proposes a tail-based summary — share above the action level, or a high percentile — rather than a measure of centre.
Rewritten title states a finding without asserting safety.
Names a single highest-impact change and defends the choice.

learningExperiences.title: Showing what you do not know

contentBlocks.content:
## The objection you will hear

*"Error bars confuse non-technical audiences, so we leave them off."*

The objection has a **real premise** and a **false conclusion**, and separating those two is what lets you win the argument without dismissing the person making it.

contentBlocks.title: Premise true, conclusion false
contentBlocks.content:
**The premise is true.** Intervals *are* frequently misread — often as ranges of possible values with hard edges, or via the belief that overlapping intervals mean no difference, which is not what overlapping intervals mean.

**The conclusion is false**, because omitting uncertainty does not remove it. **It transfers it, invisibly, to the decision-maker**, who now acts on false precision and does not know they are doing so.

You have not simplified the chart. You have moved the risk somewhere it cannot be seen — and moved it onto someone with less context about the data than you have.

contentBlocks.altText: The same estimate of 62 shown four ways. As a bare point with no range indicated. As a point with a 95% interval spanning roughly 44 to 80. As a gradient fan that fades toward the tails, conveying decreasing plausibility without requiring interval literacy. As a quantile dotplot of twenty dots stacked into the distribution's shape, so a reader can count that one dot in twenty falls below 46.
contentBlocks.caption: Four ways to show the same uncertainty.

contentBlocks.content:
## The real design problem

The question is not *whether* to show uncertainty. It is **which representation matches this audience's numeracy and this decision's stakes**.

**Error bars and confidence intervals.** Compact, conventional in technical settings, widely misread outside them. Fine for an audience that reads them daily.

**Gradient or fan encodings.** Opacity fading toward the tails. Communicates *less certain out here* without demanding interval literacy. Good for forecasts, and it avoids the hard-edge misreading entirely because there is no edge.

**Quantile dotplots.** The distribution as a countable set of discrete dots. Strong empirical results with general audiences, because people reason well by counting — *one dot in twenty falls below this line* — and badly about continuous densities.

**Hypothetical outcome plots.** Animated draws from the distribution. Replaces a static abstraction with observed variability, and tests well precisely because it requires no statistical vocabulary at all.

**Explicit textual framing.** Sometimes right for a single number: *"between 4 and 12, most likely around 7."*

contentBlocks.title: The selection rule
contentBlocks.content:
**Higher stakes and lower numeracy push you toward frequency-based, countable formats.**

A quantile dotplot for a public-facing decision. Intervals for an audience of analysts. A fan for a forecast where the shape of the uncertainty matters more than any specific bound.

And when someone asks you to remove it: do not refuse. **Offer the alternative.** "They'll misread the error bars" is a solvable design problem, and treating it as one keeps you in the conversation.

terms.definition: A range summarising sampling uncertainty in an estimate.
An animated sequence of draws from a distribution, conveying uncertainty as observed variability rather than as a static abstraction.
A distribution shown as a countable set of discrete dots, supporting frequency-based reasoning by non-technical audiences.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Omitting uncertainty to avoid confusing the audience.** *(gi-uncertainty-confuses)* — It transfers the uncertainty invisibly to the decision-maker rather than removing it.

**2. Insisting on error bars as the only valid form.** — Wrong on the facts, and it turns a solvable design problem into a standoff.

**3. Putting the uncertainty in an appendix.** — The audience reads the chart. This is omission with a paper trail.

**4. Showing intervals on the inputs but not on the difference.** — When the difference is the quantity of interest, show its interval directly. Readers cannot subtract two intervals by eye, and the overlap heuristic they will reach for is wrong.

**5. Treating uncertainty as a technical embellishment.** — It is a property of the estimate. A chart without it asserts a precision the data does not have.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **Omitting uncertainty does not remove it — it transfers it invisibly** to whoever acts on the number.
- The premise behind the objection is true: intervals are widely misread. The conclusion does not follow.
- Match the representation to **numeracy and stakes**: intervals for technical audiences, fans for forecasts, **quantile dotplots and hypothetical outcome plots for general ones**.
- Frequency-based formats work because people reason well by counting and badly about continuous densities.
- When the **difference** is the quantity of interest, show its interval directly rather than expecting readers to compare two.
- Do not refuse the request. Offer the alternative.

interactionSequence.prompt: An executive asks you to remove confidence intervals from a forecast chart because they will confuse the board. Best response?
options: Removing them does not remove the uncertainty — it transfers it invisibly to the board, who then decide on false precision. Propose a quantile dotplot or fan encoding instead.
Agree: non-technical audiences should not be shown uncertainty, as it undermines confidence in the analysis.
Refuse, on the grounds that error bars are the only statistically valid way to show uncertainty.
Remove them from the chart and put the numbers in an appendix.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. It accepts the real premise, rejects the false conclusion, and offers a specific alternative — which is what makes it persuasive rather than merely principled.
This relocates risk to where nobody can see it, and the board acts on a precision the data never had.
Wrong on the facts — fans, dotplots, hypothetical outcome plots and textual framings are all valid — and it turns a design problem into a standoff.
The board reads the chart, not the appendix. This is omission with a paper trail.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The sentence that usually lands: *"the uncertainty is in the forecast whether or not it's on the chart — the only question is whether the board can see it. Let me show you a version they'll read correctly."*

It concedes nothing about the analysis, treats their concern as legitimate, and moves immediately to a solvable problem.

interactionSequence.prompt: You are showing a treatment effect to a public patient panel with mixed numeracy. The decision has high personal stakes. Which representation?
options: A quantile dotplot, because it lets people reason by counting rather than by interpreting a continuous range.
A 95% confidence interval, because it is the statistical standard.
A point estimate with a footnote describing the uncertainty in words.
A violin plot, because it shows the full distribution shape.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Frequency framings test well with general audiences precisely because counting is a robust everyday skill and density interpretation is not.
The standard in technical settings, and among the most misread formats outside them — particularly through the overlap heuristic.
Better than nothing, and a footnote is read by a small minority while the point estimate is read by everyone.
Violin plots require reading a density curve, which is a harder demand than an interval, not an easier one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The two variables in the selection rule are pulling in the same direction here — **low numeracy and high stakes both push toward frequency framing**, so this is an easy case.

The hard cases are mixed: a technical audience making a low-stakes routine decision is fine with intervals; a technical audience making an irreversible high-stakes one may still be better served by seeing draws from the distribution, because expertise does not fully protect against the overlap heuristic.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: name a number your organisation publishes with no uncertainty attached, where a decision is made on it. Who is currently absorbing that uncertainty without knowing?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Common answers: forecast revenue quoted as a single figure; a churn prediction; an A/B test result reported as a percentage lift with no interval; survey findings from a few hundred respondents presented as if from a census; any model output shown as a number.

The A/B one is worth dwelling on. A lift reported as "+4.2%" with no interval, on a test that was underpowered, is a decision made on noise — and the person absorbing that risk is usually whoever ships the change, who has no way to know the number was uncertain.

workedExamples.problem: The drug efficacy slide is going to two audiences: a conference of clinicians, and a patient advocacy group. Specify the uncertainty representation for each.
steps: **Identify the quantity of interest.** Not the two response rates. The **difference** — 3.7 points — because that is what the claim rests on.
**Establish what the data supports.** Difference 3.7 points, 95% interval −0.4 to 7.8. The interval crosses zero, so the result is compatible with no difference.
**Clinicians — assess numeracy and stakes.** High numeracy, and the stakes are professional judgment rather than an immediate personal decision. Intervals are read daily in this setting.

**Clinicians — specify.** A dot plot of both arms with intervals, plus a **second panel showing the difference with its interval and a zero reference line**. The second panel is what makes the crossing-zero fact unmissable rather than inferable.
**Patient group — assess numeracy and stakes.** Mixed numeracy, high personal stakes. Both variables push toward frequency framing.

**Patient group — specify.** A **quantile dotplot** of the difference: twenty dots, so a reader can see that some of them fall below zero and count how many. Paired with plain text: *"in roughly one in twenty plausible outcomes, the drug performs no better."*
**Check both against the title.** Neither version can carry "superior response demonstrated," because the interval crosses zero. Both need a title stating the observed difference and its uncertainty.

**Decide what happens if the request is to remove it.** Prepared response: offer the dotplot version, and if that is refused, state plainly in writing that the chart asserts a precision the study does not support. **This is the point at which the design decision becomes an ethical one, and it is worth having decided in advance rather than in the room.**
workedExamples.conclusion:
**Two audiences, two representations, one honest claim.**

The important move is step 1. Showing intervals on the two arms and expecting readers to compare them invites the overlap heuristic, which is wrong — two intervals can overlap while the difference is clearly non-zero, and vice versa. **If the difference is the claim, chart the difference.**

And step 8 is not rhetorical. Most of this course concerns judgment; this is one of a small number of places where a designer may be asked to publish something they believe misrepresents the evidence. Deciding your position before the meeting is what makes it possible to hold it during one.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why is omitting uncertainty not a simplification? State what happens to it instead.
What two properties of the situation select an uncertainty representation, and which direction do they push?
Name two frequency-based uncertainty formats and say why they outperform intervals with general audiences.
When the difference between two estimates is the claim, why is showing intervals on each estimate insufficient?

learningExperiences.title: Usable by everyone, everywhere

contentBlocks.content:
## The procedural failure that causes all the others

Accessibility is routinely scheduled as a QA pass. It cannot be one, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of diligence.

The decisions that determine whether a chart is accessible are made **in the first hour**: whether hue alone carries meaning, whether values are reachable only on hover, whether the takeaway exists anywhere in text. By the time an audit runs, those choices are load-bearing, and remediation means redesign rather than adjustment.

This is why the material sits here rather than in a compliance section. **These are encoding decisions**, and Section 3 already made most of them.

## Four requirements, all encoding decisions

**1. No single channel is load-bearing.** If hue alone distinguishes series, viewers with colour-vision deficiency lose the chart. **Redundant encoding** fixes it — direct labels, distinct shapes or dash patterns, ordered luminance differences.

**2. Contrast and size.** WCAG 2.x requires **4.5:1** for normal text and **3:1** for large text and for non-text elements essential to understanding. Thin gridlines and three-pixel scatter marks routinely fail. And remember from Section 3 that small marks lose apparent saturation, so a palette validated on swatches can fail on the actual marks.

**3. Non-pointer access to values.** Hover is unavailable on touch, invisible to keyboard navigation, unreachable by screen readers, and undiscoverable. Anything *required to read the chart* must be reachable without a pointer: keyboard-navigable points, an adjacent table, or values printed on the marks.

**4. A meaningful text alternative** — and this is where most teams get it wrong.

contentBlocks.altText: A red and green status pair and a blue and orange status pair, each shown three ways: as designed, converted to greyscale, and under a deuteranopia simulation. The red and green pair converts to two nearly identical greys and becomes indistinguishable under deuteranopia, losing the entire good-versus-bad distinction. The blue and orange pair remains clearly separable in both conditions.
contentBlocks.caption: The ten-second test: greyscale and colour-vision simulation.

contentBlocks.title: A data table is not a text alternative
contentBlocks.content:
A table is a fallback for **values**. The chart exists to communicate a **pattern** — a trend, a cluster, a gap.

Equivalence means equivalent *information*, and the information in a chart is structural. Asking a screen-reader user to reconstruct a trend from two hundred rows is not equivalent access; it is handing them the raw material and calling it a deliverable.

**What to write instead:** *"Line chart: enrolment fell steadily from 2019 to 2022, then rose sharply in 2023 to slightly above the 2019 level."* Then, separately, provide the numbers.

A useful discipline: **write the alt text before you build the chart.** If you cannot state the pattern in one sentence, the chart may not have a takeaway yet — which is a finding about the chart, not about the alt text.

## Two more that get missed

**Motion.** Animated transitions must respect reduced-motion preferences. If a transition carries information — object constancy through a sort, covered in the next experience — a non-motion equivalent has to convey the same thing.

**Numeracy.** A chart requiring log-scale literacy or interval interpretation is inaccessible to part of a general audience in a different but equally real way. The FT log-scale decision in Section 4 and the uncertainty formats in the last experience were both this problem.

## Localisation is not a translation step

Locale changes the artifact structurally, and none of it is fixable by swapping strings in a finished design:

- **Separators invert.** 1,240.50 becomes 1.240,50 in much of Europe.
- **Date order differs**, and an ambiguous 03/04 is a different day in two markets.
- **Units and currency** change magnitude and label width.
- **Translated labels run 40–60% longer**, which breaks direct labelling — the technique Section 3 recommended precisely to avoid legends.
- **Right-to-left layout mirrors** axis direction and reading order, so the whole composition flips.

These are layout rules, and they have to be decided when the layout is.

contentBlocks.altText: The same three-series chart in three locales. In English the direct labels fit beside the line endpoints. In German the longer translated labels overflow the plot area and collide. In Arabic the axis, the series direction and the reading order are all mirrored right to left. The decimal separator differs in each: a point, a comma, and Arabic-Indic numerals.
contentBlocks.caption: Localisation is not a translation step.

terms.definition: Carrying the same meaning in two or more channels so that no single channel is load-bearing.
Minimum contrast ratios required for legibility: 4.5:1 for normal text, and 3:1 for large text and for non-text elements essential to understanding, such as data marks and gridlines.
A description conveying a chart's type, scope and takeaway pattern — not merely its values.
Reduced ability to distinguish certain hues, most commonly red and green; makes hue-only encoding of meaning a structural failure for part of any large audience.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Treating a CVD-safe palette as accessibility done.** *(av-palette-is-enough)* — Contrast, redundant encoding, pointer-free access and text alternatives all remain open.

**2. Scheduling accessibility as a QA pass.** *(av-accessibility-is-qa)* — The determining choices are made in hour one; late audits produce redesigns, not fixes.

**3. Offering a data table as the accessible equivalent.** *(av-table-satisfies)* — A table gives values; the chart's job was the pattern.

**4. Treating localisation as string replacement.** *(av-localisation-is-translation)* — Label expansion, separator inversion and right-to-left mirroring are layout consequences.

**5. Putting required information in a tooltip.** *(iad-tooltips-for-key-values)* — Fails on touch, keyboard and screen readers, and is undiscoverable. Section 7 treats this as architecture.

**6. Validating contrast on the text and not on the marks.** — A three-pixel scatter dot is a non-text element essential to understanding, and it must meet 3:1.

**7. Assuming numeracy is universal.** — A log scale or a confidence interval excludes part of a general audience as surely as a low-contrast palette does.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Accessibility is decided **in the first hour**, in the encoding, not in a QA pass.
- Four requirements: **no load-bearing single channel**, adequate **contrast and size**, **non-pointer access** to required values, and a **text alternative conveying the pattern**.
- A data table supplies values, not the structure the chart existed to communicate.
- **Write the alt text before building the chart.** If the pattern will not fit in a sentence, the chart may not have one.
- **Greyscale is a ten-second proxy test** for most colour-vision failures.
- Localisation changes layout: separators, date order, label expansion, right-to-left mirroring.
- Numeracy is an accessibility constraint too.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which statement about accessible data visualization is correct?
options: A text alternative must convey the chart's takeaway pattern, not only its values, because the pattern is what the chart existed to communicate.
Providing the underlying data table fully satisfies the accessibility requirement.
Selecting a colourblind-safe palette makes a chart accessible.
Accessibility is best handled in a QA pass before release, when the design is stable.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Equivalence means equivalent information, and the information in a chart is structural.
A table is a fallback for values. Reconstructing a trend from two hundred rows is not equivalent access.
A safe palette addresses one condition. Contrast, redundant encoding, pointer-free access and text alternatives remain open.
Hue-as-sole-carrier and hover-only values are decided in hour one; by QA they are load-bearing.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All three distractors are things teams genuinely believe they have done when they say a chart is accessible. The useful diagnostic question in a review is not *is this accessible* but **which of the four requirements have we checked?** — because the answer is almost always "the palette" and the other three have not been examined.
hints: What does the chart exist to communicate?
Could a reader reconstruct it from the values alone?

interactionSequence.prompt: A chart system built for an English-language product is rolling out across twelve markets including Arabic and German. What is most likely to break **structurally**?
options: Direct labels sized for English overflow under longer translations, separators and date order differ by locale, and right-to-left layout mirrors axis direction and reading order.
Nothing structural — localisation is a matter of swapping the label strings.
Only the font, since the layout is numeric and therefore locale-neutral.
Only the colour palette, since colour meanings differ between cultures.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Each of these is a layout rule, and none is fixable after the design is finished.
Label expansion of 40–60%, separator inversion and mirrored layout are structural consequences that strings cannot absorb.
Numbers are among the least locale-neutral elements: separators, grouping, currency and date order all vary.
Cultural colour association is worth considering and is not the main structural risk here.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
There is a cheap test that catches most of this: **render every chart with the longest available translation of every label, in a right-to-left locale, with comma decimal separators — before you sign off the layout.** Ten minutes, and it moves the whole class of failures from post-launch to pre-launch.

Note also that label expansion attacks direct labelling specifically, which is the technique Section 3 recommended to escape legends. That tension is real and needs a documented fallback.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: write the text alternative for a chart you have shipped. One sentence, stating the pattern rather than the values. Then say whether writing it revealed anything about the chart.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The common discovery is that the sentence is hard to write — not because describing is difficult, but because the chart shows several things and emphasises none. That is a finding about the chart.

When the alt text writes itself, the chart usually has a clear takeaway. When it comes out as "it shows revenue, cost and margin by quarter for five regions," you have written a description of the axes rather than of a pattern, and the chart probably needs the annotation work in the next experience before it needs alt text.

workedExamples.problem: Audit a clinical trial results dashboard against the four requirements. It uses red and green to mark arms above and below the control, values appear on hover, the palette was chosen for CVD safety, and a CSV download is provided.
steps: **Requirement 1 — is any single channel load-bearing?** The palette is CVD-safe, so the two arms remain distinguishable. But above-versus-below control is carried by **hue alone**, and in greyscale the distinction disappears. *Fails.* Fix: add position — sort arms by effect with a zero reference line — plus a direct label. Note that the sorting fix also improves the chart for everyone, which is usually the case.

**Requirement 2 — contrast and size.** Text passes. The scatter marks are 3px and the gridlines are 1px at low contrast; both are non-text elements essential to understanding and must meet 3:1. *Fails.* Fix: increase mark size and gridline contrast, and re-check at the actual rendered size rather than in the design tool.

**Requirement 3 — non-pointer access.** All values are hover-only. *Fails, and this is the most consequential one.* Fix: print effect sizes on the marks, make points keyboard-focusable with accessible names, and keep hover for supplementary detail only.

**Requirement 4 — text alternative.** A CSV download is provided and no pattern description exists. *Fails.* Fix: write the pattern — *"Dot plot of six trial arms; four show effects above control, two below, and only one interval excludes zero."*

**Check the CSV claim specifically.** The team believes the download satisfies the requirement. It does not: it supplies values without the structure, and it is also the thing they will point to when challenged. **This is worth naming explicitly in the audit** so the belief is corrected rather than left in place.
**Check motion.** Arms re-sort with an animated transition on filter change, with no reduced-motion handling. *Fails.* Fix: respect the preference and provide a non-motion equivalent.

**Check numeracy.** Effects are shown with 95% intervals to a mixed audience including patient representatives. Not a WCAG issue and a real access barrier. Fix: consider the quantile dotplot from the previous experience for the patient-facing view.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**A chart that the team believed was accessible failed five of the four requirements — because the one they had checked was the palette.**

That is the characteristic shape of this failure. Palette selection is visible, satisfying, and the easiest of the four, so it becomes a proxy for the whole. Meanwhile hover-only values exclude every touch, keyboard and screen-reader user, and nobody has looked.

Notice too how many fixes improved the chart generally. Sorting by effect with a zero line, printing values on marks, larger marks — none of these is a concession. **Accessible encoding decisions are usually just better encoding decisions**, which is the argument that gets them prioritised.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the four accessibility requirements, all of which are encoding decisions.
What must a text alternative convey that a data table does not, and when should you write it?
State the WCAG contrast minimums for normal text and for non-text elements essential to understanding.
Name three things that break structurally when a chart system is localised, and the ten-minute test that catches them.

learningExperiences.title: Saying what the chart shows

contentBlocks.content:
## "Let the data speak for itself"

It can't, and the belief that it can is the most consequential misconception in this section.

Section 4 established that every representation reveals some structures and conceals others. A chart therefore arrives **already framed**. Declining to annotate does not produce neutrality — it produces an **unguided viewer** who supplies their own interpretation from whatever is most visually salient, which is frequently the wrong thing.

contentBlocks.title: Where the line actually is
contentBlocks.content:
**Legitimate:** stating what the chart shows. *"Renewable share rose 11 points since 2021."*

**Illegitimate:** asserting what it does not show. *"Renewables caused the price decline."* — correlation stated as causation. *"Superior response demonstrated."* — a statistical claim the data does not support.

**The line is fidelity to the data, not absence of guidance.**

A chart with an accurate, specific takeaway title is *more* honest than one with a neutral topic title, because it makes the designer's framing explicit and therefore **contestable**. "Q3 Revenue by Region" hides a framing. "West region drove 70% of Q3 growth" exposes one, and can be checked.

## The annotation layer, in order of value

1. **Takeaway title.** A sentence, not a topic. The single highest-leverage element in explanatory work and the one most often wasted.
2. **Subtitle carrying scope** — units, population, date range, comparator, source. Everything a reader needs to know the boundaries of the claim.
3. **In-plot annotation** marking the specific features that support the takeaway.
4. **Reference marks** — targets, thresholds, prior periods, benchmarks. These convert difficult absolute judgments into easy comparative ones, which is a *perceptual* upgrade as much as a narrative one.
5. **Direct labels** replacing legends, per Section 3.
6. **Source and method note.** What makes the chart auditable.

contentBlocks.altText: The same adherence series twice. The first has only a topic title reading Medication Adherence and an unmarked line. The second carries a takeaway title stating that adherence rose thirteen points with most of the gain after the programme launch, a subtitle giving population, definition, date range and the absence of a control group, a vertical reference line marking the launch, a horizontal line at the eighty percent clinical target showing the endpoint remains below it, endpoint values labelled, and a source and method note.
contentBlocks.caption: The annotation layer, added one element at a time.

contentBlocks.title: The element that proves you are not selling
contentBlocks.content:
In that figure, the 80% target line is the one a purely persuasive version would have omitted — because it shows the endpoint is **still below target**.

Including what complicates your own claim is what makes the rest of it credible. A sceptical reader who finds the inconvenient fact already on the chart stops looking for what else you hid.

Make this a habit: **every annotated chart carries one element that complicates its own headline**, where the data warrants one.

## Sequence and motion

For multi-step narratives, the same principles operate over time.

**Staged reveal.** Introduce one layer at a time so the reader builds the chart's structure before being asked to read it. Most useful when the encoding is unfamiliar — the justified-novelty forms from Section 5, for instance.

**Object constancy.** When a chart changes state — sorts, filters, updates — a staged transition that preserves mark identity lets the viewer *track which mark became which*. An abrupt swap forces them to re-read from scratch. This is Gestalt common fate from Section 3, doing real work.

**And the counterweight:** gratuitous motion competes for the same attention budget as a highlight, and can defeat the pop-out it was meant to support. Animation is not free.

**Every animation must name the relationship it preserves**, and must have a reduced-motion equivalent that conveys the same thing.

terms.definition: A title stating what the chart shows as a sentence, rather than naming its topic.
A target, threshold, benchmark or prior-period line that converts a difficult absolute judgment into an easy comparative one.
Preservation of mark identity through a transition so that a viewer can track which element became which across a state change.
A visualization that constrains to a single reading and makes it unmissable.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Using a topic title to stay neutral.** *(na-data-speaks-for-itself)* — Neutrality is not achieved by silence; an unguided reader invents a takeaway from whatever is salient.

**2. Believing an explicit takeaway is editorialising.** *(na-annotation-is-editorialising)* — Stating what the chart shows differs from asserting what it does not. An explicit claim is more auditable, not less.

**3. Annotating only what supports the story.** — The reference line showing you are still below target is what makes the rest credible.

**4. Treating explanatory design as polished exploratory design.** *(na-explanatory-is-polished-exploratory)* — The requirements invert rather than intensify.

**5. Treating transitions as polish.** *(na-animation-is-decoration)* — They carry identity information. An abrupt swap makes the viewer re-read the chart.

**6. Putting the scope in surrounding copy.** — Section 4's screenshot problem: anything outside the frame is optional as far as a sharing reader is concerned.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **There is no neutral chart.** Declining to annotate produces an unguided reader, not an unbiased one.
- The ethical line is **fidelity to the data**: state what the chart shows, never what it does not.
- An explicit takeaway is **more auditable** than a topic title, because the framing becomes contestable.
- The layer, in order: **takeaway title → scope subtitle → in-plot annotation → reference marks → direct labels → source and method note**.
- Reference marks convert absolute judgments into comparative ones — a perceptual upgrade as well as a narrative one.
- **Include one element that complicates your own claim.** It is what makes the rest credible.
- Transitions carry information. Name the relationship each preserves, and provide a reduced-motion equivalent.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which chart title stays within what a two-series line chart of advertising spend and revenue over twelve months can support?
options: Revenue and ad spend both rose through 2025, with revenue growth concentrated in the third quarter.
Increased ad spend drove 2025 revenue growth.
Advertising Spend and Revenue, 2025.
Marketing efficiency improved in 2025.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. It states the co-movement and its timing — exactly what is visible — without asserting a mechanism.
Two co-moving series support association, not causation; the chart cannot exclude reverse causation or a common cause.
A topic title feels safe but hands framing to the reader, who takes it from whatever is most salient.
Efficiency is a ratio the chart does not display; the claim requires a quantity that is not shown.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Note that option C is the one most designers pick when they are being careful — and it is the option that leaves the causal reading fully available while taking no responsibility for it. A reader who sees two rising lines under a neutral title will very often conclude option B on their own.

**The neutral title does not prevent the causal reading. It just means you did not make it and cannot be corrected on it.**

interactionSequence.prompt: A dashboard re-sorts its bars instantly when a filter is applied. Users report they 'lose track of what happened'. What is at stake?
options: Object constancy: a staged transition preserving mark identity lets viewers track which bar became which, so the change is understood rather than re-read from scratch.
Animation is decoration, so the fix is to remove the sorting behaviour entirely.
The bars should be re-coloured after sorting so users can find them again.
Users need onboarding explaining that the chart re-sorts.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct — and it needs a reduced-motion equivalent, because the transition is carrying information rather than decorating.
Transitions carry identity information; treating them as polish is what produced the abrupt swap.
Recolouring adds a second identity system and spends attention without conveying the movement itself.
Explaining a comprehension failure is not the same as removing it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The reduced-motion requirement is the part that gets missed, and it has a real design consequence: if the transition is the only thing conveying *what moved where*, then users who have disabled motion lose that information entirely.

The usual answer is a non-motion equivalent that shows change explicitly — a rank-change indicator, a previous-position ghost, or an explicit 'moved up 3' label. Deciding that is part of specifying the animation, not an afterthought.

interactionSequence.prompt: Take a chart you have made. Write its takeaway title, then write the one annotation that complicates that takeaway. If nothing complicates it, say why you are confident of that.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Something almost always complicates it: the trend that reverses in the last two periods, the segment moving the other way, the target still unmet, the sample that shrank, the comparison period that was unusual.

If you genuinely found nothing, the useful check is whether you looked or whether the chart was built to avoid the question. Charts that survive scrutiny usually do so because someone went looking for the inconvenient fact first.

interactionSequence.prompt: Have you ever been asked to make a chart's message stronger than you thought the data supported? What did you do, and what would you do differently with this section's framing available?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Most people have. The framing that tends to help is that the request is usually not for dishonesty — it is for **confidence**, and confidence is often available honestly through better annotation, a clearer takeaway, and a reference mark that makes the real finding land harder.

Where that is not enough, the distinction to hold is between the title and the data: you can decline to write a title the data does not support while still helping them find the strongest true claim. "I can't write that it's proven, and I can tell you what we *can* say and make it land" keeps you useful and keeps the artifact honest.

Section 7 gives this an organisational form: a review process with an integrity pass means this conversation happens in a room with criteria rather than one-to-one under deadline.

workedExamples.problem: A line chart shows medication adherence rising from 61% to 74% over eighteen months, with a patient-support programme launched at month six and no control group. Build the annotation layer.
steps: **State the honest takeaway.** What does the chart show? Adherence rose 13 points over 18 months, with the increase concentrated after month six. What does it *not* show? That the programme caused the rise — there is no control group, and seasonal or cohort effects are unexcluded.

**Write the title inside that boundary.** ❌ *"Support programme boosts adherence 13 points"* asserts causation. ✅ *"Adherence rose 13 points over 18 months, with most of the gain after the programme launch"* states the temporal association, which is exactly what is visible.

**Write the subtitle for scope.** *"Patients with ≥2 refills, N=4,120. Adherence = PDC ≥ 80%. Jan 2024–Jun 2025. No control group."* That last clause is the one people omit and the one that makes the chart trustworthy.
**Add in-plot annotation.** A vertical reference line at month six labelled *Programme launch*. This converts "did it change after month six?" from a memory task into a direct visual comparison.

**Add the reference mark that complicates the story.** A horizontal line at the 80% clinical target — so the reader sees both the improvement *and* that the endpoint remains below target. **This is the integrity check on your own narrative.**
**Direct-label the endpoints.** 61% at the start, 74% at the end, so the headline figure is verifiable on the chart rather than only in the title.
**Add the source and method note.** Where the data came from, how PDC was computed, what was excluded.

**Write the text alternative**, per the previous experience: *"Line chart of medication adherence, January 2024 to June 2025. Adherence is roughly flat near 61% through month five, then rises steadily to 74% by month 18, remaining below the 80% clinical target throughout."*
**Check placement against the screenshot problem.** Title, subtitle and both reference lines sit inside the plot frame. Anything a reader needs must survive a crop.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The annotated chart makes a narrower claim than the unannotated one implied, and is far more persuasive to a sceptical audience.**

Every element of its framing is stated and checkable — which is the whole argument. A reader who can see the population, the definition, the date range, the missing control group and the unmet target has no reason to suspect anything further is hidden.

**Annotation is not decoration applied on top of analysis. It is where the analysis declares its boundaries.** The unannotated version was not more neutral; it was the same claim with the boundaries left off.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the boundary between legitimate framing and editorialising in a chart title, in one sentence.
List the annotation layer in order of value, from most to least.
Why does including an annotation that complicates your own headline make the chart more persuasive rather than less?
What does a staged transition preserve that an abrupt state swap destroys, and what must accompany any animation?

transferExercises.context: Employee compensation reporting — internally political, externally scrutinised.
transferExercises.scenario: An HR team publishes an annual pay-gap report. The headline chart shows the mean gap narrowing from 14.2% to 11.8% over three years. The underlying distribution is skewed, the workforce composition changed substantially over the period, and the median gap moved much less.
transferExercises.task: In under 300 words: write a takeaway title that stays inside what the data supports; specify the subtitle's scope fields; name the one annotation that complicates the headline and explain why you would include it; and state what you would do if asked to remove it.
successCriteria: Title states the mean change without implying the underlying gap closed by that amount.
Subtitle covers population, statistic used, period, and the composition change.
Identifies the median — or the composition effect from Section 2 — as the complicating annotation.
The response to removal offers an alternative framing rather than either capitulating or refusing flatly.
Does not assert a cause for the narrowing.

learningExperiences.title: When a chart identifies someone

contentBlocks.content:
## Aggregation is not anonymisation

An internal dashboard breaks engagement survey results down by department, office and seniority, with free filtering. It shows aggregates only — no names, no individual records.

Two filters in, a cell contains three people. Anyone who knows the team knows who they are, and the dashboard has just published their survey responses.

contentBlocks.altText: A nine-row breakdown of headcount by department and location shown twice. As built, three cells contain fewer than ten people, including one with two and one with three, each rendered as a small bar with its count visible. With a minimum-cell threshold applied, those three cells are replaced by a visible hatched pattern labelled suppressed, so the reader can see that a value exists and is withheld rather than being absent.
contentBlocks.caption: Aggregation is not anonymisation.

contentBlocks.content:
## Three mechanisms

**Small cells re-identify.** A regional breakdown where one category contains three people, a filter combination isolating a single team, a cross-tab with one occupied cell. Aggregation reduces disclosure risk; it does not eliminate it.

**Differencing.** Two published views that differ by one record reveal that record. This is the mechanism free filtering multiplies — every additional filter dimension multiplies the number of views an observer can compare against each other. **A dashboard with eight filters is publishing an enormous number of aggregates, most of which nobody designed.**

**Outliers self-identify.** A scatterplot of salary against tenure identifies the longest-serving employee to any colleague, regardless of aggregation, because they know who that is.

contentBlocks.title: Controls
contentBlocks.content:
**Minimum cell threshold.** Suppress cells below a stated n — commonly 5 or 10 depending on sensitivity. **Suppress visibly, never silently**: a hatched cell labelled *suppressed* tells the reader a value exists and is withheld, where a blank cell reads as zero or as missing data and reintroduces Section 1's null-versus-zero failure.

**Complementary suppression.** If one cell in a row is suppressed and the row total is shown, the suppressed value is recoverable by subtraction. A second cell must be suppressed too.

**Constrain the filter space.** Section 7's argument arriving early: fewer filter dimensions means fewer derived views, which means less differencing surface. Scoping is a privacy control as well as a design one.

**Round or band.** Reporting ranges rather than exact counts reduces precision and disclosure risk together.

terms.definition: Techniques preventing identification of individuals from published aggregates, including minimum cell thresholds, suppression and limits on differencing across filtered views.
Withholding or masking aggregate values computed from too few records, shown visibly rather than silently omitted.
The pattern of absent values and, critically, the reasons for their absence — unmeasured is not the same as measured as zero.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Believing aggregation is anonymisation.** *(gi-aggregation-is-anonymous)* — A cell of three is close to a named list to anyone who knows the group.

**2. Suppressing silently.** — A blank cell reads as zero or as missing. Suppress visibly and label it.

**3. Suppressing one cell and showing the total.** — The suppressed value is recoverable by subtraction. Complementary suppression is required.

**4. Treating this as legal's problem.** — The filter architecture that creates the differencing surface is a design decision, made by you.

**5. Assuming internal means safe.** — Colleagues are the people most able to re-identify a small cell, because they know who is in it.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **Aggregation reduces disclosure risk without eliminating it.** Small cells re-identify.
- **Free filtering multiplies the differencing surface** — every extra dimension publishes more aggregates than anyone designed.
- Apply a **minimum cell threshold**, and **suppress visibly** rather than silently, or you recreate the null-versus-zero failure.
- Use **complementary suppression** where a row total would let the value be recovered.
- Constraining the filter space is a privacy control as well as a design one.
- Internal audiences are the ones most able to re-identify, not the least.

interactionSequence.prompt: An internal dashboard breaks engagement metrics by department, office and seniority with free filtering. Some cells contain two or three people. What is the integrity concern?
options: Small cells re-identify individuals, and free filtering lets a user difference views against each other — so a minimum cell threshold with visible suppression is required.
There is no concern: the data is aggregated, so individuals cannot be identified.
The only concern is that small cells produce noisy percentages, which should be rounded.
The filter panel is too complex and should be simplified for usability.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Aggregation reduces disclosure risk without eliminating it, and interactivity multiplies the number of comparable views.
Aggregation is not anonymisation; a cell of three is close to a named list to anyone who knows the department.
Instability is a real and separate statistical issue. Rounding does not prevent identification.
Usability matters, and simplifying for clarity does not by itself address the disclosure risk the filters create.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Option D is interesting because the *action* is right for the wrong reason. Reducing the filter dimensions genuinely does reduce disclosure risk — Section 7 argues for it on design grounds and it turns out to have a privacy dividend.

But arriving there by accident means the threshold never gets set, and the remaining filters still expose small cells. The control has to be deliberate.

interactionSequence.prompt: You suppress one cell in a row for having n=3. The row total is displayed and all other cells are shown. What have you actually protected, and what would you do?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Nothing.** The suppressed value is the total minus the visible cells — recoverable by anyone with a calculator, and the suppression marker helpfully tells them exactly where to look.

The control is **complementary suppression**: suppress a second cell in the same row, conventionally the next-smallest, so that neither can be recovered. If the table has both row and column totals, the analysis extends in both directions and gets genuinely fiddly — which is why disclosure control belongs in the specification rather than being improvised at build time.

The design consequence worth noting: suppression is not a filter applied at the end. It changes what the table can show, so it has to be decided when the table is designed.
hints: Can the reader compute the suppressed value?
What else in the row would have to be hidden?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that diagnosis?

interactionSequence.prompt: Find the filter combination in a dashboard you have access to that isolates the fewest records. How few can you get it to? Did anyone design that view?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
People are routinely able to get to n=1 or n=2 in under a minute, and the answer to the second question is almost always no — nobody designed that view, it simply exists because the filters compose.

That is the argument to bring to a team: **the dashboard publishes every combination, not just the ones anyone imagined.** It reframes a filter panel from a feature into a surface with a size, and makes the threshold an obvious requirement rather than an imposition.

workedExamples.problem: Specify disclosure control for an internal engagement dashboard with five filter dimensions and a workforce of 1,800 across departments ranging from 4 to 300 people.
steps: **Size the differencing surface.** Five filter dimensions compose into a large number of derived views. Nobody designed most of them. State this in the specification, because it is the fact that justifies everything else.

**Set a threshold and justify it.** Engagement responses are sensitive, and colleagues can re-identify easily, so **n ≥ 10** rather than 5. Record the reasoning, since the number will be challenged as too conservative.

**Specify visible suppression.** Suppressed cells render with a distinct hatched treatment and the label *suppressed (n < 10)*. **Never blank**, because a blank reads as zero — Section 1's null-versus-zero failure, arriving with a privacy consequence.
**Specify complementary suppression.** Where a row or column total is displayed and exactly one cell is suppressed, suppress the next-smallest cell in that row or column as well.

**Constrain the filter space.** Restrict simultaneous filtering to two dimensions, or pre-compute the permitted breakdowns. This is scoping, which Section 7 argues for on design grounds and which turns out to shrink the disclosure surface at the same time.

**Handle the small departments explicitly.** A department of four can never be shown alone. Either roll it into a parent grouping, or exclude departmental breakdown entirely for units below threshold — and say which, so its members know their responses are not being displayed.

**Specify the empty state honestly.** When a filter combination returns a suppressed result, the message must distinguish *no data matches* from *result withheld for privacy*. These are different facts and conflating them is a data-semantics error.
**Write the disclosure row into the state inventory.** Section 7's specification format has a row for it, alongside empty, loading, partial, error and stale.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The controls that protect people here are the same controls that make the dashboard better.**

Constraining the filter space, distinguishing suppressed from empty, and rolling small units into meaningful parents are all things Section 7 will argue for on pure design grounds — fewer unmade decisions handed to users, honest empty states, scoping to a role.

That alignment is worth naming when you propose this, because disclosure control is frequently heard as a constraint imposed from outside. **It is mostly the same discipline as good dashboard architecture, arriving with a different justification.**

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the three mechanisms by which an aggregated chart can identify an individual.
Why must suppression be visible rather than silent, and which earlier failure does silent suppression recreate?
You suppress one cell in a row whose total is displayed. What has been protected, and what further control is needed?

learningExperiences.title: Case study: the chart that was not made

contentBlocks.content:
## The situation

On 28 January 1986 the Space Shuttle *Challenger* broke apart shortly after launch, killing all seven crew members. The night before, engineers at Morton Thiokol argued against launching, believing cold temperatures degraded the resilience of the solid rocket booster O-rings. They lost the argument. The Rogers Commission subsequently identified O-ring failure in cold conditions as the physical cause.

## The graphical reading

Edward Tufte's widely-taught analysis examines the charts used that night. His central claim: the engineers possessed data sufficient to make the case, and the charts they produced did not organise it so the case became visible.

The material presented emphasised individual damage incidents and rocket-by-rocket detail rather than the single relationship that mattered — **damage plotted against launch temperature**.

Critically, the flights with **no damage** were largely absent from the presented material. Those are precisely the observations that establish the pattern, because they clustered at warm temperatures. And the forecast launch temperature was far colder than any prior launch — an extrapolation beyond the entire observed range, which a temperature-axis scatterplot would have made unmissable and which the presented format did not.

contentBlocks.title: Integrity runs in both directions
contentBlocks.content:
The familiar failure mode in this section is a chart that **overstates** — a truncated axis, a selected range, an over-claiming title.

This is the opposite. Correct data, arranged so the decisive relationship was **not visible**.

**Concealment through arrangement is a distortion**, and it is the harder one to audit for, because nothing on the page is wrong. There is no lie factor to compute. The finding is about what is absent.

## The contested reading, which matters

Tufte's account has been challenged. Historians of the episode — most notably Diane Vaughan — have argued that the failure was substantially **organisational**: normalised deviance, production pressure, and a reversed burden of proof in which engineers were asked to prove the launch was *unsafe* rather than being asked to establish that it was safe. Vaughan also documents that the underlying data was messier and more ambiguous than a clean retelling suggests.

**Both readings are useful, and the disagreement is itself the lesson.**

It would be comfortable to conclude that a better chart would have saved the crew. That conclusion is not supported, and believing it would leave you badly prepared. Charts operate inside organisations, under pressure, with burdens of proof set by someone else. **Being right and being heard are different problems**, and no amount of encoding skill solves the second one.

That is precisely why `critique-and-leadership` exists as a competency, and why Section 7 spends its time on process rather than on pixels.

terms.definition: The pattern of absent values and, critically, the reasons for their absence — unmeasured is not the same as measured as zero.
A target, threshold, benchmark or prior-period line that converts a difficult absolute judgment into an easy comparative one.
A decision about time range, comparison group, denominator or aggregation statistic that shapes the reading without altering any number.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors this case illustrates
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Auditing only for overstatement.** *(gi-accurate-numbers-honest)* — A chart can fail by concealing the decisive relationship while every value is correct.

**2. Omitting the non-events.** *(ds-file-is-ground-truth)* — The zero-damage flights were data. Excluding them removed the contrast that made temperature the story. Section 1's missingness lesson at maximum consequence.

**3. Withholding the conclusion from the artifact.** *(na-data-speaks-for-itself)* — The engineers had the conclusion and did not put it in the chart. In a contested, time-pressured room, the audience will not do the analytical work for you.

**4. Not marking the extrapolation.** — The forecast temperature was outside the entire observed range. A reference mark showing that would have made the risk structural rather than arguable.

**5. Believing a better chart is sufficient.** — Vaughan's account is the corrective. Encoding skill does not fix a reversed burden of proof.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **Graphical integrity runs in both directions.** Concealment through arrangement is a distortion, and it is harder to audit because nothing on the page is wrong.
- **Omitting the non-events destroyed the pattern.** The zero-damage flights were the contrast that made temperature visible.
- The **annotation layer was the missing element**: the engineers held the conclusion and left it out of the artifact.
- A **reference mark** showing that the forecast temperature lay outside all prior experience would have made the extrapolation unmissable.
- The organisational reading is a genuine corrective. **Being right and being heard are different problems** — which is Section 7's subject.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which omission most damaged the engineers' case, on the graphical reading?
options: The flights with no O-ring damage, which clustered at warm temperatures and supplied the contrast establishing the relationship.
The exact numerical values of the damage measurements.
The names of the engineers who conducted the analysis.
The cost implications of delaying the launch.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Without the non-events there is no contrast, and damage incidents alone look scattered rather than temperature-dependent.
Precise values were available; the problem was the absence of a whole class of observations, not the precision of the ones shown.
Attribution does not affect whether the relationship is visible.
Cost was a live organisational pressure and not a missing element of the technical case.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
This generalises beyond the case, and it is worth carrying: **when you show only the events, you cannot show a rate or a relationship.** A chart of incidents alone answers 'where did incidents happen', never 'what makes incidents more likely'.

It is Section 2's denominator problem in a different costume — the non-events are the denominator, and leaving them out makes the pattern uncomputable as well as invisible.

interactionSequence.prompt: You believe a decision your organisation is about to make is unsupported by the data, and you have one chart and five minutes. Using this section, what do you build — and what do you accept the chart cannot do?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Build:** the single relationship the decision turns on, with the non-events included; a reference mark showing where the proposed condition sits relative to all prior experience — especially if it sits outside it; a takeaway title stating the finding in one sentence; and the scope subtitle, so the claim's boundaries are visible and cannot be attacked as overreach.

**Accept:** the chart cannot change who bears the burden of proof, cannot create time that does not exist, and cannot make a room that has already decided reconsider. Vaughan's account is the evidence for that.

What it *can* do is make your position legible, checkable and on the record — which is a real thing to achieve, and is sometimes the most that is available. Section 7 addresses the rest: getting an integrity pass into the review process *before* the pressured meeting, so the argument happens where criteria exist.
hints: What observations are you tempted to leave out?
Where does the proposed condition sit relative to everything previously observed?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you this would land in your organisation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Tufte's reading says the chart failed. Vaughan's says the organisation did. Which reading is more useful to you in your current role, and what does your answer suggest about where to put your effort?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Both, and the balance shifts with seniority. Early in a career the graphical reading is more actionable — you control the artifact and you can make it better. As you take on a lead role, the organisational reading becomes the one that matters, because you start being able to change *when* the argument happens, *what criteria* it is held against, and *who* has to prove what.

If your answer leaned organisational, Section 7 is written for you. If it leaned graphical, Section 7 is the part you will find least intuitive and most necessary.

workedExamples.problem: Reconstruct the chart the engineers needed, using this section's tools only.
steps: **Identify the relationship the decision turns on.** O-ring damage against launch temperature. One relationship, two variables.

**Include every observation, not only the events.** All prior launches, damaged and undamaged. The undamaged flights are not absence of data — they are measurements of zero, and Section 1 established that the distinction matters.

**Choose the encoding.** Scatterplot: temperature on x, a damage index on y. Position on a common scale, rank 1, for both variables. No aggregation, because the sample is small enough to show entirely.

**Add the reference mark that carries the argument.** A vertical line at the forecast launch temperature. It falls far to the left of every prior observation, and *that spatial fact is the case*: the proposal is an extrapolation beyond all experience.

**Check what the reference mark does perceptually.** It converts "is 29°F unusually cold for a launch?" — a question requiring knowledge of the launch history — into "is this line left of all the dots?", which is immediate and requires nothing.

**Write the takeaway title inside what the data supports.** Not *"launching will cause failure"*. Something like *"All prior launches occurred above 53°F; tomorrow's forecast is 29°F, and damage incidents cluster at the cold end of our experience."* Every clause is checkable on the chart.
**Write the scope subtitle.** Number of prior launches, how the damage index is defined, what is excluded.
**Add the element that complicates it.** The relationship is noisy and the sample is small. Say so. A sceptical engineer who finds that acknowledged stops looking for what else was smoothed over.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The chart that was needed is a scatterplot with a reference line, and it uses nothing from this course beyond Sections 1, 3 and 6.**

The reference mark is doing most of the work, which is worth noticing given how routinely reference lines are treated as optional polish. It converts a judgment requiring domain memory into a spatial comparison a tired person can make at midnight — which is exactly the condition under which the decision was actually taken.

And the honest coda: **this chart might not have changed the outcome.** Vaughan's account suggests the burden of proof had already been reversed, and a better artifact entering that room may have lost anyway. Building it would still have been the right thing to do, and Section 7 is about the other half of the problem.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Give an example of an integrity failure that understates rather than exaggerates, and say why it is harder to audit.
Why can a chart of events alone never establish a relationship? Connect it to the Section 2 idea it resembles.
What does the organisational reading of the Challenger episode add that the graphical reading omits?

learningExperiences.title: Section quiz: integrity, accessibility and narrative

contentBlocks.content: Answer from memory. This is the largest section in the course and the one whose material most often has to be defended out loud, so pay attention to which items you were confident and wrong about.

contentBlocks.title: How this is scored
contentBlocks.content: Formative; shapes your review queue. The graded assessments are `assess-graphical-integrity`, `assess-accessible-viz` and `assess-narrative-annotation`.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** If every number in a chart is arithmetically correct, the chart cannot be misleading.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Range, comparison group, denominator, aggregation statistic and aspect ratio all mislead while every number stays correct.
Correct. Arithmetic correctness is necessary and badly insufficient — framing does the work that numbers do not.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Arithmetic correctness is necessary and badly insufficient — framing does the work that numbers do not.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Every quantitative axis must start at zero.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. True for length encodings, where the mark's length is the value. For position encodings of quantities with no meaningful zero, forcing zero conceals the signal.
Correct. The baseline must match what the encoding claims — zero for length, the data's meaningful reference for position.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. The baseline must match what the encoding claims — zero for length, the data's meaningful reference for position.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Omitting uncertainty from a chart shown to a non-technical audience protects them from confusion.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. It transfers the uncertainty invisibly to the decision-maker, who acts on false precision without knowing. The premise about misreading is true; the conclusion is not.
Correct. Choose a representation matched to numeracy and stakes — quantile dotplots and fan encodings work where intervals do not.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Choose a representation matched to numeracy and stakes — quantile dotplots and fan encodings work where intervals do not.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Providing the underlying data table satisfies a chart's text-alternative requirement.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. A table supplies values; the chart existed to communicate a pattern. Equivalence means equivalent information.
Correct. Describe the pattern in a sentence, then provide the values separately.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Describe the pattern in a sentence, then provide the values separately.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Accessibility is best addressed in a QA pass once the design is stable.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Hue-as-sole-carrier and hover-only values are decided in the first hour; by QA they are load-bearing and remediation means redesign.
Correct. The four requirements are encoding decisions and belong in the definition of done at wireframe stage.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. The four requirements are encoding decisions and belong in the definition of done at wireframe stage.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Localising a chart system for new markets is essentially a matter of translating the labels.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Label expansion, separator inversion, date order and right-to-left mirroring are layout consequences that strings cannot absorb.
Correct. These are layout rules and must be decided when the layout is.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. These are layout rules and must be decided when the layout is.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** A topic title such as 'Q3 Revenue by Region' is more neutral than a title stating a finding.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. It hides a framing rather than removing one, and leaves the reader to construct a takeaway from whatever is salient. An explicit claim is contestable; a hidden one is not.
Correct. Stating what the chart shows is legitimate and auditable; the line is fidelity to the data, not absence of guidance.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Stating what the chart shows is legitimate and auditable; the line is fidelity to the data, not absence of guidance.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Once data is aggregated, a chart cannot identify an individual.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Small cells re-identify, free filtering permits differencing, and outliers self-identify to anyone who knows the group.
Correct. Aggregation reduces disclosure risk without eliminating it — apply a minimum cell threshold and suppress visibly.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Aggregation reduces disclosure risk without eliminating it — apply a minimum cell threshold and suppress visibly.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** A charity's report shows a bar chart of programme spend per beneficiary, y-axis from £180 to £240, three years, titled 'Sustained investment in our beneficiaries'. Give your findings.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Baseline truncation on a length encoding** — bars run from £180, so bar length no longer represents the value and year-on-year differences are visually exaggerated. Estimate the lie factor if the values allow.

**Denominator doing invisible work** — spend *per beneficiary* rises if beneficiary numbers fall. The chart is compatible with the charity serving far fewer people.

**Title over-claims and is vague** — 'sustained investment' asserts a trajectory the truncated bars manufacture, and names no quantity.

**Range possibly selected**, and no definition of 'beneficiary' or 'programme spend' anywhere.
