**Remediation:** zero baseline or re-encode as a dot plot; a title stating the actual change with its magnitude; a subtitle carrying beneficiary counts, definitions and source.

Strong answers note that the denominator finding is more consequential than the baseline one, even though the baseline is what an auditor sees first.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which item did you answer confidently and get wrong? Name the belief you held instead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The zero-baseline item catches the most people, and usually the most conscientious ones — it is a rule learned early, applied faithfully, and taught without its scope.

If that was yours, the repair is to hold the principle rather than the cases: **the baseline must match what the encoding claims.** You will be able to derive both cases from it, and you will not misapply it to the next encoding type you meet.

retrievalPractice.prompt: In what order do you audit a chart, and why does the axis come after the framing?

sections.title: Interactive Systems and Design Leadership
sections.description: Scaling from artifact to system to practice. Covers dashboard architecture and the primacy of the default view, metric definition as governed design surface, visualization design systems and engineering specification, and structured critique with mode-matched success measures. Introduces no new theory: each competency is the organisational form of one established earlier.

learningObjectives.description: Design the information architecture of a multi-view dashboard for a defined role and decision, with a default view that stands alone without interaction.
Convert filters into scope or drill-down, accounting for the function of every removed control, and retain filters only where the next question is genuinely unpredictable.
Specify interaction and responsive behaviour such that no information required to read a chart depends on hover or pointer input.
Construct a metric register entry — grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh — and identify a visual claim the definition does not support.
Define the six parts of a visualization design system, distinguishing semantic encoding tokens from a styled component library.
Produce an engineering-ready specification using the grammar decomposition plus conditional encoding rules, scale domain behaviour, the full state inventory, and responsive rules.
Facilitate a structured critique in fixed order with the brief as a hard gate, and convert a stalled disagreement into a pre-registered empirical test.
Define success measures matched to an artifact's mode, including at least one indicator of practice health.

motivationHooks.prompt:
Everything so far has been about producing a correct artifact. **A design lead is not paid to produce artifacts.** They are paid so that hundreds of artifacts produced by other people are correct, and so that decisions get made well when they are not in the room.

That changes the unit of work three times over. One chart becomes a coordinated system where the hardest problem is what the viewer sees before touching anything. One system becomes rules and defaults that let forty teams ship coherent charts without consulting you. One set of rules becomes a practice, sustained by how disagreements get resolved and how success gets measured.

Nothing in this section is new theory. **Each of its three competencies is the organisational form of one you already have.**

A design system is `encoding-effectiveness` made durable. Critique is `graphical-integrity` made social. Dashboard architecture is `analytic-task-framing` applied to a whole workspace instead of one chart.

If you find yourself unsure what to do here, the move is almost always to return to the earlier competency and ask what it implies at scale.

Hold this and test it as you go:

> **A container terminal dashboard has twelve tiles, eleven filters, and every value on hover. Telemetry shows 78% of sessions involve zero interaction and the median session is 41 seconds. Managers call it "the wallpaper."**

Write one line now: what is the primary problem, and what would you change first?

**The resolution.** The primary problem is that **the default view was never designed** — it was assembled from requests, and twelve equally-sized tiles assert that twelve metrics matter equally to whoever opens it.

Most sessions contain no interaction, so the unmanipulated first render *is* the dashboard for the overwhelming majority of use. The eleven filters were never a feature; **they were a record of questions nobody answered**, handed to a manager with 41 seconds and less context about the data model than the designer had.

If your first change was "improve filter discoverability" or "add onboarding," notice the diagnostic move that distinguishes it: **41-second sessions with no interaction are glances, not failed hunts.** Long sessions with no interaction would suggest people searching and failing. Short ones suggest people looking and leaving — and for them, only the default exists.

The fix was not a better tile grid. It was one role, one decision, and a ranked view that answers it before anyone touches anything.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following.

**The default view is the product.** Most sessions involve no interaction, so design the unmanipulated render as if it were the only view — for one role and one decision. Filters are unmade decisions handed to someone with less context and less time.

**Nothing required to read a chart lives in a tooltip.** That is an architecture decision, settled in the wireframe, not a styling one.

**Metric definitions are design surface.** Grain, denominator and population fix the space of honest visual claims. You do not need to own the pipeline; you need the definition to be legible enough to check charts against.

**A component library governs appearance; a design system governs meaning.** Semantic tokens are the difference, and shipping them as code beats publishing guidance — because defaults reach everyone.

**A mockup shows one state of a system with at least a dozen.** Stale and null-versus-zero are the two most often omitted and the two that cause integrity failures in production.

**Most visualization disputes are empirical.** Structured critique with a hard brief gate, and converting stalled arguments into pre-registered tests, is what makes a practice rather than a series of opinions.
keyTakeaways: Design the default view for one role and one decision; interaction serves the minority.
Account for every filter you remove — scope, drill-down, or deleted.
Nothing required to read the chart lives in hover.
Keep a metric register: grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh.
Ship semantic tokens as code; defaults reach the teams guidance never will.
Specify the state inventory, especially stale and null-versus-zero.
Run critique in four passes with the brief as a hard gate.
Pre-register the result that would change your mind, then run the fifteen-minute test.
Match success measures to mode, and track the share of briefs that arrive with a decision.

learningExperiences.title: The default view is the product

contentBlocks.content:
A container terminal operator commissions a dashboard for terminal managers. What arrives: a five-by-three grid of tiles, a left rail with eleven filters, and every value available on hover.

Six months of telemetry: **78% of sessions involve zero filter interaction. Median session length: 41 seconds.** Managers describe it as "the wallpaper."

Nothing here is a rendering problem. It is three architectural failures, each with a name.

contentBlocks.altText: Two dashboard states. As built: a panel of eleven filters beside a grid of twelve equally-sized metric tiles, each showing a percentage and a small sparkline, with no ordering or emphasis. Rescued: a single enclosed band listing four berths sorted worst-first by deviation from plan, with bar length showing the shortfall, a dashed threshold line, a twenty-four-hour trend line per row, and one accent colour reserved for the single berth past threshold and worsening.
contentBlocks.caption: The default view is the product.

contentBlocks.title: Most viewers never interact
contentBlocks.content:
They glance. The **unmanipulated first render** is what the dashboard *is* for the large majority of its use.

This is the most consequential fact in dashboard design and it is routinely inverted: teams design a flexible system and treat the default as an arbitrary starting position. **The correct order is the reverse.** Design the default view as if it were the only view, then add interaction to serve the minority of sessions that need to go further.

**The test:** if all interactivity were disabled tomorrow, what percentage of this dashboard's value survives? Under half means the default is under-designed, and no amount of interaction will rescue it.

## Filters are unmade decisions

Eleven filters is not flexibility. It is a designer declining to decide, and passing the decision to a terminal manager who has 41 seconds and less context about the data model than the designer does.

Every filter asks the user to know four things: **that it exists, what it does, what value is appropriate, and what the current state is.** Four things, times eleven, before any information is obtained.

The alternative is **scoping**: define the view for a *role and a decision* (Section 1) and set the parameters yourself. A yard-utilisation view for the shift supervisor, pre-scoped to their shift and their yard blocks, with one or two parameters exposed, outperforms a configurable everything-view. It also **fails more visibly when wrong**, which is a feature — a wrong default gets reported; an unused filter never does.

**Where filters remain right:** genuinely exploratory work, where the analyst's next question is unpredictable by construction. That is the exploratory branch of the Section 1 fork, and it is a smaller share of enterprise dashboard work than the filter counts imply.

contentBlocks.caption: Interaction patterns and what each costs
rows: Two coordinated views: the whole, and a selected region
Screen space, plus the viewer maintaining the relationship
One view magnifying or emphasising a region while surroundings remain
Distortion of the context — must not be one read quantitatively
Selection in one view highlights corresponding data in others
Implementation complexity, shared identity keys. **Highest value, most under-used**
Discoverability — and the pattern most often abused
Lost context; always show where they are and how to return
Continuous parameter adjustment with immediate feedback
Genuinely powerful in exploration; the eleven-filter rail is its degenerate form

contentBlocks.title: The tooltip rule
contentBlocks.content:
Hover is **unavailable on touch**, **invisible to keyboard navigation**, **unreachable by screen readers**, and **undiscoverable** by anyone not already exploring.

**Nothing required to read the chart may live in a tooltip.** Tooltips carry supplementary detail — the exact figure behind a bar whose approximate value is already legible, a record ID, a timestamp.

This is Section 6's accessibility material arriving as an **architecture** constraint rather than a styling one. When a value must be available: print it on the mark, put it in an adjacent table, or make points keyboard-focusable with an accessible name. **The decision about where required information lives is made in the wireframe.**

terms.definition: The unmanipulated first render of a dashboard, which carries the majority of its communicative load because most sessions contain no interaction.
Defining a view for a specific role and decision with parameters pre-set by the designer, instead of exposing filters.
Two coordinated views shown together, one presenting the whole and one the selected region.
A single view that emphasises or magnifies a region of interest while retaining the surrounding context.
Selection in one view highlighting the corresponding data in others, making cross-view relationships visible rather than inferred.
Supplementary detail revealed on selection; must never carry information required to read the chart.
Navigation from an aggregate to its components, requiring a visible breadcrumb and a return path.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Designing the flexible system first and the default last.** *(iad-interaction-fixes-default)* — Most sessions contain zero interaction. Design the default as if it were the only view.

**2. Adding a filter instead of making a decision.** *(iad-filters-always-needed)* — Filters transfer your unmade choices to someone with less context and less time.

**3. Putting required values in tooltips.** *(iad-tooltips-for-key-values)* — Fails on touch, keyboard and screen readers, and is undiscoverable.

**4. Treating low interaction as a discoverability defect.** — It is usually a signal about glance-based use. Teaching people to use filters they do not need helps nobody decide anything.

**5. Building one dashboard for the analyst and the executive.** *(atf-one-viz-all-audiences)* — Section 1's fork, at workspace scale. Their requirements invert.

**6. Drill-down without a breadcrumb.** — The viewer loses context and cannot get back. Always show where they are and how to return.

**7. Ignoring the surface people actually use.** — If the dashboard is read on a phone at shift handover, the desktop layout is the secondary case, not the primary one.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **The default view is the product.** Most sessions involve no interaction; design it as if it were the only view.
- Test: if interactivity vanished tomorrow, how much value survives?
- **Filters are unmade decisions**, each costing the user four things. Scope to a role and a decision instead.
- Filters are right where the next question is genuinely unpredictable — real exploratory work, which is rarer than filter counts suggest.
- **Brushing and linking** is the highest-value and most under-used pattern, because it makes cross-view relationships visible rather than inferred.
- **Nothing required to read the chart lives in a tooltip.** This is settled in the wireframe.
- Degrade toward the primary task on small screens; name what never drops.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Predict:** 78% of sessions on this dashboard involve no interaction at all. Before reading on — what is the most likely explanation, and what would you do about it?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The instinctive reading is a discoverability problem — people cannot find the filters. The more likely reading is that **41-second sessions are glances**, and a glancing user does not want to configure anything; they want an answer already on screen.

Hold your answer. The difference between those two diagnoses leads to completely opposite redesigns: one adds onboarding, the other removes controls.

interactionSequence.prompt: Analytics show 80% of sessions involve no interaction. What does that imply for the redesign?
options: The unmanipulated default view carries the majority of the communicative load and must stand alone for a specific role and decision.
Interaction discovery needs improving — add onboarding and affordance cues so more users engage the filters.
Add more filters so users have a reason to interact.
Broaden it so the same dashboard also serves the analytics team, who would use the filters.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Interaction serves the minority of sessions that go further; the default is what the dashboard actually is for most users.
Low interaction usually signals glance-based use rather than a discoverability defect. Teaching people to use filters they do not need helps nobody decide anything.
Filters offload unmade decisions onto users; adding them raises cost and lowers the chance the default answers anything.
Wrong. An artifact serving both a glancing manager and an exploring analyst optimises for opposite things and typically fails both — Section 1’s fork, arriving at workspace scale.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Worth noticing that option B is what most teams do, and it is not stupid — it is the correct response to a *discoverability* problem. The error is diagnostic rather than logical.

The evidence that distinguishes them is session length. Long sessions with no interaction suggest people are hunting and failing. **Forty-one-second sessions with no interaction suggest people are glancing and leaving**, and for them the only thing that exists is the default render.

interactionSequence.prompt: A stakeholder asks for date, region and product filters 'like the other dashboards have'. What is the design-lead response?
options: Ask which role and which decision the view serves, then set those parameters yourself — a filter is an unmade decision handed to someone with less context and less time.
Add all three, since filters are what make a dashboard flexible.
Add them but hide them behind an advanced panel so the default view stays clean.
Refuse all filters on principle, since scoped views are always superior to configurable ones.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it leaves room for the legitimate exception: filters belong where the next question is genuinely unpredictable.
Each filter costs the user four things before any information is obtained — knowing it exists, what it does, what value is right, and its current state.
Hiding a control does not resolve the undecided scope; it makes the unmade decision harder to find.
Over-corrects. Genuinely exploratory work needs dynamic query, and a single role can legitimately span multiple scopes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
There is an evidence route worth taking before the conversation: **check interaction analytics on the dashboards being cited as precedent.** Very often they show near-zero filter use, which turns "like the other dashboards" from an argument for filters into an argument against them.

That move — going to the data about how the artifact is used — is the same instinct this whole section is built on.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: take a dashboard you have access to. Write, in one sentence, the decision its default view supports. If you cannot, say what you would have to find out — and from whom.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The common outcome is that the default view supports no single decision, because it was assembled from requests rather than designed for a role. That is the finding, and it is usually visible in the artifact itself: equally-sized tiles in a grid signal that nobody decided what matters most.

**Equal visual weight is a claim of equal importance.** If twelve tiles are the same size, the dashboard is asserting that all twelve metrics matter equally to whoever opens it — which is almost never true and is the fastest thing to fix.

workedExamples.problem: Re-architect the port operations dashboard: 12 tiles, 11 filters, hover-only values, 41-second sessions.
steps: **Recover the role and decision.** Terminal managers, during shift handover, deciding where to reallocate crane and yard resources for the next four hours. **Not** monitoring everything — that was never a decision.

**Derive the task hierarchy.** Primary: **deviation** — which berths or yard blocks are off plan right now? Secondary: **comparison** — by how much, relative to each other? Tertiary: **drill** — what is driving the worst one?

**Design the default view for the primary task alone.** A single ranked view of berths by deviation from plan, sorted worst-first, with a threshold reference mark. Position and length carry the quantity — ranks 1 and 3 from Section 3. Exactly one pop-out, reserved for past-threshold-and-worsening.
**Scope by default rather than filtering.** Time-scoped to the current shift, because the decision is about the next four hours. This is a scoping decision, not a filter.

**Add the secondary layer as context, not configuration.** A compact 24-hour sparkline per row giving direction of travel. This answers *is it bad and getting worse* with **no interaction**, which matters because most sessions have none.

**Add interaction only where the tertiary task requires it.** Selecting a row brushes a linked detail panel showing container flow for that berth. Brushing and linking is chosen because the value is in seeing the relationship between the ranked view and the detail.

**Reduce eleven filters to two parameters.** Shift, defaulting to current, and yard area, defaulting to the manager's own. Everything else moves into the default scope or the drill-down. **Account for each removed control** — nothing simply disappears.
**Provide non-pointer access.** Row values printed in the row; rows keyboard-focusable; the ranked view available as an accessible table with the same sort order. Nothing required lives in hover.

**Specify responsive behaviour.** On a phone at shift handover — which is where this is actually read — the layout collapses to the ranked list with sparklines, and the detail panel becomes a separate view. It **degrades to the primary task**, which is the correct thing to preserve.
**Instrument one measure.** Share of sessions ending in a recorded reallocation action, so the redesign can be evaluated rather than admired.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**Fewer views, fewer controls, more decisions supported.**

Almost all of the gain came from step 1 — recovering the role and the decision — and from accepting that the default view is the product. The eleven filters were never a feature. **They were a record of questions nobody answered.**

Notice also how much of this is Section 1 arriving at workspace scale. "Monitoring everything" is a topic; "where to move two cranes before 6pm" is a decision. The entire architecture follows from which of those you write down.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why must the default view stand alone, and what is the test for whether yours is under-designed?
What is a filter, from a design-decision standpoint, and what four things does each one cost the user?
Which interaction pattern is highest-value and most under-used, and why?
State the tooltip rule, and name the three user situations that make it necessary.
What does a grid of equally-sized tiles assert, and why is that assertion usually false?

transferExercises.context: University admissions — mobile-first, seasonal, used by non-analysts.
transferExercises.scenario: A dashboard used by forty regional recruiters during a six-week decision window has nine filters, twelve tiles, and all values on hover. Median session is fifty-five seconds, filter use is near zero, and it is mostly opened on phones between school visits.
transferExercises.task: Produce: **(a)** the role and decision, with the resulting task hierarchy; **(b)** a default view designed as if it were the only view, with encoding choices justified against Sections 3 and 4; **(c)** which filters survive as parameters and where the function of each removed one went; **(d)** the mobile degradation rule, naming what never drops; **(e)** the non-pointer access provisions; **(f)** one measure you would instrument.
successCriteria: The decision line contains an action verb.
The default view supports one decision and stands alone without interaction.
Every removed control is accounted for as scope, drill-down, or deleted.
The degradation rule names what never drops, and it is the primary task.
Required values are reachable without a pointer.
The instrumented measure would actually change the design if it came back badly.

learningExperiences.title: The definition decides what every chart can say

contentBlocks.content:
Two dashboards in the same company report different figures for **active customers**. Both are correct against their own definitions. Neither definition is written down anywhere a designer can find it.

Section 1 opened with the MTA case, where the definition of a row — a train arriving at a terminal, rather than a rider completing a journey — determined what every downstream chart could possibly say. That was not a story about transit. It is the general case, and this is where it gets a name.

contentBlocks.title: Why this is design surface
contentBlocks.content:
A metric definition fixes the **grain**, the **denominator** and the **population**. Those three fix the entire space of honest visual claims available downstream.

A designer who declines to engage does not avoid the decision. **They inherit someone else's unexamined choice and then publish it under their own annotation** — which is precisely the position the engineers were in during the MTA reporting.

You do not need to own the pipeline. You need the definition to be legible, and to be able to say when a chart is making a claim the definition does not support.

## The metric register

For each governed metric, five fields — and the discipline is that a chart cannot ship against a metric whose register entry is incomplete.

| Field | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Grain** | What is one unit of this? A user, a session, a user-day? |
| **Denominator** | If it is a rate, what population is it over? |
| **Inclusions** | What counts? Which events, which statuses, which sources? |
| **Exclusions** | What was deliberately removed, and on what rule? Internal traffic, test accounts, cancelled orders? |
| **Refresh** | How current is it, and what is the staleness threshold beyond which it should not be shown? |

Every one of these traces to something earlier in the course. Grain is Section 1. Denominator is Section 2. Exclusions are a Section 6 framing choice. **Refresh is the one that only becomes visible at system scale**, and it is the one that produces silent integrity failures in production.

## The semantic layer

When these definitions live in a governed layer — a shared modelling layer, a metrics store, or simply a maintained register — three things follow.

**Charts stop disagreeing.** Two dashboards computing the same metric from the same definition produce the same number, and the disagreements that remain are real rather than definitional.

**Design decisions become traceable.** When someone asks why a chart shows what it shows, the answer exists.

**A designer can spot an unsupported claim.** If the register says a metric excludes trial accounts, a chart titled *"total customer growth"* is over-claiming, and you can say so with a citation rather than a suspicion.

Where no such layer exists, the register is still worth maintaining as a design artifact. **The value is in the definitions being written down, not in the tooling.**

terms.definition: The specification of what a named measure counts and excludes; fixes the space of visual claims available downstream.
The governed set of metric definitions — grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh — that determines what any downstream chart can honestly claim.
What a single row of a dataset represents — one transaction, one customer-day, one store-month.
A visible signal that displayed data is older than its refresh contract, preventing a dashboard from silently showing yesterday's numbers.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Treating metric definition as the data team's job.** *(vsg-metrics-are-not-design)* — It determines what every downstream chart can honestly claim. Declining to engage means publishing an unexamined choice.

**2. Accepting a metric with no written definition.** — If nobody can state the grain, denominator and exclusions, that absence is a finding and should be reported as one.

**3. Assuming two identically-named metrics are the same metric.** — The most common source of contradictory dashboards, and the hardest to detect because both parties are confident.

**4. Charting a metric whose exclusions contradict the title.** — A title claiming totality over a metric that excludes a population is over-claiming, which is Section 6's annotation line.

**5. Ignoring refresh.** — A dashboard silently showing yesterday's numbers is an integrity failure, not a caching quirk. Specify a staleness threshold and what renders past it.

**6. Averaging an ordinal metric because the register does not forbid it.** *(ds-ordinal-averaging)* — A register entry that records the scale type is what makes this catchable at review rather than after publication.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- **The metric definition fixes grain, denominator and population** — and therefore the whole space of honest visual claims.
- Declining to engage does not avoid the decision; it means inheriting and publishing someone else's.
- The **register** has five fields: grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh.
- Each traces to earlier material — Section 1 grain, Section 2 denominator, Section 6 exclusions. **Refresh only becomes visible at system scale.**
- A governed **semantic layer** makes charts stop disagreeing and makes design decisions traceable.
- Where none exists, maintain the register anyway. The value is in the writing down.

interactionSequence.prompt: Two dashboards in the same company report different figures for 'active customers' and both are correct against their own definitions. Whose problem is this?
options: It is design-governed: the definition fixes grain, denominator and population, and therefore the space of honest visual claims — so definitions belong in the system's register alongside tokens and taxonomy.
It is purely a data-engineering problem and should be escalated out of design.
It is not a problem, since each dashboard is internally consistent.
It should be resolved by having both dashboards display both figures.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The metric determines what any downstream chart can say, which makes it design surface even though design does not own the pipeline.
Escalating without engaging means inheriting an unexamined choice and then publishing it under your own annotation.
Internal consistency does not help a reader comparing the two, and it guarantees a contradiction reaches a decision-maker.
Showing both without resolving or labelling the definitions transfers the confusion to the reader.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The framing that gets this taken seriously by a data team is not ownership but **legibility**: you are not asking to control the definition, you are asking for it to be written down so that charts can be checked against it.

That is a much easier request to grant, and it produces most of the benefit.

interactionSequence.prompt: A dashboard's data feed fails silently and it continues displaying yesterday's figures. How should this be classified?
options: An integrity failure — the chart asserts currency it does not have, so a staleness threshold and a visible indicator belong in the specification.
A caching bug for engineering to fix, with no design implication.
Acceptable, since yesterday's figures are usually close to today's.
A minor issue, since users can check the refresh timestamp if they need to.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. A dashboard that shows stale data without saying so is making a false claim about what it depicts, and the remedy is a specified state rather than a fix after the fact.
The failure mode is a design decision — what the artifact renders when it cannot render truthfully — and only design will specify it.
Sometimes true and unknowable to the reader, which is the point. During an incident it is exactly when yesterday's figures are most wrong.
Requiring users to verify currency before trusting a chart inverts the burden and will not happen at 41-second session lengths.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Worth specifying two thresholds rather than one: a **soft threshold** where a timestamp becomes visually prominent, and a **hard threshold** past which the view refuses to render normally and shows an explicit stale state.

The second one is the argument you will have to defend — teams resist a dashboard that declines to show numbers. The response is that a dashboard which cannot be trusted to be current is worse than one that says so.

interactionSequence.prompt: A register entry for **crew satisfaction** records the grain as one survey response, and the metric is reported as a mean of 1–5 ratings. What should the register capture that would have caught this at review?
options: The measurement scale of the underlying responses — ordinal, which makes the mean an unlicensed operation and should trigger a distribution or top-box report instead.
Nothing: a mean of survey ratings is standard practice and needs no further specification.
The number of decimal places to display, so the figure is reported consistently.
The survey vendor, so the source can be cited.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Recording the scale type is what makes the averaging question catchable at review rather than after publication — Section 1’s rule, given an organisational enforcement point.
Averaging ordinal ratings assumes equal spacing between response options, which the scale does not guarantee. Ubiquity is not licence.
Consistent formatting on an unlicensed statistic makes the problem less visible, not smaller.
Provenance is worth recording and does not address whether the reported statistic is licensed by the scale.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
This is the argument for a register in miniature. The Section 1 knowledge was already in the course; what the register adds is **a place where it gets applied by someone other than the person who happens to remember it.**

A sixth register field — measurement scale — is a reasonable local extension, and it turns a recurring judgement into a checkable property.

interactionSequence.prompt: Reconstruct one headline metric from your organisation using the five register fields — grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh. Which field could you not fill in, and who would you have to ask?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Exclusions** is the field almost nobody can fill in, and it is frequently the one carrying the most weight — internal traffic, test accounts, refunded orders, employees, bot sessions, a region that was onboarded mid-period.

It is also the field most likely to make an existing chart's title wrong. If your metric excludes a population and a chart claims a total, you have found something concrete to raise, and Section 6 gives you the language for it.

workedExamples.problem: The terminal operator has a headline metric, 'berth productivity'. Two teams report different values. Build the register entry and identify what it fixes.
steps: **Establish the grain.** Team A computes moves per crane-hour. Team B computes moves per berth-hour. **These are different metrics with the same name** — a berth may have three cranes working or one, so the two diverge by a factor of three on the same shift.

**Establish the denominator, and notice it is the same question.** Crane-hours against berth-hours is a denominator choice, and Section 2 says the right one is the exposure the decision concerns. For crane utilisation, crane-hours. For berth turnaround commitments to shipping lines, berth-hours.

**Conclude that both are legitimate.** This is the common outcome and the one people resist. The problem is not that one team is wrong; it is that **one name is carrying two metrics**, so any comparison between their dashboards is meaningless.
**Establish inclusions.** Which moves count? Loaded containers only, or empties too? Restows? Hatch covers? Each inclusion decision moves the number by a few percent and none is visible in a chart.

**Establish exclusions.** Crane breakdown time — excluded by Team A as unavoidable downtime, included by Team B as part of real productivity. **This single choice can move the figure by 10–15%**, and it is invisible in every chart either team produces.

**Establish refresh.** Computed hourly from the terminal operating system, with a 90-minute soft threshold and a four-hour hard threshold beyond which the view shows a stale state rather than a number.

**Rename, rather than pick a winner.** `berth.productivity.crane_hour` and `berth.productivity.berth_hour`, each with a full register entry. The naming is the fix; forcing one team onto the other's definition would destroy a real measure someone depends on.
**Audit existing charts against the register.** Any chart titled simply 'berth productivity' is now identifiable as under-specified, and the fix is a subtitle naming which metric and its exclusions.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The resolution was not to choose. It was to make the two metrics distinguishable and their exclusions visible.**

That is the characteristic shape of metric governance work, and it is why it fails when framed as arbitration. Both teams were measuring something real; what did not exist was any way for a reader — or a designer — to know which one a chart depicted.

Notice the exclusion finding in step 5. **A 10–15% swing, invisible in every chart, decided by a judgment nobody wrote down.** No amount of encoding skill downstream detects that, which is the whole argument for the register.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the five fields of a metric register entry.
Why is metric definition design surface, given that design does not own the pipeline?
Two teams report different values for the same named metric and both are correct. What is the fix, and why is arbitration the wrong frame?
Why is silently showing yesterday's data an integrity failure rather than a caching bug, and what two thresholds should a specification define?

learningExperiences.title: Making the routine automatic

contentBlocks.content:
## A component library is not a design system

Components with no encoding rules let two teams build charts that look identical and mean incompatible things — the same blue meaning *at risk* in one product and *in review* in another.

That is worse than visible inconsistency, because it is **confidently wrong**. Nobody notices, and both teams believe they are complying.

contentBlocks.altText: Two products each use the same blue token from a shared palette: in one it means at risk, in the other it means in review, and both teams believe they are consistent with the system. Beside them, a semantic token layer assigns each colour a named business meaning such as status.risk and status.forecast. Below, the six parts of a visualization design system are listed, with semantic encoding tokens highlighted as the missing piece.
contentBlocks.caption: A component library is not a design system.

contentBlocks.content:
## The six parts

**1. Chart taxonomy with selection guidance.** Not a catalogue — a decision aid. For each form: the tasks it supports, its cardinality limits, and **when not to use it**. The "when not to" column does the work and is the first thing cut for length.

**2. Encoding tokens with semantics.** Categorical, sequential and diverging ramps from Section 3, with **semantic assignments fixed at system level**: which colour means positive, negative, forecast, current, comparison, disabled. Semantics are what make it a system rather than a palette.

**3. Scale and axis rules.** When zero baselines are required — length encodings — and when not, per Section 6. Default number and date formatting. Log-scale policy. Handling of negatives and nulls.

**4. Accessibility acceptance criteria.** Contrast minimums, the redundant-encoding requirement, non-pointer access, a mandatory text-alternative field. Written as things a chart **must pass**, not things a designer should consider.

**5. Annotation and titling standards.** The takeaway-title convention, required subtitle fields, where the method note lives. This is Section 6 turned into a template so the good behaviour survives the designer leaving.

**6. Contribution and review model.** How a team proposes a new form, who decides, what evidence is required, how exceptions are recorded. Without it the system ossifies, teams route around it, and you find out eighteen months later.

contentBlocks.title: On the standardisation objection
contentBlocks.content:
*"A system kills expressiveness."*

This gets the purpose backwards. The point is to make **routine cases automatic so scarce design attention goes to the genuinely novel ones**.

The alternative is not creative freedom. It is redesigning bar charts forever while nobody has time to think about the hard problem — which is exactly the state most teams are in when they say this.

A useful move: audit where the team's chart hours actually went last quarter and classify each as routine or novel. The ratio usually settles the argument without anyone having to concede.

contentBlocks.title: On defaults
contentBlocks.content:
Section 3's viridis case: published critique changed some behaviour, **changing the library default changed most of it.**

Your highest-leverage act is usually to change what happens when nobody is thinking. Guidance reaches the people who read guidance. **Defaults reach everyone.**

Ship the tokens as code.

## Specification: a mockup shows one state

A high-fidelity mockup shows plausible data, all values present, a comfortable row count. Production will reliably produce none of those.

contentBlocks.altText: On the left, a signed-off mockup showing one bar chart with plausible data. On the right, eight further states the mockup says nothing about: empty, loading, partial, stale, single row, overflow, out of range, and null versus zero. Stale and null-versus-zero are outlined in accent colour as the two most often omitted and most consequential.
contentBlocks.caption: What a mockup cannot specify.

contentBlocks.content:
The specification format is the **grammar decomposition from Section 4** — data, transform, mark, encoding, scale, guide, facet — plus four things a mockup cannot carry:

**Conditional encoding rules.** *"Colour = single accent applied only when deviation > threshold AND 3-hour trend is worsening."* That is a rule, not a value, and it cannot be drawn.

**Scale domain behaviour.** Fixed or data-driven? *"Domain fixed at ±40% so views are comparable across shifts; values beyond clamp to the axis edge and render a clipped-mark indicator."* Both halves are needed — the second is what stops an outlier silently rescaling the view.

**The state inventory**, including the two that get omitted: **stale** and **null versus zero**. Stale data displayed silently is an integrity failure. A missing reading rendered as 0 is Section 1's rule arriving as an engineering requirement.

**Responsive rules.** Breakpoints, what drops in what order, and **what never drops**.

And one line of rationale per decision — not for the engineers, but for whoever is asked in eight months to *"just make the bars start at the minimum so the differences show up better."*

terms.definition: A system-level visual value with a fixed business meaning attached, such as the colour that always denotes a forecast.
A catalogue of approved chart forms with the tasks each supports, its cardinality limits, and explicit guidance on when not to use it.
The full set of render states a production chart must handle: empty, loading, partial, error, stale, single-row and overflow.
A visible signal that displayed data is older than its refresh contract, preventing a dashboard from silently showing yesterday's numbers.
The abstraction that treats any chart as a composition of data, transform, mark, channel encodings, scales, guides and faceting rather than as an indivisible type.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Shipping a component library and calling it a design system.** *(vsg-library-equals-system)* — Without encoding rules and semantic assignments, teams build consistent-looking charts that contradict each other.

**2. Treating standardisation as an enemy of craft.** *(vsg-standards-kill-creativity)* — It exists to free attention for the novel cases, not to eliminate them.

**3. Handing engineering a mockup as the specification.** *(vsg-mockup-is-spec)* — Encoding logic, domain behaviour, states and responsive rules are all invisible in it.

**4. Omitting the "when not to use this" column.** — The only part that prevents misuse, and the first cut for length.

**5. Publishing guidance without changing defaults.** — Guidance moves some behaviour; defaults move most of it.

**6. Reusing the UI palette for data.** — UI colour signals interactivity and state; data colour encodes values and must satisfy ordering, uniformity and CVD constraints. Different problems.

**7. No contribution model.** — The system ossifies, teams route around it, and nobody tells you.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- A **library governs appearance; a system governs meaning.** Semantic tokens are the difference.
- Six parts: **taxonomy with "when not to use", semantic encoding tokens, scale and axis rules, accessibility acceptance criteria, annotation standards, contribution and review model.**
- Standardisation makes the routine automatic so attention reaches the novel. The alternative is redesigning bar charts forever.
- **Ship the tokens as code.** Defaults reach everyone; guidance reaches readers of guidance.
- The **specification** is the Section 4 grammar plus conditional rules, scale domain behaviour, the full **state inventory** and responsive rules.
- **Stale** and **null-versus-zero** are the two states almost always omitted and the two that cause integrity failures in production.
- One line of rationale per decision, for the person who will question it in eight months.

interactionSequence.prompt: A team ships a chart component library with consistent styling and reusable components across eight products. What is still missing for this to be a visualization design system?
options: Encoding rules, semantic colour assignments and selection guidance — without them, teams build consistent-looking charts that mean incompatible things.
Nothing — a consistent component library is a design system.
More component variants, so teams have enough options not to build their own.
Nothing structural, but the constraints should be relaxed, since standardisation limits expressiveness.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Semantics are what make it a system; visual consistency without semantic consistency is confidently wrong rather than merely inconsistent.
Components govern appearance; a system governs meaning, selection, accessibility acceptance and how it changes over time.
Variant proliferation without selection guidance raises the chance of misuse; the missing piece is knowing when *not* to use each form.
The purpose is to make routine cases automatic so scarce attention reaches the genuinely novel ones.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The diagnostic that makes this concrete in your own organisation: **find two charts from different teams that use the same visual token for different meanings.** It takes about twenty minutes and it is almost always there.

Once you have the example, the semantic token layer stops being an abstraction and becomes the obvious fix to a specific, embarrassing problem.

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these by leverage in getting forty product teams to ship accessible, semantically consistent charts — highest first.
options: Publish a written guideline document
Ship encoding tokens and accessible defaults as installable code
Run a lunch-and-learn on chart accessibility
Add accessibility criteria to the chart review checklist

optionFeedback.feedback: **Third.** Necessary as a reference and as something the review gate points at — read by a minority.
**First.** Defaults propagate to everyone, including teams that never read anything. This is the viridis lesson.
**Last on leverage** — highest engagement per attendee, smallest and least durable reach. Not worthless: it builds the constituency that defends the default when someone asks to override it.
**Second.** A recurring gate tied to shipping applies whether or not anyone remembers the training.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The ordering is about **reach per unit of effort**, not about worth. A design system that consists only of defaults and gates, with no teaching and no constituency, tends to be resented and eventually routed around.

You need the bottom two to make the top two survive contact with the organisation — which is what the contribution and review model is for.

interactionSequence.prompt: Why is a pixel-accurate mockup insufficient as an engineering specification?
options: It shows one state of a system with at least a dozen: encoding logic, scale domain behaviour, empty, loading, partial, error, stale and overflow states, and responsive rules are all invisible in it.
It is sufficient if the values shown are real production data.
It is insufficient only because engineers prefer written documents to images.
It is sufficient provided a redline file accompanies it.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct — and the omitted decisions do not disappear. They get made by whoever is closest to the deadline.
Real values still show a single state, and say nothing about what renders when the feed is stale or a value is out of range.
Format preference is not the issue; the missing content is behavioural rules, which no image can express.
Redlines specify geometry, not conditional encoding logic or state behaviour.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
A cheap forcing function: **hand the mockup back to yourself with the state list and try to answer each one.** Empty, loading, partial, error, stale, single row, overflow, out of range, null versus zero.

Most designers can answer three or four. The rest are decisions that will be made without them, and the specification exists so that they are not.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: pick one chart component in your product and write its **conditional encoding rule** — the thing that changes appearance based on a data condition. Then say what a mockup of it would fail to communicate.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Common ones: a bar turns red past a threshold; a trend arrow flips direction; a row is emphasised when it changed rank; a value renders as a dash when suppressed.

Every one of these is a rule with a boundary condition, and every mockup shows it in exactly one state. The questions that surface when you write it out — *what happens exactly at the threshold? what if the value is null? what if every row qualifies?* — are the ones engineering would otherwise have to guess at, and the last one is how you end up with a chart where everything is red.

workedExamples.problem: Specify the port dashboard's ranked deviation view for engineering handoff, using the Section 4 grammar plus what a mockup cannot carry.
steps: **Data.** Berth-hour records for the current shift, filtered to berths with a scheduled plan. Grain: one row per berth per shift. Metric per the register: `berth.productivity.berth_hour`, exclusions stated.
**Transform.** Compute deviation = (actual − planned) ÷ planned. Sort descending by absolute deviation. No aggregation beyond the shift.
**Mark.** Rect for the deviation bar; line for the 24-hour sparkline; text for the row label and value.

**Encoding.** y = berth (categorical, sorted by transform); x = deviation (quantitative, length from a shared baseline); colour = **conditional accent** (see rules below); sparkline y = hourly deviation.

**Scale.** Domain **fixed** at ±40% so views are comparable across shifts. Values beyond the domain **clamp to the axis edge and render a clipped-mark indicator** — without that second clause an outlier silently rescales the view and destroys the cross-shift comparison the fixed domain was chosen for.
**Guide.** Threshold reference line at the operational trigger; row labels direct; values printed in-row, **not** on hover.
**Facet.** None at default. Yard area becomes a facet in the expanded view only.

**Conditional encoding rule.** Accent applied only when `deviation > threshold AND 3-hour trend is worsening`. At exactly the threshold, not applied. If **every** row qualifies, accent the worst three only and show a system-level warning — otherwise the pop-out budget is spent on nothing, which is Section 3.

**State inventory.** Empty: no berths in scope → explanatory message naming the scope. Loading: skeleton rows, no spinner over data. Partial: rows present with a per-row missing indicator, never a gap. Error: feed unavailable → explicit state, no numbers. **Stale**: soft indicator at 90 minutes, hard refusal at 4 hours. Single row: renders without the ranking affordance. Overflow: cap at 20 rows with a count of those hidden. **Null vs zero**: a missing reading renders as a null glyph, **never** as 0.
**Responsive.** Below 480px, sparklines drop. The ranked list, the threshold line and the accent **never** drop.

**Accessibility acceptance criteria.** Focus order top to bottom; accessible name per row combining berth, deviation and trend direction; contrast tokens; text-alternative template with the top three rows interpolated.
**Rationale, one line each.** Especially for the fixed domain, which will be questioned by the first person who sees a clamped bar.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**A mockup could have shown you row eight of this specification. It could not have shown you any of the others.**

The two clauses worth carrying: the **clamp indicator** in step 5, without which a fixed domain silently misleads; and the **all-rows-qualify** case in step 8, which is how a conditional accent becomes a wall of red that nobody can read.

Both are cases nobody sketches, both will occur in production within a month, and both are decided by an engineer under deadline if the specification is silent. **That is what the specification is for** — not to constrain engineering, but to ensure the decisions that were made carefully do not get remade carelessly.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the six parts of a visualization design system, and say which one is most often cut and why that matters.
What does a component library govern, and what does a design system govern? Give the failure that follows from having only the first.
Why ship tokens as code rather than as guidance? Name the earlier case study that established this.
Name six states a mockup does not show, and identify the two most often omitted and most consequential.
You fix a scale domain so views are comparable across periods. What second clause must the specification contain, and what goes wrong without it?

learningExperiences.title: Resolving disagreements and knowing whether it worked

contentBlocks.content:
## Critique degrades into preference exchange without an anchor

The fix is structural: **critique against stated criteria, in a fixed order.** Four passes, and you hold the room to the order.

contentBlocks.caption: The four passes
rows: Is the audience, decision, task and mode stated? **If not, stop.**
Baseline, scale, range, comparison group, denominator, statistic, uncertainty
Expressiveness, channel-to-task fit, pop-out budget, cardinality
Takeaway title within support, annotation layer, greyscale, non-pointer access, text alternative

contentBlocks.title: The brief pass is a hard gate
contentBlocks.content:
If the artifact has no stated audience, decision and mode, **stop the review and write the brief instead.**

This kills the majority of unproductive critique before it starts. Every downstream criterion is relative to a goal; critiquing an artifact with no stated goal produces contradictory direction and teaches the team that reviews are unpredictable — after which they stop bringing work early, which is the real cost.

Only after all four passes does anyone discuss preference. By then most disagreements have dissolved, because they were empirical.

## Most visualization disputes are empirical

*"Can people read this ratio accurately?"* *"Does this audience know what a log scale is?"* *"Will they notice the alert?"* *"What do they think this chart says?"*

These are answerable — with the literature, or with a fifteen-minute test.

**That is your leverage as a lead: you can convert a status contest into an experiment**, and the person arguing from seniority is the one who loses when a result arrives. It also means nobody has to back down in the room, which is why it works socially as well as epistemically.

## Testing visualizations

The claim that they cannot be usability-tested is false and expensive. Established protocols:

- **Takeaway recall.** Show the chart for 10–20 seconds, remove it, ask what it showed. Brutal, cheap, and **the single most informative test for explanatory work**.
- **Timed value retrieval.** "What was the value for X?" Measures accuracy and time.
- **Comparison accuracy.** "Which is larger, and by roughly how much?" Directly tests the encoding.
- **Prediction.** "What would you expect next?" Reveals whether the trend reads as the data supports.
- **Misconception probes.** "What does this chart imply?" Count how many state something it does not support. **This is the test that catches over-claiming annotation.**

Five participants surfaces most catastrophic comprehension failures. The cost of not testing is that the loudest opinion wins.

And pre-register what would change your mind. A test you run after deciding is theatre.

## Measuring the practice

If you cannot say what success looks like, you will be evaluated on aesthetics by default. Match the measure to the mode:

**Explanatory work** — takeaway recall accuracy; misconception rate in probes; time to correct answer.

**Exploratory work** — task completion on realistic analyst questions; time to first correct insight; depth of interaction reached.

**Systems work** — token and component adoption; proportion of new charts passing accessibility criteria at first review; time from request to shipped chart; **count of one-off custom charts, which should fall**.

**Practice health** — the proportion of incoming briefs that arrive stating a **decision** rather than a chart type. This is a lagging indicator of whether Section 1 has landed in your organisation, and it is the most telling number on the list.

terms.definition: Review against stated criteria in a fixed order — brief, integrity, encoding, narrative and access — with preference discussion deferred until the passes complete.
Timed exposure to a chart followed by its removal and free recall of the message, the most informative single test for explanatory work.
Asking what a chart implies in order to count unsupported inferences, which catches over-claiming annotation.
The specific cognitive operation the viewer must perform: comparison, trend, distribution, part-to-whole, correlation, deviation, ranking or flow.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Critiquing without the brief on the table.** *(cl-critique-is-finding-faults)* — Without a stated goal, critique becomes preference exchange and the team stops bringing work early.

**2. Settling encoding disputes by seniority.** *(cl-taste-or-seniority-decides)* — Most are empirical. Converting a status contest into a test is the highest-leverage move available.

**3. Assuming visualizations cannot be tested.** *(cl-viz-cannot-be-tested)* — Recall, retrieval, comparison and probe protocols are established, cheap, and routinely overturn confident internal opinion.

**4. Testing after deciding.** — Pre-register the result that would change the design, or the test is decoration.

**5. Measuring output volume.** — Charts shipped is not a quality measure and will drive exactly the wrong behaviour.

**6. Applying one measure to every artifact.** — Recall accuracy is meaningless for an exploratory tool; task completion is meaningless for a one-shot graphic.

**7. Treating explanatory work as polished exploratory work.** *(na-explanatory-is-polished-exploratory)* — Their requirements invert, and so do their success measures.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Structured critique runs **brief → integrity → encoding → narrative and access**, with preference last if at all.
- **The brief pass is a hard gate.** No stated audience, decision and mode means the session becomes brief-writing.
- **Most visualization disputes are empirical.** Convert the status contest into a test — nobody has to back down.
- Protocols: **takeaway recall** (most informative for explanatory work), timed retrieval, comparison accuracy, prediction, **misconception probes**.
- Five participants finds most disasters. Pre-register what would change your mind.
- Match success measures to mode. **The share of briefs arriving with a stated decision** is the number that tells you whether the practice has actually changed.

interactionSequence.prompt: In a structured critique, the artifact has no stated audience, decision or mode. What is the correct action?
options: Stop and write the brief — every downstream criterion is relative to a goal, and critiquing without one produces preference exchange.
Proceed to the visual passes, since the encoding can be assessed independently of purpose.
Ask each reviewer for their personal reaction first, then synthesise the common themes.
Defer the critique until a more senior stakeholder can attend and set direction.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Making the brief a hard gate kills most unproductive critique before it starts.
Encoding quality is only assessable against a task; without one, reviewers substitute assumed purposes and give contradictory direction.
Collecting reactions without an anchor is the failure mode itself — a list of preferences presented as findings.
Deferring to seniority replaces the missing goal with a missing person, and the same problem returns.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The social benefit is worth naming: a hard gate means **the designer is never criticised for an artifact whose purpose was never agreed.** That protects people, and it is why teams tend to accept the rule once they have experienced it.

Without it, the person who brought the work absorbs feedback aimed at a goal they were never given.

interactionSequence.prompt: A designer and a data scientist have deadlocked over whether a log-scale y-axis will confuse the audience for a public-facing chart. As design lead, what is your move?
options: Convert it into an empirical question and run a short comprehension test with representative users — the disagreement is about how people read the chart, which is measurable.
Decide it yourself, since resolving deadlocks by seniority is what a lead is for.
Publish both versions and let readers choose the one they prefer.
Note that visualizations cannot really be usability-tested and default to the linear scale.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. This is the lead's core leverage: evidence resolves the dispute without anyone having to lose an argument.
It unblocks the ticket and teaches the team that status settles questions, forfeiting a cheap better answer.
This doubles maintenance and pushes an encoding judgment onto the readers least equipped to make it.
Wrong on the facts: comprehension and recall protocols are established, cheap, and routinely overturn confident internal opinion.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The part that makes it work in practice is **pre-registering the threshold**. Agree beforehand what result changes the design — *"if fewer than four of six readers correctly rank the growth rates, we go linear"* — because a test with no pre-agreed threshold produces an argument about the test.

Section 4's FT case is this same decision, taken publicly, with the comprehension cost accepted and mitigated rather than denied.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which method most directly tests whether an explanatory chart communicates its intended message?
options: Timed exposure, then removing the chart and asking for free recall of what it showed.
Asking stakeholders in review whether they find the chart clear.
Counting how long users spend looking at the chart in analytics.
Comparing the chart against a checklist of visual design best practices.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Takeaway recall measures what survived rather than what was noticed, which is exactly the claim an explanatory chart makes.
Reviewers who already know the intended message cannot assess whether it is recoverable by someone who does not.
Dwell time measures attention, not comprehension, and long dwell can indicate confusion as easily as engagement.
A checklist catches known defects and cannot tell you what a reader actually took away.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The removal is the essential part and the part people skip. Leaving the chart on screen turns the test into reading comprehension; **taking it away tests what the chart deposited**, which is what a glancing reader gets.

Given that Section 7 opened with 41-second sessions, that is the realistic condition.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: take a live disagreement in your team about a chart. Phrase it as an empirical question, name the protocol you would use, and **pre-register the result that would change your own mind**.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The pre-registration is where most people hesitate, and the hesitation is informative. If you cannot name a result that would change your position, you are not in a disagreement about evidence — you are defending a preference, and the honest move is to say so and argue it on those terms.

Doing this publicly is also the single most effective way to change how a team argues. **A lead who visibly changes their mind on a result makes evidence the currency**, and after that the seniority argument stops being available to anyone, including you.

interactionSequence.prompt: You are seven sections into this course. Which competency do you expect to be hardest to actually use in your organisation — and is the obstacle knowledge, process, or authority?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Most people name a process or authority obstacle rather than a knowledge one, which is the right diagnosis and the reason this section exists.

If the obstacle is **process**, you can usually move it yourself: a brief template, a review gate, a register. These are cheap and nobody objects to them in the abstract.

If it is **authority**, the route is evidence rather than escalation — which is what the testing material is for. A lead who arrives with a comprehension result does not need authority for that decision.

And if it is **knowledge**, your spaced-review queue already has the items. The Day 90 review interleaves across all seven sections deliberately.

workedExamples.problem: Run a structured critique on the original port dashboard — 12 tiles, 11 filters, hover-only values — as it would actually go.
steps: **Pass 1 — Brief.** Ask: who is this for, what decision does it support, is it exploratory or explanatory? Answer offered: *"terminal managers, to monitor operations."* **Monitor is not a decision.** The gate fails. **Stop the visual review** and spend the session recovering the decision instead.

**What that costs and saves.** It costs a scheduled review. It saves the four rounds of contradictory feedback that would follow from four reviewers each assuming a different purpose — and it means the designer is not criticised for missing a goal nobody set.
**Reconvene with a brief.** *Terminal managers, at shift handover, deciding crane and yard reallocation for the next four hours. Explanatory, glanceable, mobile.* Now the passes can run.

**Pass 2 — Integrity.** Tiles show percentages with no denominators stated. Two use different date ranges without saying so. No staleness indicator, and the feed is known to lag. *Three findings, none visible in the visual design.*

**Pass 3 — Encoding and perception.** Twelve equally-sized tiles assert equal importance, which contradicts the brief's single decision. No sorting, so position encodes nothing. Pop-out budget spent on nothing — no element is emphasised. Deviation, the decision variable, is not encoded at all.
**Pass 4 — Narrative and access.** No takeaway anywhere. All values hover-only, so touch, keyboard and screen-reader users cannot read it — and it is used on phones. No text alternative.
**Only now: preference.** By this point there is nothing left to discuss. Every finding named a mechanism, and the redesign follows from the brief rather than from anyone's taste.

**Convert one finding into a test.** The team disputes whether managers would prefer a ranked list to the tile grid. Protocol: takeaway recall with five managers, 15-second exposure, on both versions, asking *"which berth needs attention first?"* **Pre-registered threshold:** if fewer than four of five answer correctly on the tile grid, the grid goes.
**Define the success measure.** Explanatory mode, so: correct-identification rate under timed exposure, plus the share of sessions ending in a recorded reallocation.
**Record the exception path.** If a manager needs the full tile grid for a monthly review, that is a second artifact with its own brief — not a reason to compromise this one.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The most valuable thing that happened was stopping at pass 1.**

A review that proceeded past the missing brief would have produced a list of visual improvements to an artifact that supported no decision, and everyone would have left feeling productive. The tile grid would have been restyled and still ignored.

Notice also that pass 2 found three integrity issues **invisible in the visual design** — undenominated percentages, inconsistent ranges, undisclosed staleness. Those are the findings a review organised around appearance never reaches, and they are the reason the passes run in this order.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the four passes of structured critique in order, and state what happens if the first one fails.
A chart disagreement has stalled. What is the lead's highest-leverage move, and what must be agreed before the test runs?
Describe the takeaway recall protocol, and say why removing the chart is the essential step.
Which single measure tells you whether the practice has actually changed, and which earlier section does it test?
Give one success measure each for explanatory, exploratory and systems work, and say why one measure cannot serve all three.

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Run one structured critique under the brief gate, and convert one finding into a pre-registered test.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: Use a real artifact from your team — ideally someone else's, with their agreement, so the gate is tested rather than self-applied.
instructions: **Part A — Set the rule (5 min).** Tell the group the four passes and the order, and state the gate explicitly: if audience, decision, task and mode are not stated, the session becomes brief-writing. Say it before the artifact appears.
**Part B — Run the gate (5 min).** Ask for the brief. If it does not exist, stop and write it. Do not proceed out of politeness — this is the part of the exercise that matters.
**Part C — Four passes, timeboxed (20 min).** Five minutes each. Rule: every finding names a mechanism. No preference comments until all four are complete.

**Part D — Convert one finding into a test (10 min).** Choose the finding with the most disagreement. Write: what you would show, to whom, for how long, what you would ask, and **the result that would change the design**.
**Part E — Define the measure (5 min).** Name the artifact's mode, and one success measure matched to it that you could instrument this quarter.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A real artifact and, ideally, its designer's agreement.
The four-pass structure visible in the room.
A timer — the timeboxing is what stops pass 3 consuming the session.
reflectionPrompts: Did the brief exist? If not, what happened when you stopped?
How many findings turned out to be preferences wearing a mechanism's clothes?
Which pass produced findings nobody would have raised in an unstructured review?
Could you name a result that would change your own mind, or only one that would change someone else's?

verification.mode: self-assessment against explicit criteria, plus one follow-up: did the test actually get run?
selfAssessmentCriteria: The gate was applied rather than waived.
Every finding named a mechanism rather than a comparative adjective.
Preference discussion was deferred until all four passes completed.
The test protocol has a pre-registered threshold that would genuinely change the design.
The success measure is matched to the artifact's mode, not applied generically.
At least one finding came from a pass that an unstructured review would not have reached.

learningExperiences.title: Case study: a published system, and what it cannot give you

contentBlocks.content:
## The situation

IBM's Carbon Design System is unusual among large public design systems in treating data visualization as a **first-class, separately-specified domain** rather than as a chart component tucked into a component library.

Its data visualization guidance publishes, as system-level artifacts: dedicated categorical, sequential and diverging palettes distinct from the product UI palette; chart-selection guidance organised by the question being asked; explicit accessibility requirements including contrast expectations and non-colour redundancy; and specifications for chart anatomy — axes, legends, labels, empty and loading states.

The palettes and components are distributed **as code alongside the guidance**, so a team adopting Carbon inherits the defaults whether or not anyone reads the documentation.

contentBlocks.title: Four things to extract
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Data-viz colour is separated from UI colour.** These are different problems. UI colour signals interactivity and state; viz colour encodes data and must satisfy perceptual uniformity, ordering and CVD constraints from Section 3. Systems that reuse the brand palette for encoding produce charts whose colours mean two things at once.

**2. Selection guidance is organised around the question.** This mirrors Section 4's argument that structure eliminates but task selects — and it is the difference between a catalogue and a decision aid.

**3. Accessibility appears as system-level requirements**, not per-project intentions. That is what turns Section 6's material from a designer's discipline into a property of the organisation's output.

**4. Distribution as code is the mechanism.** Guidance persuades; defaults propagate. The same lesson as viridis in Section 3, arriving from the enterprise side.

## What no published system can give you

Here is the limit, and it is the reason this case sits at the end of the course rather than the start.

**No external system can encode your organisation's semantics.** What *at risk* means in your domain. Which comparison is the standard one. Which thresholds are regulatory. What your metrics are defined as.

That layer is yours to build, and **it is the part that actually prevents two teams from meaning different things by the same blue.** Adopting Carbon gives you excellent palettes, real accessibility defaults and a serious taxonomy. It does not give you a semantic token layer for your business, a metric register, or a contribution model staffed by anyone.

So the honest summary: **adopting an external system is a strong starting point and not a governance model.** Teams that adopt one and stop are frequently surprised eighteen months later to find the same semantic collisions they thought they had solved.

terms.definition: A system-level visual value with a fixed business meaning attached, such as the colour that always denotes a forecast.
The governed set of metric definitions — grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh — that determines what any downstream chart can honestly claim.
A catalogue of approved chart forms with the tasks each supports, its cardinality limits, and explicit guidance on when not to use it.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors this case illustrates
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Treating adoption as completion.** *(vsg-library-equals-system)* — The external system supplies palettes and components; organisational semantics remain undefined and ungoverned.

**2. Reusing the UI palette for data.** — Different constraints entirely; Carbon separates them for a reason.

**3. Publishing guidance without shipping defaults.** — Carbon does both, and the code is what reaches teams who never read.

**4. Adopting without a contribution model.** — Nobody can propose a new form, so teams build outside the system and nobody finds out.

**5. Assuming a system exempts you from selection reasoning.** *(csc-flowchart-decides)* — Carbon's guidance is organised around the question precisely because structure alone cannot decide.

contentBlocks.title: Summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Carbon treats data visualization as a **separately-specified domain**, with viz colour kept distinct from UI colour.
- Selection guidance is organised **around the question**, which is what makes it a decision aid rather than a catalogue.
- Accessibility appears as **system-level requirements**, turning it into a property of output rather than of individual diligence.
- **Distribution as code is the mechanism** — the same lesson as viridis, from the enterprise side.
- **No external system can supply your organisation's semantics**, metric definitions, or a staffed contribution model.
- Adoption is a strong starting point and not a governance model.

interactionSequence.prompt: Your organisation adopted a well-regarded external design system twelve months ago, including its data visualization palettes and components. Two teams have nonetheless shipped charts where the same colour means 'at risk' in one and 'in review' in the other. Diagnose and prescribe.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Diagnosis:** an external system supplies palettes and components but cannot supply your organisation's semantics. Consistent visual tokens with unassigned meanings produce charts that look coherent and mean different things — worse than visible inconsistency, because nobody notices. This is a **governance gap, not an adoption failure**, and framing it as the latter will make both teams defensive when neither did anything wrong.

**Prescribe:** a semantic token layer defined at org level and shipped as code, mapping each business meaning onto the adopted palette; selection and semantics added to the taxonomy including 'when not to use'; a contribution and review model so new semantic states get registered rather than invented locally; and a semantic check added to the review gate.

**And note how it surfaced.** Somebody happened to compare two teams' output. That implies a need for periodic cross-team review, because nothing in the current process would have caught it.
hints: What did the external system supply, and what could it not?
How was the collision detected, and what does that imply?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you this diagnosis would land with both teams?

interactionSequence.prompt: If you were given one quarter and no additional headcount to improve visualization quality across your organisation, which of the six system parts would you build first — and what makes it the highest-leverage choice in *your* context?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
There is no universally right answer, and the reasoning matters more than the choice. Some useful patterns:

**Semantic tokens** win where teams already share a component library — the collision is live and the fix is cheap and visible.

**Accessibility acceptance criteria** win where there is regulatory pressure, because the mandate already exists and you are supplying the mechanism.
