**The taxonomy with 'when not to use'** wins where teams are building reasonable charts for the wrong tasks.

**The contribution model** wins where a system already exists and is being routed around — which is the most common state in organisations that adopted one two years ago.

What rarely wins first is the annotation standard, valuable as it is: it needs the review gate to exist before it has any enforcement surface.

workedExamples.problem: You are adopting an external design system. Specify the layer you must build on top of it, and in what order.
steps: **Take what it gives you, without modification if possible.** Palettes, chart components, accessibility defaults, anatomy specifications. Modifying these is how organisations end up maintaining a fork and losing upstream improvements.

**Build the semantic token layer first.** Map each business meaning onto the adopted palette: `status.risk`, `status.review`, `status.ok`, `series.forecast`, `series.actual`, `state.suppressed`. Ship as code. **This is the piece that prevents the collision**, and it is small enough to do in weeks.

**Build the metric register second.** Grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh, per governed metric. It does not need a metrics platform — a maintained document beats nothing by a wide margin, and it is what lets a designer catch an over-claiming title.

**Extend the taxonomy with your domain's cases.** The external taxonomy covers general forms. Add the forms your domain actually needs, each with its 'when not to use'. For a logistics operator that might be berth timelines and yard occupancy views that no general system contains.
**Add the acceptance criteria to your review gate.** The external system states accessibility requirements. Only your process can enforce them, and an unenforced requirement is a wish.
**Write the annotation standard.** Takeaway-title convention, required subtitle fields, method-note placement. This is Section 6 turned into a template that survives the designer leaving.

**Design and staff the contribution model last, and actually staff it.** Who proposes, who decides, what evidence is required, how exceptions are recorded, how often cross-team review happens. **An unstaffed contribution model is the most common failure**, because it is the only part that requires ongoing time rather than a one-off build.

**Instrument adoption.** Token usage, first-review accessibility pass rate, count of one-off custom charts. Without these you will be asked next year whether the system worked and will have only anecdotes.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The external system is the bottom two-thirds. The top third is irreducibly yours, and it is the part that carries meaning.**

Order matters here. Semantic tokens first because the collision is live and the fix is cheap; the contribution model last because it needs the other parts to exist before there is anything to contribute to — but it must actually happen, and it is the piece most often left as an intention.

And notice step 8. **A system you cannot measure is a system you cannot defend at the next budget conversation**, which is how good ones quietly stop being maintained.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What can no published design system supply, and why is that the part that matters most?
After adopting an external system, which layer do you build first and which last? Give the reason for each.

learningExperiences.title: Section quiz: interactive systems and design leadership

contentBlocks.content: The final check. Several items reach back across the whole course — this section introduced almost no new theory, only the organisational form of things you already knew.

contentBlocks.title: How this is scored
contentBlocks.content: Formative; shapes your review queue. The graded assessments are `assess-interaction-and-dashboards`, `assess-viz-systems-governance` and `assess-critique-and-leadership`. Your Day 90 review will interleave items from all seven sections.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Because interaction lets users reach any view they need, a weak default view is acceptable in an exploratory tool.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Even in exploratory tools the default sets the frame, determines what users believe the data contains, and is the only view many sessions ever see.
Correct. A weak default does not only underserve glancers — it misdirects explorers about where to look.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. A weak default does not only underserve glancers — it misdirects explorers about where to look.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** A high-fidelity mockup is an adequate specification if it is pixel-accurate and uses real data.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. It shows one state. Conditional encoding rules, scale domain behaviour, empty, loading, partial, error, stale and overflow states, null-versus-zero policy and responsive drop order are all invisible in it.
Correct — and everything not written down gets decided by whoever is closest to the deadline.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct — and everything not written down gets decided by whoever is closest to the deadline.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** If a critique opens on an artifact with no stated audience, decision or mode, you should proceed with the visual passes and raise the brief at the end.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Every downstream criterion is relative to a goal. Stop and write the brief — otherwise the designer absorbs feedback aimed at a purpose nobody agreed.
Correct. The brief pass is a hard gate, and holding it kills most unproductive critique before it starts.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. The brief pass is a hard gate, and holding it kills most unproductive critique before it starts.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Standardising chart production reduces the amount of genuinely creative visualization work a team does.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. It makes routine cases automatic so scarce attention reaches the novel ones. The alternative is redesigning bar charts forever.
Correct — and the audit that settles this is classifying last quarter's chart hours as routine or novel.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct — and the audit that settles this is classifying last quarter's chart hours as routine or novel.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Visualization comprehension is too subjective to test meaningfully.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Takeaway recall, timed retrieval, comparison accuracy, prediction and misconception probes are established, cheap, and routinely overturn confident internal opinion.
Correct. Five participants surfaces most catastrophic comprehension failures; the cost of not testing is that the loudest opinion wins.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Five participants surfaces most catastrophic comprehension failures; the cost of not testing is that the loudest opinion wins.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Values required to read a chart may be placed in a tooltip provided the tooltip is fast and clearly styled.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Hover is unavailable on touch, invisible to keyboard and screen readers, and undiscoverable. Styling does not address any of that.
Correct. Tooltips carry supplementary detail only, and where required information lives is settled in the wireframe.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Tooltips carry supplementary detail only, and where required information lives is settled in the wireframe.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** Metric definitions are the data team's responsibility and outside the designer's scope.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. The definition fixes grain, denominator and population, and therefore the whole space of honest visual claims. Declining to engage means publishing an unexamined choice.
Correct — and you do not need to own the pipeline, only for the definition to be legible enough to check charts against.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct — and you do not need to own the pipeline, only for the definition to be legible enough to check charts against.

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false:** An explanatory graphic and an exploratory dashboard are the same problem at different levels of polish.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Their requirements invert — one constrains to a single reading, the other preserves many — and so do their success measures.
Correct. Treating them as a polish gradient produces underspecified dashboards and overbuilt graphics.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: Correct. Treating them as a polish gradient produces underspecified dashboards and overbuilt graphics.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Short answer.** You have been asked to define what success looks like for your organisation's visualization practice over the next year. In four or five sentences, propose measures and say how you would run critique so they are achievable.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Mode-matched measures.** Explanatory: takeaway recall accuracy, misconception rate in probes. Exploratory: task completion on realistic analyst questions, time to first correct insight. Systems: token adoption, first-review accessibility pass rate, count of one-off custom charts — which should fall. **Practice health: the share of incoming briefs that arrive stating a decision rather than a chart type.**

**Critique.** Four ordered passes — brief, integrity, encoding, narrative and access — with the brief as a hard gate and preference deferred until all four complete. Name one recurring disagreement and the fifteen-minute protocol that would settle it, including the pre-registered threshold.

Strong answers note that the practice-health measure is the only one that tests whether Section 1 landed, and that output measures such as charts shipped will drive exactly the wrong behaviour.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Final elaboration.** In your own words: name the single change you will make to how you work as a result of this course, and the first artifact you will apply it to. Be specific about both.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The changes people most often name, and what each requires:

**Recovering the decision before designing** — costs four minutes per brief, needs nothing from anyone else, and changes the most.

**Asking for the denominator** — one question, and it catches a whole class of failure invisible in the artifact.

**Running the greyscale test** — ten seconds, no tooling.

**Writing the alt text first** — reveals whether the chart has a takeaway at all.

**Holding the brief gate in critique** — the hardest socially and the highest-leverage, because it changes how a whole team argues.

Whichever you named: your spaced-review queue now spans all seven sections, with the Day 90 review interleaving across them deliberately. **The habits fade faster than the concepts, so the specific artifact you named matters more than the principle.**

retrievalPractice.prompt: Section 7 introduced almost no new theory. Name the earlier competency that each of its three competencies is the organisational form of.

assessments.title: Reading the data before the chart

questions.prompt: A retail dataset has a column `store_id` with values from 100 to 899. A designer plots `store_id` on the x-axis of a line chart against monthly revenue. What is the primary error?
options: The line chart implies an ordered, evenly spaced sequence, but store_id is nominal — the numbers carry identity only.
There is no error: store_id is stored as a number, so it is a quantitative variable.
Revenue should have been shown as a percentage of the company total rather than in currency.
A line chart is the wrong form because bar charts are always clearer than line charts.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Store IDs are labels that happen to be numeric; a continuous position axis plus a connecting line asserts both order and spacing that the variable does not have.
Storage type tells you nothing about measurement scale — zip codes, SKUs and route numbers are all numeric and all nominal.
That is a different framing choice and leaves the actual defect untouched: a nominal variable is sitting on a continuous axis.
Context-free chart verdicts substitute slogans for reasoning; a line chart is excellent for trend over a genuinely ordered dimension.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats a numerically stored identifier as quantitative and accepts a continuous positional encoding for it.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-run the two-question classification drill on every numeric column in the learner's own current dataset: does order mean anything, and does the gap between values mean anything. Require a written verdict per column before any encoding is proposed.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why can a column full of numbers still be disqualified from a continuous axis? Name the property that decides it.

questions.prompt: A product team reports 'average customer satisfaction: 3.7' from a 1–5 rating scale and asks you to chart it over time. What is the most important thing to raise?
options: Averaging the ratings assumes equal spacing between response options, which an ordinal scale does not guarantee — show the distribution or a top-box share instead.
Nothing needs raising: 3.7 is arithmetically correct, so the chart will be accurate.
The scale should be relabelled from 1–5 to 0–4 so that the arithmetic is cleaner.
The average should be shown to two decimal places to preserve precision.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The mean silently imposes an interval assumption the data never made, and it presents that assumption with the authority of a measurement.
Arithmetic correctness is not the issue — the operation itself is unlicensed by the measurement scale.
Renumbering the labels changes nothing about spacing; the gaps between response options remain unknown.
Adding decimal places increases apparent precision on a number whose underlying assumption is unverified — it makes the problem less visible, not smaller.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner accepts a mean of ordinal responses as a measured quantity and charts it without distributional context.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Show the same Likert dataset as mean, median with interquartile range, and full response distribution, using a case where the mean stays fixed while the distribution moves from unimodal to bimodal. Then have the learner script the sentence they would give a stakeholder demanding a single number.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A stakeholder wants 'average satisfaction' from a 1–5 scale charted over time. What is the objection, and what do you offer instead?

questions.prompt: A hospital gives you a file with one row per ward per quarter containing `avg_wait_minutes`. Ward B shows 24 minutes, comfortably within target. What is the strongest reason to request record-level data before charting?
options: A quarterly ward average can conceal concentrated variation — severe waits confined to particular shifts — which is exactly what the target metric exists to detect.
Record-level data is always more honest than aggregated data, so it should always be requested.
Averages are never valid for time-based measures such as minutes.
The file is unusable because it does not contain patient identifiers.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. This is the grain problem: the collapse is arithmetically valid and destroys precisely the variation the decision depends on.
Raw data can obscure through overplotting just as an average obscures through collapse; the question is whether this aggregation hides this task's signal.
Means are legitimate for ratio data like minutes — the problem is the grain the mean was computed at, not the operation.
Identifiers are irrelevant here and would introduce privacy exposure without improving the analysis.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner charts a pre-aggregated file without establishing its grain, inheriting an invisible collapse as a published claim.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Give the learner the record-level source alongside the aggregate, have them state a claim from the aggregate, then re-aggregate at a different grain until the claim reverses. Install the three data-owner questions as a required step in their brief template.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A file arrives with one row per ward per quarter. What must you establish before charting it, and why?

questions.prompt: A product manager sends you a file of `nps_score` averaged per country and asks for a map showing which countries love the product most. In three to five sentences, name what you must establish before designing, and state what each could change about the design.
successCriteria: Names at least two of: measurement scale of the underlying responses, grain and sample size per country, the decision behind the request, or the pattern of missingness.
States a concrete design consequence for each item named.
Does not answer solely in terms of map projection, palette or styling.

rubric.excellent: Identifies that NPS is built from an ordinal 0–10 rating so a country mean carries an equal-spacing assumption, and that a mean over eleven respondents renders identically to one over forty thousand — then states the specific design consequences (distribution or top-box display; uncertainty encoding or suppression of low-n countries). Also distinguishes 'no responses' from 'low score' as a rendering requirement and reframes 'love us most' into an actionable decision.
rubric.adequate: Names one or two of the required items with a plausible design consequence, but treats the country mean as a straightforward measurement or omits the sample-size problem.
rubric.weak: Answers in terms of visual styling only — projection, colour ramp, labelling — or accepts the delivered averages as the ground truth and proceeds to chart them.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Before designing a map of country-level NPS averages, what must you establish about the data, and what would each answer change?

errorPatterns.description: Learner accepts a delivered aggregate at face value and moves directly to visual decisions without auditing scale, grain or missingness.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the four-property audit table — scale, cardinality, grain, aggregation state — as a gate before any encoding work on the learner's next three real briefs, with a written note on what the file cannot determine.

assessments.title: Rates, change and the numbers behind the chart

questions.prompt: A city publishes a map of total reported burglaries by district. The three districts with the highest counts are also the three most populous. What is the primary problem?
options: Raw counts confound the phenomenon with the size of the population producing it, so the map largely shows where people are rather than where risk is concentrated.
Nothing is wrong: counts are the raw facts, and rates introduce assumptions.
The problem is the map's colour scale, which should be diverging rather than sequential.
The districts should be sorted alphabetically so no district appears to be singled out.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Choosing a count rather than a rate is a claim about what is being measured, not a neutral default — and here it produces a map of population.
Counts are facts about a compound of phenomenon and population; presenting them as if they answered a risk question is the claim being smuggled in.
A different palette renders the same misleading quantity more attractively; the defect is the numerator-denominator pairing.
Ordering does not address which quantity is displayed, and the concern named is not a design criterion.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A map of total incidents by district ranks the most populous districts highest. Name the problem and the fix.

errorPatterns.description: Learner displays raw counts where the question concerns risk or intensity, producing a view dominated by the denominator.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require every quantity in the learner's next three briefs to be labelled count, rate, share or index with its denominator named, and to be built at least twice so the ranking change is observed rather than described.

questions.prompt: A support team reports that first-response time 'averaged 14 minutes, well within our 20-minute target'. The distribution is strongly right-skewed. What should you raise?
options: In a skewed distribution the mean can sit above most cases or conceal a long tail of very slow responses; report the median with a spread indicator, or the share breaching the target.
Nothing: 14 minutes is under 20 minutes, so the target is met by definition.
The target should be raised to 25 minutes so that the average has more headroom.
The average should be recalculated excluding the slowest cases so it better reflects normal operation.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. A mean over a skewed distribution can describe no actual case, and the decision here concerns breaches, which is a tail question rather than a centre question.
The aggregate meeting the target says nothing about how many individual cases breached it, which is what the target exists to control.
Adjusting the target to fit the statistic inverts the purpose of having one.
Removing the slow cases removes precisely the observations the target was written to detect.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A skewed response-time distribution has a mean inside target. What do you raise, and what do you report instead?

errorPatterns.description: Learner reports a mean as descriptive of typical experience on a skewed distribution, concealing the tail the decision depends on.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner display one skewed dataset as mean, median with interquartile range, and full distribution, stating which claims survive each. Establish that any mean ships with a shape indicator.

questions.prompt: A conversion rate moved from 4% to 6%. Which description is precise?
options: A two percentage-point increase, which is a fifty percent relative increase — and the relative figure should be shown with its base.
A two percent increase.
A fifty percent increase, which is the only meaningful way to express it.
A six percent conversion rate, which makes any change description redundant.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Both measures are legitimate and they carry very different rhetorical weight, so the label must be exact and the base visible.
This conflates percentage points with percent, the most common vehicle for overstating a small effect.
Relative change without its base is how a move on a tiny denominator is made to look large; it is one legitimate measure, not the only one.
Stating the endpoint discards the comparison the audience asked about.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A rate moved from 4% to 6%. Give the precise description, and say what must accompany the relative figure.

errorPatterns.description: Learner conflates percentage-point and relative change, or reports relative change without its base, overstating small effects.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Drill paired statements on the same data — percentage points, relative percent and absolute counts — requiring all three to be written and the decision-relevant one chosen, with any relative figure accompanied by its base.

questions.prompt: A national body publishes a chart showing that, in a given month, more people who had received a treatment experienced a given outcome than people who had not. Coverage of the treatment in that population is roughly ninety percent. Explain what is wrong with reading this as evidence that the treatment is ineffective, and specify how you would present the data instead.
successCriteria: Identifies that the two groups have very different sizes, so raw counts cannot be compared.
Names the correct denominator for each group.
Recognises that comparison may still be confounded by differences between the groups.
Specifies a presentation that makes the base rates visible.

rubric.excellent: Identifies that when ninety percent of the population is treated, the treated group is roughly nine times larger, so a larger raw count among the treated is expected even if the per-person rate is substantially lower; states that the comparison must be made as rates within each group, each with its own denominator; notes that even rate comparison remains confounded if the groups differ systematically in age, exposure or health, so age-standardised or stratified rates are needed; and specifies a presentation showing rates per group with the group sizes visible, ideally faceted by the confounding variable. Strong answers observe that this is the base-rate structure generally, not a fact about one topic, and that the same shape appears whenever a majority group is compared to a minority one by count.
rubric.adequate: Identifies the group-size problem and proposes rates, but does not address confounding or does not specify how the base rates become visible in the artifact.
rubric.weak: Treats the counts as comparable, or rejects the chart as simply wrong without identifying the denominator structure.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: More treated than untreated people experienced an outcome, in a population with ninety percent coverage. Why is that not evidence of ineffectiveness, and how would you present it?

errorPatterns.description: Learner compares raw counts across groups of very different sizes, mistaking a base-rate artifact for an effect.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the learner to state, for every group comparison, the size of each group and the denominator used, and to build one faceted version showing rates with group sizes annotated before any aggregate claim is published.

assessments.title: From stakeholder request to analytic task

questions.prompt: A stakeholder says: 'Build me a donut chart of support tickets by product area for the exec review.' What is your first move as design lead?
options: Ask what decision the exec review will produce, then derive the analytic tasks from that decision.
Build the donut chart as specified — the stakeholder knows their audience better than you do.
Add every available ticket dimension so the executives can see the full picture.
Build one artifact that serves both the exec review and the support team's daily triage.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The named chart is a guess at a solution; only the decision reveals what the artifact actually has to support.
Delivering the guess forfeits the expertise you were brought in for and leaves the real requirement untested until review.
Unfiltered volume raises visual search cost; insight comes from the task-relevant comparison being available, not from coverage.
Explanatory and exploratory artifacts optimise for opposite things, and merging them usually fails both audiences.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats a named chart type as the requirement and begins production without recovering the decision.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Practise the decision question on five solution-shaped requests, requiring an action verb before any form is proposed. Include one case where the stakeholder's guess proves correct, so the habit reads as verification rather than contradiction.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A stakeholder names a specific chart type. What do you recover first, and why is the named chart not the requirement?

questions.prompt: Which pair of properties, once established, most changes what you build for a given dataset?
options: The decision the viewer will make, and whether the artifact is exploratory or explanatory.
The number of variables available, and the file format they arrive in.
The stakeholder's seniority, and their previously expressed chart preferences.
The brand palette in use, and the presentation software the deck will run in.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The decision generates the analytic tasks, and the mode determines whether you constrain to one reading or preserve many — these have inverted requirements.
Variable count and file format are logistics; they constrain implementation without telling you what the artifact must let someone do.
Preference is an input to fluency at best; deciding by seniority forfeits the judgment you are being paid to make.
These affect execution, not requirements — a correct chart in the wrong mode is still the wrong artifact.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner proceeds without resolving the exploratory–explanatory fork, producing an artifact that is too rigid to explore and too dense to explain.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Give the learner one dataset and two audiences, require two separate artifacts, then have them list every requirement that inverted between the two versions.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Which two properties of a brief most change what you build, and why do they change it?

questions.prompt: A city wants to show residents how recycling participation has changed over twenty-four months. Which analytic task is most central to that brief?
options: Trend, because the dimension named in the brief is time and the question is about direction of change.
Distribution, because you should always show the spread across households first.
Part-to-whole, because participation is a share and shares are best shown as composition.
Correlation, because participation must be explained by some driver to be meaningful.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The brief explicitly concerns change over an ordered time dimension; comparison to a baseline is implied but secondary.
Spread across households is a different brief. Nothing in the stated decision requires it, and adding it dilutes the primary comparison.
Participation does have a whole, but composition answers 'what share', not 'has it changed' — the brief asks the second.
Explaining the driver is a further question the brief does not pose; answering it requires data and claims not in scope.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner expands the brief beyond the stated decision, adding tasks and variables that raise search cost without serving the decision.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner strip a dense dashboard to the single comparison its decision requires and time their own answer on both versions, then connect the cost to serial visual search.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A brief asks how participation has changed over two years. Which analytic task leads, and which ones are out of scope?

questions.prompt: Take this request: 'Can you make us a heatmap of engineering velocity by team for the quarterly business review?' Rewrite it as a design brief. State audience, decision, analytic tasks, delivery surface and mode, and name one thing you ruled out with its reason.
successCriteria: The decision line names an action rather than a topic.
Analytic tasks are drawn from the standard vocabulary: comparison, trend, distribution, part-to-whole, correlation, deviation, ranking or flow.
The requirements contain no chart type.
Mode is stated as exploratory or explanatory and justified from audience and surface.

rubric.excellent: Produces a brief whose decision line names a concrete action (for example, where to move headcount next quarter), lists two or three tasks from the standard vocabulary, specifies surface and viewing conditions, classifies the mode with justification from at least two of audience, decision and surface, and rules out the heatmap or another candidate on a named ground such as cardinality or task mismatch. Strong answers also flag that 'velocity' is an undefined metric whose grain must be established before anything is charted.
rubric.adequate: Recovers a plausible decision and names tasks, but leaves the mode unjustified, keeps a chart type inside the requirements, or omits the delivery surface.
rubric.weak: Restates the request with cosmetic edits, keeps the heatmap as the requirement, or produces a brief whose decision line names a topic rather than an action.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Rewrite a solution-shaped stakeholder request as a design brief. What five things must the brief state?

errorPatterns.description: Learner rewrites the request without extracting a decision, leaving the stakeholder's proposed solution embedded in the requirements.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the five-line brief template — audience, decision, tasks, surface, mode — as a gate on the learner's next three real requests, with the rule that no chart type may appear above the line.

assessments.title: How the visual system reads marks

questions.prompt: A dashboard uses six saturated accent colours to highlight six different alert types. Users report that alerts 'don't stand out'. What is the mechanism?
options: Pop-out depends on the highlight being unique on its distinguishing attribute; six competing highlights return the viewer to serial search.
Preattentive attributes are processed quickly, so six should be faster than one — the saturation level must be too low.
Colour is inherently unsuitable for alerts and should never be used for them.
The alerts need to be larger, since size ranks above colour in the effectiveness ranking.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Preattentive speed comes from scarcity, not from the attribute itself, so the six cancel one another.
Speed depends on the target being the only instance; multiplying pop-out channels cancels the effect regardless of saturation.
Hue is an excellent categorical identity channel — the failure here is scarcity, not colour as such.
The ranking concerns magnitude judgment, and this task is detection; enlarging all six reproduces the same cancellation.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner deploys multiple simultaneous pop-out channels and expects additive salience, producing a display with no effective emphasis.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Run a timed find-the-target exercise at one, three and six highlight colours so the cancellation is experienced directly, then impose a one-per-view pop-out budget on the learner's next design.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Six highlight colours are on screen and nothing stands out. Name the mechanism and the constraint that fixes it.

questions.prompt: A colleague argues that because people disagree about which charts look better, the channel effectiveness ranking is essentially a matter of taste. What is the strongest response?
options: Aggregate error rates by channel have been measured in controlled experiments and replicated at scale; variation between individuals is not the absence of a reliable effect.
They are right, and the ranking should be treated as one designer's opinion among many.
They are right about charts generally, but the ranking still applies to scientific work.
The ranking is authoritative because it appears in most visualization textbooks.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it is the form of argument that works in review: it moves the conversation from whose preference wins to what has been measured.
Judgment accuracy for position, length, angle, area and colour has been quantified for decades; treating it as opinion discards usable evidence.
Human vision does not change between audiences; the findings are about perception, not about a professional context.
Appeal to textbook authority is not evidence and will not survive a reviewer who asks how the effect was measured.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner reframes empirical perceptual findings as stylistic preference and therefore cannot defend an encoding decision under challenge.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Walk the learner through the Cleveland–McGill methodology rather than its conclusion, then have them run a two-minute comparison test on colleagues and observe the effect reproduce on their own sample.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Someone calls the channel effectiveness ranking 'just taste'. What is the response, and what makes it work in a review?

questions.prompt: Which statement about colour as a visual channel is correct?
options: Colour is strong for categorical identity and coarse magnitude at overview scale, and weak for precise quantitative comparison.
Colour is the most powerful channel available, so the most important numbers should be encoded in it.
Colour should be reserved entirely for decoration and never used to carry data.
Colour outperforms position for magnitude judgment provided the palette is perceptually uniform.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Importance and precision are different requirements, and colour serves only one of them.
Importance is not the criterion — precision is. Position and length substantially outperform colour for magnitude judgment.
This over-corrects: colour is the right channel for nominal identity and for density at overview scale.
Perceptual uniformity improves ordering, but it does not lift colour above position for accuracy of ratio judgment.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner assigns the most decision-critical quantitative variable to a colour channel, degrading the accuracy of the judgment the chart exists to support.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner state, for every variable, whether the viewer must identify it or must measure it, and assign channels from that answer. Contrast a cluster-detection heatmap with a ratio-judgment bar chart so colour's legitimate role is preserved.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: When is colour the right channel for a quantity, and when is it the wrong one?

questions.prompt: An analyst insists that a scatterplot's third variable — region, seven categories — should be encoded as point size 'so the important regions look important'. In three or four sentences, diagnose the proposal and state what you would do instead.
successCriteria: Identifies that region is nominal and size is an ordered channel, so the encoding asserts magnitude the categories do not have.
Separates encoding from emphasis: importance is an editorial judgment, not a data property.
Proposes a specific alternative for both the identity encoding and any warranted emphasis.

rubric.excellent: Names the expressiveness violation explicitly — an ordered channel carrying nominal data asserts ranking and magnitude among categories that have neither — then separates the two goals: identity belongs in hue or, at seven categories with overplotting risk, in faceting, while emphasis on a genuinely important region belongs in a single pop-out spend or in annotation. Strong answers note that 'look important' reveals the real request is editorial and should be handled explicitly rather than smuggled into the encoding.
rubric.adequate: Recognises that size is the wrong channel and proposes hue or faceting, but does not name why nominal data cannot take an ordered channel, or conflates the emphasis question with the encoding question.
rubric.weak: Accepts size-for-importance, or rejects it only on grounds of clutter or appearance without identifying the expressiveness violation.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Someone proposes encoding a seven-category nominal variable as point size so important categories 'look important'. Diagnose it.

errorPatterns.description: Learner evaluates an encoding proposal on appearance rather than on channel-to-scale fit, and cannot separate data encoding from editorial emphasis.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require a channel inventory table — channel, variable, measurement scale, verdict of matched, over-claiming or decorative — before any critique of a chart's appearance, and have the learner state the pop-out budget separately.

questions.prompt: A team must display four thousand sensor readings so operators can spot spatial clusters of abnormal values. A designer proposes a colour-coded grid heatmap; a reviewer objects that colour is near the bottom of the effectiveness ranking. Who is right?
options: The designer. The ranking measures accuracy of quantitative magnitude judgment, and this task is pattern detection at scale, where a colour heatmap is often correct.
The reviewer. Colour should never carry quantitative information.
The reviewer. The ranking is a hierarchy and the highest available channel should always be preferred.
Neither. The readings should be shown as a data table so that nothing is lost.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Task governs: position-based encodings for four thousand points would defeat overview, and no operator needs to read exact ratios from the grid.
This over-corrects. Colour is poor for precise comparison, not unusable for quantity — coarse magnitude at overview scale is what it is good for.
Applying the ranking without reference to task is its single most common misuse.
A four-thousand-row table makes spatial clustering essentially undetectable; completeness is not communicativeness.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner applies the effectiveness ranking as a top-down hierarchy without reference to the analytic task, rejecting correct low-ranked encodings.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Pair every effectiveness exercise with an explicit task statement and include at least one case whose correct answer is a low-ranked channel. Require the learner to state what the ranking does not rank before applying it.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What exactly does the channel effectiveness ranking measure, and what does it not measure?

questions.prompt: Which statement about diverging colour scales is correct?
options: They are appropriate only when the data has a genuinely meaningful midpoint such as zero, a target or a baseline.
They should be used whenever the data spans both high and low values, since the contrast aids reading.
They are interchangeable with sequential scales as long as the endpoints are distinguishable.
They are preferable to sequential scales because more hues carry more information.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The palette's pivot is read as a threshold, so an arbitrary midpoint fabricates a boundary the data never contained.
All continuous data spans high and low; that describes range, not a meaningful centre.
A diverging scale makes a structural claim about a centre and a sequential scale a claim about monotonic order — different claims.
Visual variation that carries no additional data is cost without informational return.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner adds visual variation — extra hues, depth, area scaling — that carries no data while degrading judgment accuracy.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner estimate values from a 3D pie and its flat equivalent and check both against the underlying numbers. Install the standing question — what does this channel encode — as a gate on every decorative dimension.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: When is a diverging colour scale legitimate, and what does an arbitrary midpoint do to the reading?

questions.prompt: A stakeholder states flatly that pie charts are bad and the team should always use bars. What is the correct evaluation of that rule?
options: It replaces reasoning with a slogan: pies are weak for precise comparison across many slices but adequate for a coarse part-to-whole read with few categories, and bars are wrong for trend, distribution or correlation.
It is correct — bar charts outperform pie charts on every task, so the rule is a useful shortcut.
It is correct for executives but not for analysts, who can read pie charts accurately.
It is incorrect because chart choice is a matter of personal preference and cannot be evaluated.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Form is only assessable against a stated task, which is why context-free verdicts fail in both directions.
Bars are disqualified when the task is trend, distribution or correlation; the shortcut hides the deciding variable.
Judgment accuracy by channel does not vary by job title; angle comparison is imprecise for everyone.
Over-corrects into relativism: encoding accuracy and task fit are assessable and measured.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner applies context-free chart verdicts, accepting or rejecting a form without reference to the analytic task it must serve.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Present four briefs where the same form is correct in two and disqualified in the other two, requiring the learner to name the deciding variable each time. Ban 'good' and 'bad' from their justifications and require a task reference instead.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Someone says 'pie charts are bad, always use bars'. What is wrong with the rule in both directions?

questions.prompt: A designer says 'we should switch from a grouped bar chart to a stacked area chart' as though choosing a different species of object. What does the grammar of graphics reveal about that framing?
options: The two differ by a transform (stacking) and a mark (area rather than rect), not by kind — so the real decision is about those components and what each one costs.
Nothing useful: chart types are discrete objects and the choice is between them as wholes.
It reveals that stacked area charts are strictly more advanced and therefore preferable.
It reveals that the underlying data must be restructured before either chart can be built.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Decomposing into data, transform, mark, encodings, scales, guides and facets makes visible exactly which component you are changing — here, that stacking costs the common baseline.
Treating forms as atomic hides which component you would actually change and makes precise specification impossible.
There is no advancement ordering among forms; stacking is appropriate for totals and composition and wrong for per-series trend.
The same tidy data supports both; no restructuring is implied by the choice.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Two charts 'differ by type'. What does the grammar of graphics say the difference actually is?

errorPatterns.description: Learner reasons about charts as indivisible types rather than as compositions, and therefore cannot specify or modify them precisely.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner decompose five familiar charts into grammar components and then produce a new form by changing exactly one component; adopt that decomposition as the standard specification format.

questions.prompt: A weather service publishes a map of rainfall anomaly — deviation from the thirty-year normal — using a rainbow colormap from dark blue to dark red. Work through the diagnosis and state your remediation.
successCriteria: Establishes whether the data has a meaningful midpoint and therefore which scale type is warranted.
Identifies the luminance problem and its consequence for how the data is read.
Notes that the palette's visual pivot and the data's meaningful pivot are in different places.
States a remediation that addresses implementation rather than switching scale type unnecessarily.

rubric.excellent: Establishes that anomaly has a genuinely meaningful zero, so a diverging scale is the correct type; identifies that the rainbow's luminance is non-monotonic, creating bright mid-scale bands that readers perceive as structure in the data, so regions of moderate anomaly appear more prominent than extreme ones; notes that the palette's perceptual centre does not coincide with zero anomaly; and prescribes a perceptually uniform diverging ramp with its neutral point anchored exactly at zero. Strong answers also run the CVD and greyscale checks and state the general rule: validate scale type, luminance monotonicity and midpoint alignment before evaluating preference.
rubric.adequate: Identifies the rainbow as problematic and proposes a perceptually uniform alternative, but does not confirm that the diverging type was correct or does not connect luminance non-monotonicity to the false-feature effect.
rubric.weak: Rejects the palette on grounds of appearance or convention, or switches to a sequential scale without recognising that the data's meaningful zero warranted a diverging one.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A rainfall anomaly map uses a rainbow colormap. Diagnose it against the three tests a continuous colour scale must pass.

errorPatterns.description: Learner evaluates a colour scale on appearance rather than on scale type, luminance monotonicity and midpoint alignment, and remediates by substitution rather than diagnosis.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Impose the three-test protocol on every continuous colour scale the learner selects — type matches data structure, luminance orders monotonically, midpoint aligns with the data's meaningful zero — with the preference question deferred until all three pass.

questions.prompt: A logistics team wants to compare month-over-month shipment volume for fourteen distribution centres, seeing the shape of each centre's year. Which composition strategy is correct?
options: Small multiples — fourteen panels on shared scales — because the task is seeing each series' shape and faceting scales past the legend ceiling.
A single line chart with all fourteen series superposed and a colour legend.
Small multiples with each panel scaled to its own data, so every centre's pattern is clearly visible.
A stacked area chart, so total volume is visible alongside each centre.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct on both counts: the task is per-series shape, and fourteen categories is far beyond the working-memory ceiling for legend use.
Occlusion plus a fourteen-item legend forces repeated memory round-trips; superposition is for comparing a few series to each other.
Independent scales make panels look comparable while destroying comparability — the layout makes a claim the scales invalidate.
Only the bottom band of a stacked chart has a common baseline; the other thirteen are read against a wiggling one.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner selects a composition strategy from data shape alone, ignoring the task and the cardinality limits that decide between structurally valid options.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Give one dataset and three decisions held by three roles, requiring three different correct answers, then have the learner locate the point in a published chart-chooser where all three collapse into one recommendation.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Fourteen series, and the task is seeing each one's shape. Superpose or facet — and what is the non-negotiable condition?

questions.prompt: A scatterplot of sixty thousand loan records shows a solid black mass in the centre with scattered points at the edges. A colleague argues that any aggregation would be less honest. Your response?
options: The overplotted version already hides the distribution while preserving the outliers, so it over-represents the rare; binning or density with a separate outlier layer is more truthful.
They are right — every data point should always be shown so that nothing is lost.
They are right, but the chart should be enlarged until the points separate.
Replace it with summary statistics, which are more rigorous than any plot.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it names the mechanism rather than asserting a preference, which is what makes it usable in review.
Nothing is lost from the file, but nearly everything is lost from the reading — the viewer sees ink density, not data.
At sixty thousand points this only postpones saturation and fails entirely on any fixed delivery surface.
Over-corrects into the opposite error: Anscombe's quartet exists precisely to show that matching summary statistics can hide radically different structures.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner equates completeness with honesty and ships an overplotted view whose central mass is unreadable.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner estimate centre and spread from a heavily overplotted scatter, reveal the binned version and their own error, then immediately present Anscombe's quartet so both failure directions are held at once.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Someone says aggregating would be less honest than plotting all sixty thousand points. What is the counter-argument?

questions.prompt: A designer proposes a custom radial encoding for a quarterly revenue-by-region report, arguing it will make the deck memorable. What is the correct evaluation?
options: Apply the novelty test — name the specific task a conventional form would prevent. Revenue by region is a ranked comparison a sorted bar chart handles at top-ranked accuracy, so the learning cost is unjustified.
It is a good idea: a distinctive visualization signals design sophistication to executives.
Radial encodings are always invalid and should never be used.
Accept it if the executives like it, since audience preference is the deciding factor.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Novelty is justified by structural necessity, not by memorability; the cost is paid by every viewer while the benefit accrues to the designer.
To analytics and engineering partners this typically reads as self-indulgence and costs credibility you will need later.
Radial forms are appropriate for genuinely cyclical data — hours of the day, months of the year — where linear layout misrepresents wraparound.
Audience fluency is an input to selection; audience preference between forms is the judgment you are being paid to make on their behalf.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner selects a non-conventional form for reasons of distinctiveness, imposing decoding cost on every viewer without a task justification.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Install the novelty test as a required gate — name in one sentence the task a conventional form would prevent — and pair it with cases where novelty is genuinely warranted, so the test reads as calibration rather than prohibition.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What single test do you apply before committing to a custom encoding, and what happens if you cannot pass it?

questions.prompt: A dashboard tile exists so that finance staff can look up the exact figure for a named cost centre among forty. A designer proposes replacing the current table with a bar chart. Evaluate.
options: The table is correct for this task: when the job is precise value lookup, reading a number beats decoding any graphical channel, and forty rows exceeds what a bar chart labels comfortably.
The bar chart is better, because visualizing data is always preferable to tabulating it.
The bar chart is better, because bar charts sit near the top of the effectiveness ranking.
Either works equally well, since the underlying numbers are identical.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and the effectiveness ranking itself predicts it — the ranking concerns judging magnitudes, not retrieving exact values.
Tables are a first-class form; treating them as a failure to visualize discards the best tool for lookup and for heterogeneous metrics.
Length ranks highly for comparing magnitudes, which is not the task here, and forty labelled bars is beyond comfortable direct labelling.
Identical numbers do not imply identical task support; the whole discipline is that representation determines what is readable.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: When is a designed table the correct answer rather than a chart?

errorPatterns.description: Learner replaces a lookup-oriented table with a chart, degrading precise value retrieval in the belief that charting is inherently superior.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner rebuild a lookup tile as a designed table with aligned figures, deliberate sorting and in-cell sparklines, then compare retrieval time against the charted version.

questions.prompt: You are handed hourly air-quality readings from sixty monitoring stations across a city, covering three years. A councillor asks for a chart showing whether air quality is improving. Walk through your selection reasoning and state your chosen form, your runner-up, and why the runner-up lost.
successCriteria: Addresses all four selection inputs: structure, task, audience and convention, delivery surface.
Names a grain decision and justifies it from the task rather than from convenience.
Eliminates at least one alternative by a named mechanism, not a comparative adjective.
Identifies the audience's likely follow-up question and where its answer lives.

rubric.excellent: Establishes structure (time at very high cardinality, sixty nominal stations far past the legend ceiling, ratio readings) and re-grains from hourly to monthly or seasonal because a three-year improvement question does not need hourly resolution; names the task as trend with an implied deviation against a regulatory threshold; classifies the councillor as non-technical and the surface as an explanatory report; selects a citywide trend line with a threshold reference mark, direct-labelled, with a faceted small-multiple set on shared scales as a planned secondary figure; and eliminates superposition on legend-ceiling and occlusion grounds and stacking on baseline-loss grounds. Strong answers note that averaging sixty stations into one line hides uneven improvement across the city, and that the councillor's predictable follow-up is exactly why the faceted figure is planned rather than optional.
rubric.adequate: Chooses a defensible form and names the task, but leaves one or two selection inputs unaddressed, eliminates alternatives with comparative adjectives rather than mechanisms, or does not address the grain decision.
rubric.weak: Names a chart type without reasoning, selects from data shape alone, or proposes superposing sixty series.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Sixty stations, three years of hourly air-quality data, a non-technical councillor asking whether things are improving. Walk through your selection reasoning.

errorPatterns.description: Learner selects a form without generating and eliminating a viable set, and so cannot name the runner-up or defend the choice under challenge.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the viable-set discipline on the learner's next three briefs: three genuinely different candidates, an elimination sentence per rejected form naming a mechanism, and an explicit statement of the runner-up.

questions.prompt: A conservation team wants to compare protected-area funding across twelve regions for a budget decision. What is the strongest first question about using a map?
options: What does the map show that a sorted bar chart would not — is any spatial relationship such as adjacency or contiguity part of this decision?
Which projection should be used to minimise area distortion?
Which sequential colour ramp best fits the funding values?
Should the regions be labelled directly or in a legend?

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Geography is expensive in space and accuracy, and it is worth paying for only when spatial relationships are part of the question; twelve regions ranked by funding is a comparison task.
A real question, but it presumes the map — and projection choice cannot rescue a form that does not serve the task.
Palette selection is downstream of whether the map is the right encoding at all.
Labelling is a refinement of a decision not yet justified.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Before building a map, what is the gate question you must answer?

errorPatterns.description: Learner selects a map because the data contains locations, spending space and accuracy on geography the decision does not use.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require both a map and a non-spatial form for one location-bearing dataset, with a written statement of which questions each answers better, and install the gate question before any future map.

questions.prompt: You aggregate the same incident points into census tracts, then into postal districts, and the spatial pattern changes noticeably. What is the correct interpretation?
options: This is the modifiable areal unit problem: the boundaries are an analytical choice, and the pattern is partly a property of the units rather than of the incidents.
One of the two aggregations must contain an error, since the same points cannot produce different patterns.
The finer aggregation is always the more accurate one and should be preferred.
The pattern difference is a rendering artifact and will disappear at higher resolution.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it means every choropleth carries an obligation to disclose which units were used and why.
Both can be computed correctly; differing patterns from differing aggregations is expected, not evidence of a mistake.
Finer units reduce some aggregation effects and worsen small-cell instability and disclosure risk; finer is not automatically better.
The effect is analytical, not a matter of pixels, and it persists at any rendering resolution.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: The same points aggregated into two different boundary sets give different patterns. What is this called, and what does it oblige you to disclose?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats administrative boundaries as a neutral container and reports a choropleth pattern as a property of the phenomenon alone.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Show one point dataset aggregated at three boundary levels so the pattern visibly changes, then require a standing disclosure on every choropleth: which units, why those, and the population range across them.

questions.prompt: A team publishes a force-directed node-link diagram of an eight-hundred-node collaboration network. Reviewers describe clusters 'in the centre' as the most important. What is your assessment?
options: Node position in a force-directed layout is largely an artifact of the algorithm and its seed, so centrality read from position is not a finding; at this density a matrix view would better support adjacency and cluster tasks.
The reviewers are right: central position in a force layout encodes network centrality by construction.
The diagram is fine, but the nodes should be coloured to make the clusters clearer.
Node-link diagrams are always the correct representation for network data.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Viewers reliably read proximity as similarity and centre as importance, so a layout that encodes neither must say so — and at eight hundred nodes the hairball defeats most tasks anyway.
Force layouts approximate some structure but do not encode a centrality measure; if centrality matters it must be encoded explicitly in a channel.
Colour cannot repair a spatial arrangement that viewers are reading as data when it is not.
Matrix representations outperform node-link views for adjacency and cluster tasks at moderate and high density.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Reviewers call the central cluster of a force-directed diagram the most important. Assess that reading.

errorPatterns.description: Learner publishes a force-directed layout without stating what position encodes, allowing algorithmic artifacts to be read as findings.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner re-run one layout with different seeds and observe the picture change while the graph does not, then rebuild the same data as an ordered matrix and compare task support. Require every published node-link view to state what position does and does not encode.

questions.prompt: A land-management agency has ten years of parcel-level land-use change records covering a large region, plus a hierarchy of ownership categories and the flows of parcels between use classes. The director asks for something showing 'how land use is changing'. Design the set of views, justifying each form.
successCriteria: Establishes the decision before choosing forms.
Justifies whether geography earns its space, and states the normalization used on any map.
Selects a defensible representation for the hierarchy and for the flow, each justified by task.
Names one distortion introduced by each chosen form.

rubric.excellent: Recovers a decision — for example where to target acquisition or restoration — and derives tasks from it. For the spatial view, justifies geography on the grounds that adjacency and contiguity matter to land management, selects a form appropriate to the normalization question (rate of change per unit area rather than raw parcel counts) and names the areal-unit and projection distortions it accepts. For the ownership hierarchy, chooses a treemap or sunburst for part-to-whole at depth, noting that area judgments are imprecise and that depth beyond two or three levels degrades quickly. For the transitions between use classes, chooses a Sankey or chord form and notes that link crossings and node ordering are layout artifacts rather than data. Strong answers apply the novelty test from the chart-selection material, state which single view carries the headline, and note that a designed table may serve the precise-value questions better than any of them.
rubric.adequate: Selects reasonable forms for each structure and justifies most choices by task, but omits the normalization question on the map or does not name the distortions each form introduces.
rubric.weak: Produces a map because the data has locations and a node-link or treemap because the data has structure, without a decision, a normalization or a stated distortion.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Parcel-level land-use change, an ownership hierarchy, and flows between use classes. Design the view set and justify each form.

errorPatterns.description: Learner selects spatial and relational forms from data structure alone, without a decision, a normalization choice or an accounting of the distortions each form introduces.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the three-part discipline on every spatial or relational brief: state what the form encodes that a simpler form would not, name the normalization, and name the distortion accepted.

questions.prompt: A line chart of a currency exchange rate over six months uses a y-axis from 1.28 to 1.34. A reviewer demands it start at zero. What is the correct response?
options: The zero rule applies to length encodings, where the mark's length is the value. This is a position encoding of a quantity with no meaningful zero, so a zero baseline would compress the signal into an unreadable flat line.
The reviewer is right: all quantitative axes must begin at zero to avoid exaggeration.
The reviewer is right, but only because currency data is volatile.
It does not matter, because the axis is labelled with its actual range.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it states the principle rather than the exception: the baseline must match what the encoding claims.
Applied universally this destroys signal in exchange rates, temperatures and pH, where zero is not a meaningful reference point.
Volatility is not the deciding variable; whether the encoding is length-based and whether zero is meaningful are.
Viewers read mark geometry preattentively, long before reading axis labels — labels do not repair a misleading geometry.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner applies the zero-baseline rule universally, either exaggerating with truncated bars or destroying signal by forcing zero on a position encoding.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Drill paired cases — the same data as bars and as a line — so the learner watches the rule apply and then not apply, and can name the property of the encoding that decided it each time.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: When must an axis start at zero, when must it not, and what principle decides between the two cases?

questions.prompt: An executive asks you to remove confidence intervals from a forecast chart because they will confuse the board. What is the best response?
options: Removing them does not remove the uncertainty — it transfers it invisibly to the board, who then decide on false precision. Offer a quantile dotplot or fan encoding instead.
Agree: non-technical audiences should not be shown uncertainty, as it undermines confidence in the analysis.
Refuse on the grounds that error bars are the only statistically valid way to show uncertainty.
Remove them from the chart and put the numbers in an appendix.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. It accepts the true premise that intervals are often misread and rejects the false conclusion, then offers a specific alternative — which is what makes it persuasive rather than merely principled.
This relocates risk to where nobody can see it, and the board acts on a precision the data never had.
Wrong on the facts — hypothetical outcome plots, quantile dotplots, gradient encodings and textual framings are all valid — and it turns a solvable design problem into a standoff.
The board reads the chart, not the appendix; this is omission with a paper trail.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner omits uncertainty to simplify a chart, transferring unquantified risk to the decision-maker without disclosure.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Present one forecast as point estimates, error bars, a quantile dotplot and a fan encoding, and have the learner match each to an audience and stakes level. Require a scripted response to the removal request that includes the alternative offered.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: An executive asks you to drop the error bars so the board is not confused. What is the argument against, and what do you offer instead?

questions.prompt: Which of these is a genuine integrity finding even when every number in the chart is arithmetically correct?
options: The time range begins at a local trough, so the subsequent series reads as recovery rather than as normal fluctuation.
The chart uses a sans-serif typeface that does not match the report's body text.
The legend is placed on the right rather than above the plot area.
The chart shows four series where three would have been sufficient.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Range selection is a framing choice that shapes the reading without altering a single value — one of the classic mechanisms alongside comparison group, denominator, aggregation statistic and aspect ratio.
A typographic inconsistency is a craft issue, not a claim about the data.
Legend placement affects reading cost, not the truth of what is claimed.
Series count affects clarity and search cost; it is not by itself a distortion of the underlying relationship.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner audits only the numbers and the axis, missing framing-based distortion introduced through range, comparison group, denominator or statistic.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Give one dataset and require two charts supporting opposite conclusions without falsifying any value, then have the learner write the framing disclosures that would make each honest.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Name four ways a chart can mislead while every number in it is correct.

questions.prompt: An internal dashboard breaks engagement metrics down by department, office and seniority, with free filtering. Some resulting cells contain two or three people. What is the integrity concern?
options: Small cells re-identify individuals, and free filtering lets a user difference views against each other — so a minimum cell threshold with visible suppression is required.
There is no concern: the data is aggregated, so individuals cannot be identified.
The concern is only that small cells produce noisy percentages, which should be rounded.
The concern is that the filter panel is too complex and should be simplified for usability.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Aggregation reduces disclosure risk without eliminating it, and interactivity multiplies the number of views that can be compared.
Aggregation is not anonymisation; a cell of three is close to a named list to anyone who knows the department.
Noise is a real statistical issue and a separate one; rounding does not prevent identification.
Usability matters, but simplifying the panel for clarity does not address the disclosure risk it creates.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A filterable breakdown produces cells containing two or three people. Name the concern and the control.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats aggregation as anonymisation and ships filterable breakdowns that expose small cells and permit differencing.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner find the filter combination isolating the fewest records in a real dashboard, implement a minimum-cell threshold with visible suppression rather than silent omission, and add a disclosure-control row to the specification template.

questions.prompt: A charity's annual report shows a bar chart of programme spend per beneficiary, y-axis from 180 to 240, with bars for three years, titled 'Sustained investment in our beneficiaries'. Audit it and state your remediation.
successCriteria: Identifies the baseline problem and connects it to the encoding type rather than stating a general rule.
Identifies at least one framing finding that involves no incorrect number.
Addresses the title's relationship to what the chart can support.
States remediations that change the encoding or disclosure, not only the wording.

rubric.excellent: Identifies baseline truncation on a length encoding — bars beginning at 180 no longer represent their values, so year-on-year differences are visually exaggerated — and estimates the lie factor where the values allow; identifies the denominator doing invisible work, since spend per beneficiary can rise because beneficiary numbers fell; flags the three-year range as possibly selected and the absence of any definition of 'beneficiary' or 'programme spend'; and notes the title asserts a positive trajectory the truncated bars manufacture. Remediation covers a zero baseline or re-encoding as a dot plot, a title stating the actual change with its magnitude, and a subtitle carrying beneficiary counts, definitions and source.
rubric.adequate: Identifies the baseline truncation and rewrites the title, but misses the denominator problem or treats the range and definitional gaps as minor.
rubric.weak: Notes only that the chart looks misleading without naming a mechanism, or proposes fixing it by changing the title alone while leaving the truncated bars in place.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A charity's per-beneficiary spend chart runs its bar axis from 180 to 240 and is titled 'Sustained investment'. Audit it by mechanism.

errorPatterns.description: Learner audits a chart impressionistically, missing framing mechanisms and remediating with wording changes rather than encoding or disclosure changes.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the eight-row mechanism table — baseline, scale, aspect ratio, time range, comparison group, denominator, statistic, uncertainty — on every audit, with a severity rating and an estimated lie factor wherever it is computable.

questions.prompt: Which statement about accessible data visualization is correct?
options: A text alternative must convey the chart's takeaway pattern, not only its values, because the pattern is what the chart existed to communicate.
Providing the underlying data table fully satisfies the accessibility requirement.
Selecting a colourblind-safe palette makes a chart accessible.
Accessibility is best handled in a QA pass before release, when the design is stable.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Equivalence means equivalent information, and the information in a chart is structural — a trend, a cluster, a gap.
A table is a fallback for values; asking a screen-reader user to reconstruct a trend from two hundred rows is not equivalent access.
