A safe palette addresses one condition. Contrast, redundant encoding, pointer-free access and text alternatives all remain open.
Hue-as-sole-carrier and hover-only data access are decided in the first hour; by QA they are load-bearing and remediation means redesign.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner supplies a data table as the accessible equivalent, providing values while withholding the structural pattern the chart existed to convey.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner attempt to state the takeaway of an unfamiliar chart from its data table alone under a time limit, then write the one-sentence pattern description that would have served. Require both in every deliverable thereafter.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why is a data table not a sufficient text alternative for a chart?

questions.prompt: A team has adopted a CVD-safe palette across all their charts. Which check is most likely to still fail?
options: Values that are reachable only on hover, which excludes touch, keyboard and screen-reader users.
Nothing — a CVD-safe palette resolves the accessibility requirements for charts.
The chart's file size, which affects load time on assistive technology.
The alphabetical ordering of the legend entries.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Palette choice and pointer-free access are independent requirements, and hover dependence is the most common surviving failure.
Contrast, redundant non-colour encoding, pointer-free access, text alternatives and reduced-motion handling are all still open.
File size is a performance concern, not an access barrier of this kind.
Legend ordering affects scanning cost; it is not an accessibility failure in itself.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats palette selection as completing accessibility work and ships charts with hover-dependent values or insufficient contrast.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Run the four-check audit — greyscale, pointer-free access, contrast, text alternative — on a chart the learner has already judged compliant, so the remaining failures are discovered rather than described.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A chart already uses a CVD-safe palette. Which accessibility checks remain open?

questions.prompt: At what point in a project do the decisions that determine a chart's accessibility get made?
options: In the first hour, when colour is or is not made the sole carrier of meaning and when it is decided where required values live.
At the end, during a QA pass, which is why accessibility is scheduled there.
During engineering implementation, since accessibility is delivered through markup.
After launch, when real users with assistive technology report problems.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Those choices become load-bearing quickly, and remediating them later means redesign rather than adjustment.
By QA the determining choices are already structural, which is why late audits produce redesigns rather than fixes.
Markup implements decisions already made; no amount of markup rescues a chart whose meaning is carried by hue alone.
Post-launch reports are a safety net, not a design method, and they arrive after the cost of change has multiplied.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner schedules accessibility as a late verification step, so encoding choices that foreclose access are already committed by the time they are examined.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Move the four criteria into the learner's definition-of-done for chart work at wireframe stage, and have them cost the remediation of a finished hover-dependent chart against designing the same chart accessibly from the start.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: When are the decisions that determine a chart's accessibility actually made, and what follows from that?

questions.prompt: A chart system built for an English-language product is being rolled out across twelve markets including Arabic and German. What is most likely to break structurally?
options: Direct labels sized for English will overflow under longer translations, decimal and date conventions differ by locale, and right-to-left layout mirrors axis direction and reading order.
Nothing structural — localisation is a matter of swapping the label strings.
Only the font will need changing, since the layout is numeric and therefore locale-neutral.
Only the colour palette, since colour meanings differ between cultures.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Each of these is a layout rule, not a string, and none is fixable after the design is finished.
Label expansion of fifty percent or more, separator inversion and mirrored layout are all structural consequences that strings cannot absorb.
Numbers are among the least locale-neutral elements: separators, grouping, currency and date order all vary.
Cultural colour association is worth considering, but it is not the main structural risk here.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A chart system is going to twelve markets including a right-to-left language. What breaks structurally?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats internationalization as end-stage string replacement, leaving layout rules that cannot absorb label expansion or mirrored reading order.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner render one chart with the longest available translation of every label, a right-to-left locale, and a comma-decimal locale, then fix the failures in the layout rules rather than in the copy.

questions.prompt: Write a text alternative for a line chart showing quarterly enrolment at a training provider from 2019 to 2024, where enrolment falls steadily from 2019 to 2022, rises sharply through 2023, and ends slightly above the 2019 level. Then state what else the chart needs to be accessible.
successCriteria: The alternative names the chart type, the scope and the structural pattern in prose.
The alternative is not a list of values.
Names at least two further requirements beyond the text alternative.

rubric.excellent: Produces a description that names the chart type and scope, then states the pattern — a steady decline through 2022, a sharp recovery through 2023, and an endpoint slightly above the starting level — in prose a listener could act on. Then names further requirements: redundant non-colour encoding so hue is not load-bearing, contrast minimums for marks and text, pointer-free access to any required values, and provision of the underlying data separately from the pattern description. Strong answers note that the alternative and the visible takeaway title should agree, and that if the pattern cannot be stated in one sentence the chart may not have a takeaway.
rubric.adequate: Writes a serviceable pattern description but drifts into listing values, or names only one further requirement.
rubric.weak: Lists the quarterly values, describes the chart's appearance rather than its content, or asserts that supplying the data table is sufficient.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Write a text alternative for a line chart with a decline, a sharp recovery and an endpoint above the start — and name what else the chart needs.

errorPatterns.description: Learner writes text alternatives that enumerate values or describe appearance rather than conveying the structural pattern.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require every chart deliverable to ship with a one-sentence pattern statement written before the chart is styled, and have the learner check it against a colleague's unaided reading of the finished chart.

questions.prompt: Which chart title stays within what a two-series line chart of advertising spend and revenue over twelve months can support?
options: Revenue and ad spend both rose through 2025, with revenue growth concentrated in the third quarter.
Increased ad spend drove 2025 revenue growth.
Advertising Spend and Revenue, 2025.
Marketing efficiency improved in 2025.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. It states the co-movement and its timing — exactly what is visible — without asserting a mechanism.
Two co-moving series support association, not causation; the chart cannot exclude reverse causation or a common cause.
A topic title feels safe but hands framing to the viewer, who takes it from whatever is most salient.
Efficiency is a ratio the chart does not display; the claim requires a quantity that is not shown.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner defaults to a topic title in the belief that withholding a takeaway is neutral, leaving the viewer to construct an unsupported reading.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Show one chart with only a topic title to several colleagues and collect the spread of stated takeaways, then repeat with an accurate takeaway title so the learner sees annotation narrow the readings toward the supported one.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why is a topic title not a neutral choice, and what does an accurate takeaway title do instead?

questions.prompt: Where is the line between legitimate framing and editorialising in a chart's annotation layer?
options: Stating what the chart shows is legitimate; asserting what it does not show is not. The test is fidelity to the data, not absence of guidance.
Any interpretation added by the designer is editorialising, so annotation should be limited to axis labels.
Annotation is legitimate whenever the underlying numbers are accurate, regardless of what the text claims.
The line depends on the audience: technical audiences can be given takeaways, general audiences cannot.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it explains why an explicit takeaway is more auditable than a topic title — it makes the framing contestable.
This confuses guidance with distortion; declining to annotate does not remove framing, it hides it.
Accurate numbers under a claim the chart cannot support is precisely the failure mode — the text must stay inside what the data establishes.
General audiences need the takeaway more, not less; withholding it leaves them to invent one.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner either withholds annotation to avoid bias or annotates past what the data supports, having no working test for the boundary.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Drill paired titles for one chart — one stating an observed association, one asserting a mechanism — requiring the learner to mark where each crosses the line and rewrite the failing one inside support.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: State the boundary between legitimate framing and editorialising in a chart title.

questions.prompt: A team treats their exploratory dashboard and their executive summary graphic as the same design problem at different levels of polish. What is wrong with that view?
options: The two modes have inverted requirements — one constrains to a single reading, the other preserves many — so treating them as a polish gradient underspecifies both.
Nothing is wrong: the summary graphic is simply the dashboard with better typography and spacing.
The dashboard should always be built first, and the summary graphic derived from it by deletion.
The two differ only in how much data they contain, so the fix is to reduce the number of series.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The requirements invert rather than intensify, which is why merged artifacts are too rigid to explore and too cluttered to explain.
Polish does not resolve a requirements conflict; the artifact still has to choose which set of requirements it satisfies.
Derivation by deletion preserves the exploratory structure and rarely produces a single unmissable takeaway.
Volume is a symptom; the underlying difference is whether the artifact constrains or preserves readings.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats explanatory design as a finishing stage applied to exploratory work, producing artifacts that satisfy neither mode's requirements.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner list both modes' requirements side by side and mark every pair that inverts, then split a merged artifact from their own work into two and note what each version could finally drop.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why are explanatory and exploratory design not the same problem at different levels of polish?

questions.prompt: A dashboard re-sorts its bars instantly when a filter is applied. Users report that they 'lose track of what happened'. What is the design principle at stake?
options: Object constancy: a staged transition that preserves mark identity lets viewers track which bar became which, so the change is understood rather than re-read from scratch.
Animation is decoration, so the correct fix is to remove the sorting behaviour entirely.
The bars should simply be re-coloured after sorting so users can find them again.
Users need onboarding explaining that the chart re-sorts.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it should respect reduced-motion preferences — the transition carries information, so a non-motion equivalent is needed too.
Transitions carry information about identity and change; treating them as polish is what produced the abrupt swap.
Recolouring adds a second identity system and spends attention without conveying the movement itself.
Explaining a comprehension failure is not the same as removing it.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Users lose track when a chart re-sorts instantly. Name the principle and the constraint that accompanies it.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats transitions as visual polish, producing abrupt state changes that force viewers to re-read the chart.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner build one state change twice — instant swap and staged transition preserving object constancy — and test which lets a colleague state what changed; require every animation to name the relationship it preserves and to have a reduced-motion equivalent.

questions.prompt: A line chart shows medication adherence rising from 61 to 74 percent over eighteen months, with a patient-support programme launched at month six and no control group. Write the title, the subtitle, and name two annotations you would add — including one that complicates your own headline.
successCriteria: The title states the temporal association without asserting causation.
The subtitle carries scope: population, definition, date range, and the absence of a control group.
One named annotation is a reference mark that makes a comparison direct.
One named annotation complicates the headline claim.

rubric.excellent: Produces a title stating that adherence rose thirteen points with most of the gain after the programme launch — the temporal association, which is what is visible — and explicitly avoids the causal phrasing. The subtitle carries population, the adherence definition, the date range and the absence of a control group. Annotations include a vertical reference line at the launch point, converting a memory task into a direct visual comparison, and a horizontal reference line at the eighty-percent clinical target which shows the endpoint remains below target — the self-complicating element. Strong answers state why including the inconvenient reference mark makes the rest of the chart more credible to a sceptical reader.
rubric.adequate: Writes a non-causal title and adds the launch reference line, but omits the scope subtitle or includes no annotation that complicates the headline.
rubric.weak: Writes a causal title, or produces a topic title on the grounds that stating a takeaway would be biased, or lists only decorative annotations.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Adherence rose thirteen points around a programme launch, with no control group. Write the title, subtitle, and two annotations — one of which must complicate your headline.

errorPatterns.description: Learner builds an annotation layer that supports the headline only, omitting the disclosures and reference marks that would let a reader assess the claim.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require every annotated chart to include one element that complicates its own claim where the data warrants, and have the learner state in review why that element strengthens rather than weakens the argument.

questions.prompt: Analytics show that eighty percent of sessions on your dashboard involve no interaction at all. What does this imply for the redesign?
options: The unmanipulated default view carries the majority of the communicative load and must stand alone for one role and one decision.
Interaction discovery needs improving — add onboarding and affordance cues so more users engage the filters.
Add more filters so users have a reason to interact.
The data is not interesting enough; source additional metrics to increase engagement.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Interaction serves the minority of sessions that go further; the default is what the dashboard actually is for most users.
Low interaction is usually a signal about glance-based use, not a discoverability defect; teaching people to use filters they do not need helps nobody decide anything.
Filters offload unmade decisions onto users; adding them raises cost and lowers the chance the default view answers anything.
Volume raises search cost. The question is whether the default view supports a decision, not how much it contains.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner relies on interaction to deliver value that the default view fails to deliver, leaving most sessions unserved.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner pull interaction analytics from a real dashboard, confront the zero-interaction share, and apply the standing test: if interactivity vanished tomorrow, what percentage of value survives before and after redesign.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Most sessions on a dashboard involve no interaction. What follows for how you design it?

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for date, region and product filters 'like the other dashboards have'. What is the design-lead response?
options: Ask which role and which decision the view serves, then set those parameters yourself — a filter is an unmade decision handed to someone with less context and less time.
Add all three, since filters are what make a dashboard flexible.
Add them but hide them behind an advanced panel so the default view stays clean.
Refuse all filters on principle, since scoped views are always superior to configurable ones.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and it leaves room for the legitimate exception: filters belong where the next question is genuinely unpredictable.
Each filter costs the user four things — knowing it exists, what it does, what value is right, and its current state — before any information is obtained.
Hiding a control does not resolve the undecided scope; it only makes the unmade decision harder to find.
Over-corrects: genuinely exploratory work needs dynamic query, and a single role can legitimately span multiple scopes.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner adds filters by convention rather than by need, transferring scoping decisions to users who lack the context to make them.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the learner to justify each filter by naming the role whose next question is genuinely unpredictable; every filter failing the test is converted to a default scope or a drill-down and the decision documented.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A stakeholder wants three filters 'like the other dashboards'. What do you ask, and when is a filter actually right?

questions.prompt: Where may a tooltip legitimately carry information?
options: Supplementary detail only — an exact figure behind a mark whose approximate value is already legible, a record ID, a timestamp.
Anywhere, since hovering is a natural interaction that all users perform.
Any value that would clutter the chart if printed on the marks.
Primary values, provided the tooltip is styled clearly and appears quickly.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Nothing required to read the chart may depend on a pointer; that constraint is settled at the wireframe, not in styling.
Hover is unavailable on touch, invisible to keyboard and screen-reader users, and undiscoverable by anyone not already exploring.
Clutter is a real cost, but the remedy is relocating or reducing what is shown, not hiding required values behind a pointer.
Styling and latency do not address the access problem; the value remains unreachable for a large group of users.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner places values required to read the chart in hover states, making them unreachable on touch, by keyboard and by screen reader.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner operate their own dashboard on a phone and by keyboard alone, list every value that became unreachable, and relocate each to the mark, an adjacent table or a focusable element, recording the decision in the specification.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: State the tooltip rule, and name the three user situations that make it necessary.

questions.prompt: A university admissions dashboard used by forty regional recruiters has nine filters, twelve tiles, and all values on hover. Median session is fifty-five seconds, filter use is near zero, and it is mostly opened on phones between school visits. Redesign it: state the role and decision, the default view, which filters survive, and the mobile degradation rule.
successCriteria: Names a role and a decision that is an action, not a topic.
Designs a default view that stands alone without interaction, with encoding choices justified.
Accounts for every removed control — scoped, moved to drill-down, or deleted.
States what drops on mobile, in what order, and what never drops.
Provides pointer-free access to any required values.

rubric.excellent: Recovers a specific role and decision — for example, which schools a recruiter should prioritise visiting in the coming fortnight — and derives a task hierarchy from it. Designs a default view for that decision alone, scoped to the recruiter's own region and current cycle, using position and length for the primary quantity with a threshold reference mark and a single pop-out spend. Reduces nine filters to at most two parameters and accounts for the rest as scope or drill-down. States a mobile degradation order in which the ranked primary view and its threshold never drop. Moves all required values off hover onto the marks or into a focusable list, and names one instrumented measure — such as time to a shortlist, or the share of sessions ending in a recorded action — to test whether the redesign worked.
rubric.adequate: Produces a scoped default view and removes most filters, but leaves the mobile degradation order unstated, does not account for where removed controls went, or leaves some required values in hover.
rubric.weak: Restyles the existing twelve tiles, keeps most filters on the grounds of flexibility, or proposes onboarding to increase filter use.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Nine filters, twelve tiles, hover-only values, fifty-five-second sessions, mostly on phones. Redesign it — role, decision, default view, surviving filters, mobile rule.

errorPatterns.description: Learner redesigns a dashboard's surface without recovering the role and decision, so the default view remains unscoped and the control count stays high.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the default-view rescue protocol on the learner's next dashboard: state the decision in one sentence, redesign for it alone, account for every removed control, and record the before-and-after answer to the disabled-interactivity test.

questions.prompt: A team ships a chart component library with consistent styling and reusable components across eight products. What is still missing for this to function as a visualization design system?
options: Encoding rules, semantic colour assignments and selection guidance — without them, teams build consistent-looking charts that mean incompatible things.
Nothing — a consistent component library is a design system.
More component variants, so teams have enough options not to build their own.
Nothing structural, but the constraints should be relaxed, since standardisation limits expressiveness.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Semantics are what make it a system; visual consistency without semantic consistency is confidently wrong rather than merely inconsistent.
Components govern appearance; a system governs meaning, selection, accessibility acceptance and how it changes over time.
Variant proliferation without selection guidance raises the chance of misuse; the missing piece is knowing when not to use each form.
The purpose is to make routine cases automatic so scarce design attention reaches the genuinely novel ones.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner equates a styled component library with a design system, leaving encoding semantics and selection guidance undefined across teams.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner find two charts in their own organisation using the same visual token for different meanings, then draft the semantic token layer that would have prevented it, with every token carrying a business meaning rather than only a value.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A team has a consistent chart component library. What is still missing before it is a design system?

questions.prompt: Rank the following by leverage in getting forty product teams to ship accessible, semantically consistent charts. Which is highest?
options: Shipping encoding tokens and accessible chart defaults as installable code.
Publishing a written accessibility guideline document.
Running a lunch-and-learn session on colour accessibility.
Asking each team to nominate an accessibility champion.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Defaults propagate to everyone, including teams that never read anything — which is why changing a library default moves behaviour that guidance does not.
Necessary as a reference and as something a review gate can point at, but read by a minority.
Highest engagement per attendee, smallest and least durable reach — valuable for building the constituency, not for leverage.
Distributes responsibility without changing what happens by default when nobody is thinking.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner relies on documentation and persuasion rather than defaults, so adoption depends on individual attention and decays.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner audit where their team's chart hours actually went last quarter, classify each as routine or novel, then design the system to absorb the routine share and reserve a documented exception path for the rest.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: What is the single highest-leverage intervention for org-wide chart consistency, and why does it beat guidance?

questions.prompt: Why is a pixel-accurate mockup insufficient as a specification for engineering?
options: It shows one state of a system that has at least a dozen: encoding logic, scale domain behaviour, empty, loading, partial, error, stale and overflow states, and responsive rules are all invisible in it.
It is sufficient if the values shown are real production data.
It is insufficient only because engineers prefer written documents to images.
It is sufficient provided a redline file accompanies it.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and the omitted decisions do not disappear — they get made by whoever is closest to the deadline.
Real values still show a single state, and say nothing about what renders when the feed is stale or a value is out of range.
Format preference is not the issue; the missing content is behavioural rules, which no image can express.
Redlines specify geometry, not conditional encoding logic or state behaviour.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner hands off a single-state mockup, leaving conditional encoding, domain behaviour and production states to be decided ad hoc during implementation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Give the learner a polished mockup and the list of production states and have them find the state it cannot answer, then require a state inventory table in every handoff with stale-data behaviour as a named row.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Name four things a pixel-accurate mockup cannot specify.

questions.prompt: Two dashboards in the same company report different figures for 'active customers' and both are correct against their own definitions. Whose problem is this?
options: It is a design-governed problem: the metric definition fixes grain, denominator and population, and therefore the entire space of honest visual claims — so definitions belong in the system's register alongside tokens and taxonomy.
It is purely a data-engineering problem and should be escalated out of design.
It is not a problem, since each dashboard is internally consistent.
It should be resolved by having both dashboards display both figures.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The metric determines what any downstream chart can say, which makes it design surface even though design does not own the pipeline.
Escalating without engaging means inheriting an unexamined choice and then publishing it under your own annotation.
Internal consistency does not help a reader comparing the two, and it guarantees a contradiction reaches a decision-maker.
Showing both without resolving or labelling the definitions transfers the confusion to the reader.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Two dashboards report different figures for the same metric, both correct. Whose problem is it, and why?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats metric definition as outside design scope, leaving the determinant of every downstream visual claim ungoverned.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner reconstruct one headline metric's definition — grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh — identify one current visual claim it does not support, and add a metric-definition register to the design system's governance scope.

questions.prompt: Your organisation adopted a well-regarded external design system including data visualization palettes and components. Two teams have nonetheless shipped charts where the same colour means 'at risk' in one and 'in review' in the other. Diagnose the situation and prescribe.
successCriteria: Separates palette and component supply from organisational semantics.
Prescribes a semantic token layer distributed as code.
Prescribes a governance mechanism, not only an artifact.
Identifies how the collision became visible and what that implies about detection.

rubric.excellent: Diagnoses that an external system supplies palettes and components but cannot supply the organisation's semantics — which state counts as at risk, which comparison is standard, which thresholds are regulatory — so consistent visual tokens with unassigned meanings produce charts that look coherent and mean different things, which is worse than visible inconsistency because nobody notices. Prescribes a semantic token layer defined at org level and shipped as code, selection and semantics added to the chart taxonomy including when-not-to-use guidance, a contribution and review model so new semantic states are registered rather than invented locally, and a semantic check added to the review gate. Strong answers note this is a governance gap rather than an adoption failure, and that the collision surfaced only because someone compared two teams' output, implying a need for periodic cross-team review.
rubric.adequate: Identifies the semantic collision and proposes a token layer, but stops at the artifact without prescribing a contribution or review mechanism.
rubric.weak: Treats it as an adoption or training problem, or proposes more documentation and stricter palette compliance without addressing meaning.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Two teams use the same colour for different meanings despite a shared external design system. Diagnose and prescribe.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats an adopted external system as complete, leaving organisational semantics undefined and ungoverned across teams.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the learner to define the six system parts for their own organisation, with the semantic token layer and the contribution model as the two mandatory deliverables and adoption measured rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: A designer and a data scientist have deadlocked over whether a logarithmic y-axis will confuse the audience for a public-facing chart. As design lead, what is your move?
options: Convert it into an empirical question and run a short comprehension test with representative users — the disagreement is about how people read the chart, which is measurable.
Decide it yourself, since resolving deadlocks by seniority is what a lead is for.
Publish both versions and let readers choose the one they prefer.
Note that visualizations cannot really be usability-tested and default to the linear scale.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. This is the lead's core leverage: most visualization disputes are empirical, and evidence resolves them without anyone having to lose an argument.
It unblocks the ticket, but it teaches the team that status settles questions and forfeits a cheap, better answer.
This doubles maintenance and pushes an encoding judgment onto the readers least equipped to make it.
Wrong on the facts: comprehension and takeaway-recall protocols are established, cheap, and routinely overturn confident internal opinion.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner resolves empirical encoding disputes by authority or compromise, forfeiting available evidence and normalising status-based decisions.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner take a live disagreement, phrase it as a testable question, run a fifteen-minute study with five participants, and pre-register the result that would change their own mind.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A chart disagreement has stalled. What is the lead's highest-leverage move, and why does it beat deciding?

questions.prompt: In a structured critique, the artifact under review has no stated audience, decision or mode. What is the correct action?
options: Stop and write the brief — every downstream criterion is relative to a goal, and critiquing without one produces preference exchange.
Proceed to the visual passes, since the encoding can be assessed independently of purpose.
Ask each reviewer to state their personal reaction first, then synthesise the common themes.
Defer the critique until a more senior stakeholder can attend and set direction.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Making the brief pass a hard gate kills the majority of unproductive critique before it starts.
Encoding quality is only assessable against a task; without one, reviewers substitute their own assumed purposes and give contradictory direction.
Collecting reactions without an anchor is exactly the failure mode — it produces a list of preferences presented as findings.
Deferring to seniority replaces the missing goal with the missing person, and the same problem returns.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner runs critique as fault-finding without a stated goal, producing contradictory direction and eroding trust in the review process.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Make the brief pass a hard gate in the learner's next three reviews: if audience, decision, task and mode are not stated, the session becomes brief-writing. Have them report what changed in the quality of findings.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A critique opens on an artifact with no stated brief. What do you do, and why is proceeding worse?

questions.prompt: Which method most directly tests whether an explanatory chart communicates its intended message?
options: Timed exposure followed by removal of the chart and free recall of what it showed.
Asking stakeholders in review whether they find the chart clear.
Counting how long users spend looking at the chart in analytics.
Comparing the chart against a checklist of visual design best practices.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Takeaway recall is brutal, cheap and the single most informative test for explanatory work, because it measures what survived rather than what was noticed.
Reviewers who already know the intended message cannot assess whether it is recoverable by someone who does not.
Dwell time measures attention, not comprehension, and long dwell can indicate confusion as easily as engagement.
A checklist catches known defects but cannot tell you what a reader actually took away.

successCriteria: Selects the option that names a mechanism rather than a preference.
Can restate why each distractor fails without re-reading the feedback.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats chart comprehension as untestable and relies on internal opinion or proxy metrics instead of direct measurement.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Run a timed takeaway-recall test on the learner's own chart with five colleagues and compare recalled messages against the intended one; the gap usually settles the objection without argument.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Name three ways to test a visualization, and say which is most informative for explanatory work.

questions.prompt: You have been asked to define what success looks like for your organisation's visualization practice over the next year. Propose success measures, and describe how you would run critique so that the measures are actually achievable.
successCriteria: Measures are matched to artifact mode rather than applied uniformly.
At least one measure concerns the health of the practice, not only individual artifacts.
The critique process is specified in a fixed order with a stated gate.
At least one disagreement type is identified as empirically resolvable, with the test named.

rubric.excellent: Proposes mode-matched measures: takeaway recall accuracy and misconception rate for explanatory work; task completion and time to first correct insight for exploratory work; token adoption, first-review accessibility pass rate and the count of one-off custom charts for systems work; and at least one practice-health measure such as the share of incoming briefs that arrive stating a decision rather than a chart type. Specifies critique as four ordered passes — brief, integrity, encoding, narrative and access — with the brief pass as a hard gate and preference discussion deferred until all four complete. Names at least one recurring disagreement and the fifteen-minute protocol that would settle it, including the result threshold that would change the design.
rubric.adequate: Proposes reasonable measures and a critique structure, but applies the same measures to all artifact types or leaves the brief gate unstated.
rubric.weak: Proposes only output or satisfaction measures such as charts shipped or stakeholder happiness, and describes critique as collecting feedback.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Define success measures for a visualization practice, and specify the critique process that makes them achievable.

errorPatterns.description: Learner defines success by output volume or stakeholder satisfaction and runs critique without ordered criteria, leaving quality unmeasured and disputes unresolved.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the learner to instrument one mode-matched measure on a live deliverable this quarter and to facilitate one critique under the four-pass rule, reporting both the measure and what the ordering changed about the findings.

retrievalSystem.algorithm: Expanding-interval spaced retrieval with per-item schedule blocks. Each item advances through its subsequentReviewDays sequence on a successful recall and resets toward initialReviewDays on failure. Interval growth is governed by the item's strengthMultiplier and bounded by minimumIntervalDays and maximumIntervalDays. Confidence modulates scheduling when confidenceSchedulingEnabled: correct-but-unconfident answers are kept in the queue rather than promoted, and confident-but-incorrect answers are flagged miscalibrated for priority review.

glossary.definition: A grid representation of a network with entities on both axes and relationships in the cells; outperforms node-link views for adjacency and cluster tasks at density.
Whether the values in a file are raw observations or the output of prior summarising by someone else.
Partial mark transparency so that overlapping marks accumulate into visible density.
The specific cognitive operation the viewer must perform: comparison, trend, distribution, part-to-whole, correlation, deviation, ranking or flow.
Four datasets with nearly identical summary statistics whose plots are radically different; the standard demonstration that statistics without a plot conceal structure.
Choosing a plot's aspect ratio so that average absolute segment slope approaches forty-five degrees, the angle at which slope differences are judged most accurately.
The underlying frequency of an outcome in a population, without which counts from differently sized groups cannot be compared.
Starting a length-encoded axis above zero, breaking the identity between a mark's length and its value.
Selection in one view highlighting the corresponding data in others, making cross-view relationships visible rather than inferred.
The number of distinct values a variable takes; frequently rules chart forms in or out before any aesthetic consideration.
A map deliberately distorting geographic area to encode a variable such as population, trading spatial fidelity for quantitative fidelity.
A set of distinct hues at roughly equal luminance, used for nominal identity; practically limited to about six to eight distinguishable categories.
The overall structural type of a visualization: bar, line, scatter, area, treemap, Sankey and so on.
A catalogue of approved chart forms with the tasks each supports, its cardinality limits, and explicit guidance on when not to use it.
A map encoding a value by shading defined areal units; requires normalization, since raw counts render as a map of the denominator.
Reduced ability to distinguish certain hues, most commonly red and green; makes hue-only encoding of meaning a structural failure for part of any large audience.
A shift in an aggregate caused by a change in the mix of subgroups rather than by change within any subgroup; can move an aggregate opposite to every part.
A range summarising sampling uncertainty in an estimate.
The unmanipulated first render of a dashboard, which carries the majority of its communicative load because most sessions contain no interaction.
The medium and conditions of viewing: projected slide, phone screen, print, embedded dashboard.
The population or exposure a count is divided by; choosing it is an analytical claim, not a formatting decision.
A table treated as a first-class visualization form, using alignment, sorting, grouping and in-cell marks to support precise value retrieval and heterogeneous metrics.
Supplementary detail revealed on selection; must never carry information required to read the chart.
Placing series labels on the marks themselves rather than in a legend, eliminating working-memory round-trips.
Techniques preventing identification of individuals from published aggregates, including minimum cell thresholds, suppression and limits on differencing across filtered views.
Two sequential ramps meeting at a meaningful midpoint such as zero, a target or a baseline; illegitimate when the midpoint is arbitrary.
A map placing marks in proportion to a count within each area, conveying magnitude and rough distribution without area-based shading.
Navigation from an aggregate to its components, requiring a visible breadcrumb and a return path.
The empirically measured ordering of visual channels by accuracy of quantitative magnitude judgment, from position through length and angle to area, saturation and hue.
A system-level visual value with a fixed business meaning attached, such as the colour that always denotes a forecast.
A visualization that constrains to a single reading and makes it unmissable.
A visualization that preserves many possible readings so an analyst can search for the one that matters.
The requirement that an encoding convey all and only the structure present in the data; a precondition for effectiveness rather than a trade-off against it.
A single view that emphasises or magnifies a region of interest while retaining the surrounding context.
A decision about time range, comparison group, denominator or aggregation statistic that shapes the reading without altering any number.
Rules by which the visual system groups marks into units: proximity, similarity, enclosure, connection, continuity and common fate.
What a single row of a dataset represents — one transaction, one customer-day, one store-month.
The abstraction that treats any chart as a composition of data, transform, mark, channel encodings, scales, guides and faceting rather than as an indivisible type.
An axis, legend or annotation that lets a viewer decode a scale; the readable counterpart of an encoding.
An animated sequence of draws from a distribution, conveying uncertainty as observed variability rather than as a static abstraction.
A series rescaled so a chosen reference period equals a fixed value such as 100, making relative movement comparable across series with different units or magnitudes.
A measurement scale with equal spacing and an arbitrary zero; differences are meaningful, ratios are not.
Placing different chart forms side by side, usually coordinated; powerful but expensive, since the viewer must learn each encoding separately.
The decoding effort a non-standard encoding imposes on every viewer on every viewing, paid repeatedly while the benefit accrues once.
The size of the effect shown in a graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data.
A scale transform on which equal distances represent equal ratios, making proportional change comparable across magnitudes; carries real comprehension risk with general audiences.
The geometric primitive a chart draws — point, line, bar, area, arc, path — one component of the grammar.
The kind of information a variable's values carry — nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio — independent of the data type used to store them.
The specification of what a named measure counts and excludes; fixes the space of visual claims available downstream.
Asking what a chart implies in order to count unsupported inferences, which catches over-claiming annotation.
The pattern of absent values and, critically, the reasons for their absence — unmeasured is not the same as measured as zero.
The effect whereby aggregating the same point data into different boundary sets produces different, sometimes opposite, spatial patterns.
A network representation drawing entities as nodes and relationships as edges; in force-directed layouts, node position is largely an algorithmic artifact.
A measurement scale carrying identity only: categories with no order.
Expressing a quantity relative to a base — population, area, time or a reference period — so that groups of different size can be compared.
Preservation of mark identity through a transition so that a viewer can track which element became which across a state change.
A measurement scale carrying ordered categories with no guaranteed equal spacing between them.
Marks obscuring one another at high density, destroying the visible distribution while preserving outliers.
Two coordinated views shown together, one presenting the whole and one the selected region.
The arithmetic difference between two percentages; distinct from percent change, which is the relative difference between them.
The property that equal steps in the data produce equal perceived steps in colour; requires monotonic luminance across the ramp.
Parallel detection of a target, where search time is independent of the number of distractors; depends on the target being unique on its distinguishing attribute.
A visual property detected in a single fixation across the whole visual field without serial search, such as hue, luminance, size, orientation, curvature, motion, enclosure or position.
The transformation from a curved surface to a flat one; every projection distorts some combination of area, shape, distance and direction.
A distribution shown as a countable set of discrete dots, supporting frequency-based reasoning by non-technical audiences.
A count divided by the population or exposure that produced it, making comparison across differently sized groups possible.
A measurement scale with equal spacing and a true zero, so ratios between values are meaningful.
Carrying the same meaning in two or more channels so that no single channel is load-bearing.
A target, threshold, benchmark or prior-period line that converts a difficult absolute judgment into an easy comparative one.
A flow representation in which link width encodes quantity moving between states or stages; node ordering and link crossings are layout artifacts rather than data.
Defining a view for a specific role and decision with parameters pre-set by the designer, instead of exposing filters.
Regular periodic variation in a time series, which must be either shown, adjusted for, or explicitly acknowledged before a trend claim is made.
The governed set of metric definitions — grain, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, refresh — that determines what any downstream chart can honestly claim.
A colour ramp varying monotonically in luminance, used for ordinal or ratio data running from low to high.
Item-by-item checking, where search time rises with item count; triggered by conjunction targets or by a distinguishing attribute shared with distractors.
Identical axis domains across faceted panels, without which the panels look comparable and are not.
The shift in a colour's appearance depending on its surround, which is why palettes validated on large swatches can fail on small marks.
Asymmetry in a distribution, under which the mean can describe no actual case and can sit above the great majority of observations.
Withholding or masking aggregate values computed from too few records, shown visibly rather than silently omitted.
Repetition of one chart form across values of a categorical variable, on shared scales, so the viewer learns the encoding once and then compares patterns.
Replacing values with a rolling or fitted summary to reveal trend; removes short-term variation, which must be disclosed as a choice.
A visible signal that displayed data is older than its refresh contract, preventing a dashboard from silently showing yesterday's numbers.
The full set of render states a production chart must handle: empty, loading, partial, error, stale, single-row and overflow.
Review against stated criteria in a fixed order — brief, integrity, encoding, narrative and access — with preference discussion deferred until the passes complete.
Overlaying multiple data series within a single coordinate space; suited to comparing a small number of series to each other.
Timed exposure to a chart followed by its removal and free recall of the message, the most informative single test for explanatory work.
A title stating what the chart shows as a sentence, rather than naming its topic.
A description conveying a chart's type, scope and takeaway pattern — not merely its values.
A space-filling representation of hierarchical part-to-whole using nested rectangles; area judgments are imprecise, and depth beyond a few levels degrades quickly.
Aggregating points into spatial cells, often hexagonal, and encoding the count, which makes density explicit and quantified.
The two to four defensible chart forms generated before selection, from which one is chosen with stated reasons and a named runner-up.
A property of a mark used to carry data: position, length, angle, area, luminance, saturation, hue, shape, size, texture or motion.
Minimum contrast ratios required for legibility: 4.5:1 for normal text, and 3:1 for large text and for non-text elements essential to understanding, such as data marks and gridlines.
